5.1|How does constitutionalism fundamentally limit the exercise of state power?|By concentrating all governmental authority in the hands of the executive branch|By ensuring that government powers are legally restricted by a fundamental law to safeguard individual liberties|By eliminating the need for any written laws or formal institutional checks and balances|By prioritizing arbitrary executive decrees over legislative enactments during peacetime|Option B|Constitutionalism is the philosophical doctrine that governmental power must be legally bound and limited by a fundamental law to protect citizens' rights.|

14.1|How does Proportional Representation (PR) fundamentally impact party competition and legislative composition?|It allocates legislative seats to parties in direct proportion to the total percentage of votes they secure nationally or regionally|It restricts legislative representation strictly to the two largest political parties|It mandates that every winning candidate must run as an independent without party backing|It ensures that smaller political parties win zero legislative seats due to threshold barriers|Option A|Proportional Representation aligns a party's share of legislative seats closely with its share of the popular vote, ensuring broader representation for minority parties.

5.1|Which term describes a constitution that is not compiled into a single document and relies heavily on conventions and statutes?|A rigid constitution|A codified constitution|An unwritten constitution|A unitary constitution|Option C|An unwritten constitution consists of a collection of statutes, judicial precedents, and constitutional conventions rather than a single codified document.

8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, what does the first principle of the rule of law entail?|Supremacy of regular law over arbitrary or wide discretionary power|Absolute immunity of government officials from legal prosecution|Primacy of military tribunals over ordinary civilian courts|Undisputed supremacy of legislative acts over individual liberties|Option A|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law is supreme over arbitrary power and wide discretionary authority, preventing government arbitrariness.
8.1|Which of the following best describes A.V. Dicey's second principle of the rule of law?|Equality before the ordinary courts of the land for all classes of persons|Exemption of high-ranking political officials from ordinary jurisdiction|Trial of government officials exclusively in specialized administrative courts|Subordination of civilian legal codes to executive decrees during peacetime|Option A|Dicey's second principle emphasizes that all individuals, regardless of rank or status, are subject to the ordinary law administered by ordinary courts.
8.1|How does Dicey's third principle frame the protection of individual rights?|Rights are primarily derived from the general constitution and judicial decisions|Rights are granted at the discretion of the executive branch of government|Rights are protected solely through temporary emergency proclamations|Rights exist only when codified explicitly into regional military decrees|Option A|Dicey argued that individual rights in the British constitution are a result of judicial decisions and the ordinary law of the land rather than abstract constitutional declarations.
8.1|In the context of Nigerian constitutional law, which provision serves as a major limitation to Dicey's principle of equality before the law?|Section 308 granting executive immunity to the President and Governors|Section 36 guaranteeing the right to a fair hearing in civil and criminal trials|Section 14 establishing the fundamental objectives and directive principles of state policy|Section 43 protecting the citizen's right to acquire and own immovable property|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution provides temporary immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to certain executive officers, limiting equality before the law.
8.1|How does delegated legislation act as a limitation on the practical enforcement of the rule of law?|It allows non-legislative bodies to make laws that can sometimes bypass strict parliamentary scrutiny|It completely abolishes the need for any legislative oversight whatsoever|It forces the judiciary to surrender its power to interpret statutes permanently|It dissolves ordinary courts and replaces them with executive administrative tribunals|Option A|Delegated legislation empowers executive bodies to create subsidiary laws, which can challenge the supremacy of regular legislative processes if poorly checked.
8.1|What is the legal effect of military ouster clauses on the enforcement of the rule of law?|They explicitly restrict or exclude the jurisdiction of courts to review certain actions|They automatically expand the scope of fundamental human rights protections|They mandate that all executive actions be subjected to rigorous judicial review|They permanently entrench Dicey's third principle into the supreme law of the land|Option A|Ouster clauses are legislative or decree provisions inserted by military or authoritarian regimes to bar courts from inquiring into the legality of specific government actions.
8.1|During a legally declared state of emergency in Nigeria, what generally happens to certain individual rights under the rule of law?|They may be lawfully derogated from or restricted as permitted by the constitution|They become entirely absolute and immune from any form of legislative limitation|They are permanently abrogated without any possibility of judicial restoration|They are transferred from the federal legislature to municipal traditional rulers|Option A|A state of emergency allows for the constitutional restriction of certain fundamental rights to restore public order, representing a practical limitation on Dicey's third principle.
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey strongly oppose the French droit administratif system of administrative courts?|He believed it violated the principle of equality by treating state officials differently from ordinary citizens|He thought it granted too much independent power to ordinary civilian juries|He argued that it made the legislature far too weak compared to the judiciary|He claimed it completely abolished the need for any written constitution whatsoever|Option A|Dicey criticized administrative law systems because they insulated government officials from ordinary courts, which conflicted with his view of universal equality before the law.
8.1|Which concept is fundamentally antithetical to A.V. Dicey's conceptualization of the rule of law?|Arbitrary power and wide discretionary authority exercised by the executive|The adjudication of civil disputes by independent and impartial judges|The enforcement of ordinary legal codes against both private citizens and public officials|The protection of personal liberty through established judicial precedents|Option A|Dicey's doctrine is built upon the absolute supremacy of regular law as an antidote to wide, unchecked discretionary power and arbitrariness.
8.1|Which scenario best exemplifies a direct violation of Dicey's second principle of the rule of law?|A government official escaping prosecution for theft solely because a special statute shields their office|A citizen being tried in an open magistrate court for a minor traffic offense|A police officer being held accountable in an ordinary court for committing assault|A judge applying established legal precedents to resolve a standard contractual dispute|Option A|Shielding a government official from prosecution via special protective statutes directly violates the principle that all people are subject to the same ordinary law and courts.

9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly during emergency sessions|Rules and orders made by executive ministers or agencies under legislative authority|Judicial pronouncements that interpret ambiguities in the constitution|Executive directives issued by the President without any statutory backing|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers or administrative agencies using powers specifically delegated to them by the legislature through an enabling act.
9.1|What is the primary function of an Enabling Act or Parent Act in relation to delegated legislation?|It provides the permanent constitutional framework for the judiciary|It grants specific, limited lawmaking powers to executive agencies and ministers|It automatically repeals all existing customary laws in the federation|It empowers the executive to amend the constitution without a referendum|Option B|An enabling or parent act is the foundational legislation passed by Parliament that transfers specific rule-making powers to an executive body or minister.
9.1|Under the doctrine of ultra vires, what happens when an administrative agency issues a statutory instrument that exceeds the powers granted in its parent act?|The National Assembly is automatically dissolved for constitutional breach|The judiciary strikes down or declares the unauthorized rule null and void|The President must issue a counter-executive order to legalize the action|The Supreme Court temporarily suspends the funding of the offending agency|Option B|The doctrine of ultra vires dictates that any delegated legislation exceeding the scope or limits authorized by the parent act is illegal and will be struck down by the courts.
9.1|Which of the following is considered a primary procedural control mechanism designed to prevent the abuse of delegated legislation?|Mandatory publication of the rules and orders in the official government gazette|A mandatory public referendum held across all states before implementation|Prior approval from international organizations such as the Economic Community of West African States|Direct ratification by traditional rulers and emirs in a special joint council|Option A|Official publication in the government gazette ensures transparency, publicity, and public awareness so that citizens are properly informed of new administrative rules.
9.1|How does parliamentary review serve as a control mechanism over delegated legislation in Nigeria?|Parliament can impeach the administrative officer who drafted the rule without a trial|The legislature retains the power to scrutinize, amend, or annul rules made under its delegated authority|Parliament appoints all junior civil servants directly responsible for drafting statutory instruments|The legislature can veto judicial rulings that invalidate executive rules|Option B|Parliamentary review allows the legislature to monitor executive rule-making and retain ultimate authority by having the power to scrutinize, modify, or reject improper statutory instruments.
9.1|Why is delegated legislation a necessary practice in modern governance systems like Nigeria?|It completely eliminates the need for the legislative branch of government|It allows specialized administrative agencies to quickly address complex, technical details without bogging down parliament|It enables the judiciary to bypass traditional court procedures during economic crises|It prevents citizens from challenging executive policies in a court of law|Option B|Modern governance requires speed and specialized technical expertise, allowing parliament to delegate detailed rule-making to executive bodies while focusing on broad policy frameworks.

9.1|Which of the following bodies is primarily responsible for exercising judicial review over delegated legislation in Nigeria?|The Federal Executive Council meeting in plenary session|The regular courts of law within the judicial hierarchy|The standing committees of the National Assembly on delegated legislation|The Civil Service Commission during annual performance reviews|Option B|Courts of law exercise judicial review to examine whether administrative agencies have acted within their statutory powers or violated the doctrine of ultra vires.
9.1|What constitutes a substantive ultra vires violation by an administrative agency making delegated legislation?|Failing to print the exact number of required physical copies for internal filing|Passing a rule that deals with a subject matter completely outside the scope authorized by the parent act|Publishing the statutory instrument on a Friday instead of a Monday morning|Using a font size that does not conform to the standard government printing press guidelines|Option B|Substantive ultra vires occurs when the administrative rule enacted deals with matters or powers that were never authorized or contemplated by the parent act.
9.1|Which of the following best captures the relationship between the legislature and the executive under the framework of delegated legislation?|The executive acts as the principal while the legislature functions as the subordinate agent|The legislature acts as the principal delegator while the executive functions as the subordinate rule-maker|Both branches share equal and concurrent constitutional powers to amend the primary constitution|The executive possesses absolute sovereignty to delegate its own powers back to the legislature|Option B|In delegated legislation, the legislature is the principal that delegates limited authority, making the executive a subordinate agent bound strictly by the terms of the enabling act.

5.1|What is the distinguishing feature of a rigid constitution?|It can be easily amended by a simple majority vote of the ordinary legislature|It requires a special, more cumbersome amendment procedure distinct from ordinary lawmaking|It is completely immune to any form of legislative revision or modification|It does not permit the judiciary to interpret its provisions during legal disputes|Option B|A rigid constitution mandates a complex and special amendment process, usually involving supermajorities or referenda, to safeguard fundamental laws.|

8.1|Which of the following is NOT one of the three core principles of the Rule of Law as expounded by A.V. 8.1|What does Dicey's first principle regarding the supremacy of regular law primarily entail?|The absolute predominance of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power or wide discretionary authority|The total superiority of military decrees over civilian legislation during a constitutional crisis|The power of the executive branch to suspend statutes whenever national security is threatened|The subordination of the judiciary to legislative directives and executive policy statements|Option A|Dicey emphasized that government officials cannot punish citizens except for a distinct breach of law established before ordinary courts, ruling out wide discretionary power.
8.1|How does Dicey's second principle define equality before the law?|Equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary legal courts|The exclusion of public officials from ordinary courts through the creation of specialized administrative tribunals|The absolute exemption of government ministers from any form of civil or criminal litigation|The requirement that all citizens possess equal wealth and property holdings before accessing justice|Option A|Dicey argued against separate administrative courts, insisting that officials and private citizens alike must be judged by the same ordinary courts of law.
8.1|According to A.V. 5.1|Which of the following best defines the core philosophical concept of constitutionalism?|The total concentration of power in a single executive authority|The principle that government powers are legally limited by a fundamental law to protect liberties|The absolute supremacy of the legislature over all other branches of government|The practice of writing down all political conventions into a single document|Option B|Constitutionalism is defined as the philosophy and practice whereby government powers are legally bounded and limited by a fundamental law to safeguard individual liberties against arbitrary rule.
5.1|How does a written constitution primarily differ from an unwritten constitution in terms of its structural composition?|A written constitution contains only judicial rulings while an unwritten one contains only executive decrees|A written constitution is codified into a single comprehensive document whereas an unwritten one consists of various statutes and conventions|A written constitution can never be amended under any circumstances unlike an unwritten constitution|A written constitution applies solely to unitary states while an unwritten constitution applies to federations|Option B|A written constitution is systematically codified and compiled into a single formal document, whereas an unwritten constitution is scattered across multiple historical statutes, judicial precedents, and unwritten conventions.

5.1|Which term describes a constitutional system where fundamental rules are not compiled into a single codified document but are derived from a body of separate statutes, precedents, and traditions?|Rigid constitution|Flexible constitution|Unwritten constitution|Federal constitution|Option C|An unwritten constitution lacks a single master document and instead relies on a cumulative collection of written statutes, judicial rulings, and accepted political conventions.
5.1|In the context of constitutional government, what is the fundamental purpose of imposing legal limits on state power?|To maximize state revenue collection and economic centralisation|To protect individual liberties and prevent the arbitrary exercise of authority|To ensure that political parties remain permanently in power without opposition|To abolish the need for legislative representation and public elections|Option B|Constitutionalism centers on the idea that state power must be legally restricted to shield citizens from tyranny and protect fundamental human rights.
5.1|Which of the following documents or sources is most characteristic of an unwritten constitution?|A single codified constitution ratified by a constituent assembly|Constitutional conventions, historical charters, and judicial statutes|Executive orders issued exclusively during a state of emergency|A supreme law text outlining fundamental human rights and state organs|Option B|Unwritten constitutions are built upon a foundation of historical charters, statutory enactments, judicial decisions, and binding political conventions rather than a single codified text.
5.1|Why are written constitutions frequently associated with rigidity?|Because they are written in permanent ink that cannot be physically altered|Because they usually require special, complex legislative majorities or referendums to amend|Because they forbid any form of judicial review by the supreme court|Because they are drafted exclusively by military dictators rather than elected assemblies|Option B|Written constitutions typically incorporate rigid amendment procedures that demand more than a simple legislative majority to safeguard core institutional frameworks.
5.1|Which political theorist framework heavily informs the doctrine of constitutionalism through the separation of powers to prevent tyranny?|Max Weber's theory of rational-legal bureaucracy|Baron de Montesquieu's institutional checks and balances|Karl Marx's historical materialism and class struggle|Thomas Hobbes's absolute sovereign Leviathan|Option B|Constitutionalism relies heavily on Montesquieu's doctrine of separation of powers and institutional checks and balances to ensure government power checks power.

14.1|How does Proportional Representation typically impact the composition of the legislature?|It ensures that only two dominant political parties hold legislative seats|It creates coalition governments and represents diverse minority political interests|It eliminates the need for any political parties by focusing purely on independents|It guarantees that every elected representative wins an absolute majority of votes|Option C|Proportional Representation fosters multi-party systems and gives smaller political factions legislative representation reflective of their total popular support.
14.1|Which administrative task forms an indispensable prerequisite for organizing credible and transparent democratic elections?|Compiling and updating a comprehensive register of eligible voters|Drafting and enacting the national constitution and penal codes|Collecting corporate taxes from businesses operating within the state|Managing the day-to-day operations of local government secretariats|Option A|A credible voter register ensures that only qualified citizens participate, serving as the foundational document for any democratic electoral process.
14.1|Which system of voting requires voters to rank candidates in order of preference rather than choosing just one?|Simple Majority System|First-Past-The-Post System|Alternative Vote or Preferential Voting System|Absolute Majority Runoff System|Option C|Preferential voting allows voters to rank candidates sequentially, ensuring winners achieve broad consensus support through preference transfers.
14.1|What is a primary criticism often leveled against the First-Past-The-Post electoral system?|It creates overly large coalition governments that are unstable|It can result in a winning candidate or party securing power with less than a majority of total votes cast|It requires complex mathematical formulas to distribute legislative seats|It makes voter registration completely unnecessary for the electorate|Option B|FPTP can lead to a plurality winner who lacks majority support, meaning a party can win government without earning the majority of overall votes.

1.1|What is the fundamental theoretical distinction between the state and the government in political science?|The state is temporary while the government is a permanent territorial entity|The state is a permanent sovereign entity whereas the government is a temporary political agent|The state and the government are synonymous terms used interchangeably in political analysis|The government possesses ultimate sovereignty while the state derives its authority from elected officials|Option B|The state is defined as a permanent, sovereign political entity, whereas the government comprises the temporary political agents who manage state apparatuses.
1.1|According to Thomas Hobbes, what is the primary justification for the establishment of government and political authority?|To maximize economic growth and industrialization through state capitalism|To eliminate all social classes and establish a completely egalitarian society|To avoid the chaotic, insecure, and violent conditions of the state of nature|To promote religious orthodoxy and moral perfection among citizens|Option C|Hobbes argued that a strong government is necessary to escape the brutish and insecure state of nature through a social contract.

1.1|In the context of POL 122, how is government perceived when viewed as a discipline?|As a temporary political administration that changes after every election cycle|As a permanent sovereign entity with a monopoly on the legitimate use of force|As an academic field of study focused on political phenomena, institutions, and behavior|As a revolutionary movement aimed at overthrowing traditional structures|Option C|When government is analyzed as a discipline, it refers to the academic study of political science, governance structures, public policies, and political behavior.

5.1|Which of the following best defines constitutionalism in the context of political science?|The absolute supremacy of the legislature over all other branches of government|The philosophy and practice that government powers are legally limited by a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|The process of drafting a new constitution after a military regime hands over power|The rigid codification of government rules into a single document|Option B|Constitutionalism is fundamentally the philosophical belief and practice that government power must be legally limited by a supreme law to safeguard the rights and liberties of citizens.
5.1|What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes a written constitution from an unwritten constitution?|A written constitution can never be amended under any circumstances|A written constitution is codified and contained within a single formal document or a specific set of documents|An unwritten constitution does not possess any legal validity or judicial enforcement|An unwritten constitution is exclusively based on religious doctrines rather than statutes|Option B|A written constitution is characterized by its formal codification into a single or primary document, whereas unwritten constitutions rely on a collection of statutes, judicial precedents, and conventions.

5.1|Which element is most commonly associated with unwritten constitutions like that of the United Kingdom?|A complete absence of constitutional conventions and political traditions|Exclusive reliance on executive decrees for governance|A reliance on uncodified constitutional conventions, historical statutes, and judicial precedents|Strict judicial supremacy where judges can rewrite laws at will|Option C|Unwritten constitutions are not embodied in a single codified text but are instead derived from a mosaic of uncodified conventions, historical documents, judicial decisions, and statutes.

5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A constitution that cannot be altered under any circumstances|A single codified legal document containing fundamental laws and principles|A collection of unwritten political conventions and historical traditions|An executive decree issued exclusively by the head of state without legislative input|Option B|A written constitution is a single, codified document that formally sets out the fundamental laws, powers of government, and citizens' rights.
5.1|What is the defining characteristic of an unwritten constitution?|It is entirely illegal and lacks any legal enforceability|It exists purely as an oral tradition with no recorded documentation whatsoever|It is derived from a combination of statutes, judicial precedents, and constitutional conventions rather than a single codified document|It can only be amended through a violent political revolution|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not codified into a single document; instead, it is sourced from historical statutes, court rulings, and enduring political conventions.
5.1|How is a rigid constitution fundamentally distinguished from a flexible one?|It requires a special, complex, and more difficult amendment procedure than ordinary legislation|It can be amended by a simple majority vote in the legislature just like regular laws|It prohibits the legislature from passing any new laws indefinitely|It applies exclusively to military dictatorships and absolute monarchies|Option A|A rigid constitution mandates a special, arduous amendment process to ensure fundamental laws cannot be altered hastily or easily by a simple legislative majority.
5.1|Which of the following best describes the core philosophy of constitutionalism?|The belief that the constitution should be completely rewritten every decade|The doctrine that government powers are legally limited by a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|The theory that executive authority should supersede judicial review during national emergencies|The practice of merging legislative and judicial powers into a single supreme council|Option B|Constitutionalism is the political philosophy asserting that government power must be legally restrained by a higher law to safeguard the rights of citizens against tyranny.
5.1|Which of the following is a primary advantage associated with having a written constitution?|It completely prevents the occurrence of political corruption or state inefficiency|It guarantees absolute economic equality among all citizens within the state|It provides clarity, certainty, and a clear reference point for determining the legality of governmental actions|It eliminates the need for an independent judiciary or court system|Option C|A written constitution offers legal clarity and transparency, enabling citizens and courts to easily verify whether government actions conform to fundamental laws.
5.1|In the context of constitutional law, what is the primary function of a constitutional convention?|To serve as a binding statutory law enforced strictly by criminal courts|To provide unwritten rules of political behavior and norms that regulate the operations of government organs|To act as a temporary legislative body created only during wartime|To formally replace the written text of the constitution every election cycle|Option B|Constitutional conventions are unwritten rules, maxims, and practices that guide political actors and govern institutional relationships despite lacking strict judicial enforcement.
5.1|Why is a rigid constitution often considered essential for federal states?|It prevents the central government from unilaterally eroding the powers and autonomy of component regional units|It ensures that all federating units have identical economic output and tax structures|It allows the executive branch to dissolve regional assemblies at will|It merges the legal systems of all regions into a single municipal code|Option A|A rigid constitution protects the federal structure by ensuring that neither the central government nor a simple legislative majority can alter the division of powers without broad consensus.
5.1|Which term describes a political system where government actions are strictly constrained by legal limits and fundamental laws?|Autocracy|Constitutionalism|Plutocracy|Totalitarianism|Option B|Constitutionalism specifically denotes a political order where the exercise of state power is legally bounded and checked by fundamental constitutional principles.
5.1|What is a major potential drawback of an unwritten constitution?|It makes constitutional interpretation overly rigid and unresponsive to modern societal changes|It creates legal ambiguity and makes it difficult for citizens to easily ascertain their precise constitutional rights|It requires a public referendum for every single minor administrative policy change|It prevents the legislature from ever passing ordinary laws|Option B|Because unwritten constitutions are scattered across various statutes and conventions, they often lack the clarity of a single code, creating potential ambiguity regarding rights and limits.
5.1|Which of the following best exemplifies the practical implementation of constitutionalism?|An absolute monarch issuing decrees that override all existing parliamentary laws|An independent judiciary striking down an unconstitutional legislative act passed by parliament|A ruling political party banning all opposition groups to maintain permanent stability|A military regime suspending all civil liberties indefinitely during a minor public dispute|Option B|Judicial review striking down unlawful government actions is a core mechanism of constitutionalism, demonstrating that the government remains subordinate to fundamental law.

8.1|Which of the following is NOT one of the three core principles of the Rule of Law as formulated by A.V. 8.1|What does A.V. 8.1|Under A.V. 14.1|Which electoral system awards a legislative seat to the candidate who secures the highest number of votes cast in a single-member constituency, even without achieving an absolute majority?|First-Past-The-Post system|Proportional Representation system|Absolute Majority runoff system|List System of representation|Option A|The First-Past-The-Post system is a plurality voting method where the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they cross the fifty percent threshold.
14.1|What is the primary defining feature of an absolute majority electoral system in comparison to a simple majority system?|It requires a candidate to secure more than fifty percent of the total valid votes cast to win|It allocates seats strictly proportional to the total percentage of votes won by political parties|It relies entirely on multi-member constituencies without any run-off provisions|It prevents independent candidates from participating in executive elections|Option A|An absolute majority system mandates that a winning candidate must achieve an overall majority of over fifty percent, often requiring a second-round runoff if no candidate meets this threshold initially.
14.1|How does Proportional Representation fundamentally differ from majoritarian electoral systems?|It translates a political party's share of the national vote directly into a corresponding share of legislative seats|It restricts political participation to only two dominant national parties|It eliminates the need for any form of voter registration or electoral commission management|It guarantees that every elected representative belongs to an independent political faction|Option A|Proportional Representation ensures that legislative seats are distributed in alignment with the percentage of popular votes received by participating political parties.

14.1|What is the main objective of implementing a runoff or second-round vote in an absolute majority system?|To ensure that the ultimate winner enjoys the mandate of a clear majority of the electorate|To penalize smaller political parties for failing to form coalitions before the primary election|To reduce voter turnout by encouraging citizens to vote only in high-stakes contests|To allow the electoral commission extra time to review disputed campaign expenditures|Option A|A runoff election ensures broad electoral legitimacy by forcing a decisive contest between the top two candidates until one secures an absolute majority.

1.1|What fundamental characteristic distinguishes a state from a government based on political theory?|A state is a temporary political agent whereas a government is a permanent legal entity|A state is a permanent sovereign entity while a government is a temporary political agent that can be changed through elections or coups|A state only exists during times of war whereas a government operates exclusively during peacetime|A state is an academic discipline while government is strictly an art of governing without theory|Option B|The state represents a permanent, sovereign political community, whereas the government serves as its temporary political agent or administration.

8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, what does the supremacy of regular law principle primarily mean in a constitutional democracy?|Absolute power of the regular law over arbitrary power and wide discretionary authority by government officials|Primacy of international treaties over domestic legislative enactments|Supremacy of military decrees during public emergencies|Absolute authority of custom over statutory enactments|Option A|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law reigns supreme and excludes the existence of arbitrariness or wide discretionary power by authorities.
8.1|Which of the following best describes Dicey's second principle of the Rule of Law?|Equality before the ordinary courts and subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land|Special courts established exclusively for government ministers and ruling elites|Immunity from prosecution for all public servants while in office|Exemption of the police force from ordinary civil liabilities|Option A|The second principle emphasizes that no person is above the law and everyone regardless of rank is subject to the ordinary courts of the land.

8.1|What is the legal effect of a military ouster clause on the operation of the Rule of Law?|It explicitly bars courts from entertaining suits challenging specific government actions or decrees|It mandates the immediate execution of parliamentary bills without presidential assent|It guarantees automatic judicial review for all human rights abuses|It compels the legislature to impeach corrupt executive officers|Option A|Ouster clauses are legislative or decree provisions that strip courts of jurisdiction to review administrative or executive actions thereby undermining judicial oversight.

9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly through a constitutional amendment process|Rules and orders made by executive ministers or administrative agencies under legislative authority granted by an Enabling Act|Judicial interpretations and rulings handed down by the Supreme Court of Nigeria to resolve constitutional disputes|Decrees and edicts unilaterally promulgated by a military head of state without legislative oversight|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers or agencies using powers specifically delegated to them by the legislature via an Enabling Act.
9.1|What is the primary function of an Enabling or Parent Act in the creation of delegated legislation?|It establishes the constitutional framework for the separation of powers between the executive and the judiciary|It grants specific legislative authority to executive bodies or ministers to make subsidiary laws|It provides a detailed financial budget for the implementation of federal government projects|It outlines the procedure for the impeachment of the president and federal cabinet members|Option B|An Enabling or Parent Act is the foundational statute passed by the legislature that delegates rule-making powers to an executive body or minister.

7.1|According to Baron de Montesquieu in his 1748 treatise, what is the primary structural arrangement required to prevent tyranny?|The centralization of all state power in a single democratic assembly|The division of governmental functions among three distinct and separate bodies|The subordination of the judiciary to the executive branch for swift justice|The elimination of legislative vetoes to ensure absolute parliamentary supremacy|Option B|Montesquieu argued that liberty is preserved only when the legislative, executive, and judicial powers are exercised by separate, independent bodies to prevent tyrannical concentrations of authority.
7.1|Which of the following best encapsulates the three distinct functions of government as outlined by Montesquieu?|Taxation, military defense, and foreign diplomacy|Legislation, execution, and adjudication|Constitutional drafting, policy implementation, and public administration|State planning, law enforcement, and ideological education|Option B|Montesquieu categorized the fundamental powers of the state into three distinct functions: making laws (legislation), executing public policy (execution), and resolving legal disputes (adjudication).
7.1|How does the system of checks and balances fundamentally differ from a rigid separation of powers?|It completely fuses legislative and executive powers into a single cabinet system|It allows distinct branches to overlap and restrain each other's powers through constitutional mechanisms|It subordinates the executive branch entirely to judicial decree and constitutional interpretation|It abolishes the legislative branch during times of national emergency to favor executive action|Option B|While a strict separation keeps branches completely isolated, checks and balances purposely interlink them by giving each branch constitutional tools to block or oversee the actions of the others.
7.1|Which constitutional mechanism allows the legislative branch to check the power of the executive branch regarding public expenditure?|Judicial review|Budget approval|Executive veto|Legislative impeachment|Option B|The power of the purse or budget approval gives the legislature critical leverage to authorize, restrict, or deny funding for executive programs and operations.
7.1|In the context of institutional checks and balances, what is the primary purpose of a legislative veto over executive actions?|To allow lawmakers to directly execute administrative policies themselves|To prevent the executive branch from exercising unchecked unilateral authority|To enable the legislature to appoint judges to the supreme court|To transfer judicial adjudication responsibilities to parliament|Option B|The veto serves as a defensive constitutional instrument that empowers one branch to block or reject actions taken by another, thereby guarding against overreach.
7.1|Which branch of government typically exercises the power of judicial review to check the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions?|The executive branch through presidential decrees|The legislative branch through parliamentary committees|The judicial branch through courts of law|The electoral commission through voter referendums|Option C|Judicial review is the power exercised by courts to examine legislative statutes and executive actions to ensure they conform to the constitution.
7.1|What is the formal constitutional mechanism through which the legislature can remove an executive official or judge for grave misconduct?|Veto override|Budget impoundment|Impeachment|Judicial injunction|Option C|Impeachment is a formal legislative process of charging and potentially removing high-ranking public officials for constitutional violations, treason, or high crimes.
7.1|Why did Montesquieu emphasize the necessity of separating the judiciary from both the legislative and executive powers?|To ensure judges can actively rewrite flawed legislation during trials|To prevent the judge from simultaneously acting as both lawmaker and law enforcer|To allow the executive branch to influence sentencing guidelines directly|To make court rulings completely independent of constitutional constraints|Option B|Montesquieu famously asserted that if judicial power were joined with legislative power, the life and liberty of the subject would be exposed to arbitrary control, because the judge would then be the legislator.
7.1|Which institutional arrangement best exemplifies the concept of checks and balances in modern democratic governance?|A parliament passing laws without executive assent|A president vetoing a bill passed by the legislature, which can then be overridden by a supermajority|A supreme court drafting national development policies independently of parliament|An executive branch unilaterally appointing all members of the legislature|Option B|The executive veto combined with the legislative power to override it demonstrates how two independent branches interact and check each other.
7.1|What is the ultimate theoretical objective of combining Montesquieu's doctrine of separation of powers with a robust system of checks and balances?|Maximizing bureaucratic efficiency and administrative speed|Eliminating the need for written constitutions altogether|Safeguarding political liberty and preventing the rise of tyrannical rule|Centralizing state authority for rapid economic industrialization|Option C|The foundational philosophy behind separating powers and instituting checks and balances is to protect citizen liberty by stopping any single entity from monopolizing absolute power.

9.1|Which procedural defect in the making of delegated legislation can render the entire statutory instrument legally defective under judicial review?|Failure to follow mandatory statutory consultation or publication procedures stipulated in the parent act|Failure of the president to personally sign every individual agency guideline|Failure of the opposition party members to vote in favor of the administrative circular|Failure to translate the regulation into all local indigenous languages simultaneously|Option A|Non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements laid down in the parent act can lead courts to strike down delegated legislation on procedural ultra vires grounds.

5.1|Which of the following best characterizes a written constitution in comparison to an unwritten one?|It is entirely immune to any form of judicial interpretation|It is codified in a single formal document and usually possesses a rigid amendment procedure|It relies exclusively on unwritten political conventions and historical traditions|It completely eliminates the possibility of legislative supremacy over executive actions|Option B|A written constitution is formally codified into a single authoritative document and typically requires a special, rigid amendment process rather than ordinary legislation.
5.1|What is the foundational philosophy behind constitutionalism?|The total concentration of power in a single revolutionary council to ensure rapid development|The belief that government powers must be legally limited by a fundamental law to protect liberties|The doctrine that economic planning supersedes all civil and political rights of citizens|The supremacy of executive decrees over legislative enactments during states of emergency|Option B|Constitutionalism is the political philosophy asserting that government power must be legally limited by a supreme fundamental law to safeguard individual rights.
5.1|Which primary characteristic distinguishes a rigid constitution from a flexible one?|It requires a special, more difficult legislative procedure or referendum for amendments|It cannot be altered under any circumstances regardless of national emergencies|It can be amended by a simple majority vote of the regular legislature at any time|It lacks any written documentation and relies solely on judicial precedent and common law|Option A|A rigid constitution requires a special or extraordinary legislative mechanism to amend, safeguarding its fundamental status against casual changes.
5.1|How are unwritten constitutions primarily constituted and sustained?|Through strict executive decrees and military proclamations issued during transitions|Through a single, comprehensive legal document ratified by a constituent assembly|Through a combination of historical statutes, judicial precedents, and political conventions|Through international treaties signed with foreign constitutional monarchies|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not codified in one document; instead, it is derived from diverse sources like statutes, common law, conventions, and precedents.
5.1|Why is a written constitution typically associated with rigidity?|Because it prohibits the judiciary from interpreting statutory laws enacted by parliament|Because its fundamental rules are formally entrenched and necessitate special amendment processes|Because it allows the executive branch to alter constitutional provisions without legislative consent|Because it completely prevents any future amendments by succeeding generations of citizens|Option B|Written constitutions are typically rigid because they establish a formal, entrenched framework requiring special procedures to alter, unlike ordinary statutes.
5.1|Which of the following scenarios best exemplifies the practical application of constitutionalism?|A president dissolving the legislature by decree to expedite emergency economic policies|A supreme court nullifying a legislative act because it violates fundamental human rights|A ruling political party extending its tenure indefinitely through a simple parliamentary vote|A military junta suspending all fundamental human rights to maintain public order and security|Option B|Constitutionalism is demonstrated when an independent judiciary enforces fundamental legal limits to invalidate government actions that infringe on rights.
5.1|What is a primary functional advantage of a codified written constitution?|It automatically eliminates all forms of political corruption within the public service sector|It provides clarity, transparency, and accessible legal standards regarding the limits of state power|It ensures that the legislature remains permanently superior to both the judiciary and executive|It prevents economic recessions by stabilizing national monetary and fiscal policies permanently|Option B|A codified constitution provides clear, accessible, and written documentation of state powers and citizen rights, promoting transparency and legal certainty.
5.1|Which term describes a constitutional system where power is dispersed and checked by fundamental law, directly opposing arbitrary rule?|Autocracy|Constitutionalism|Plutocracy|Technocracy|Option B|Constitutionalism is the antithesis of arbitrary rule, ensuring that government authority is circumscribed by fundamental laws that protect individual liberties.
5.1|In the context of constitutional classification, what role do political conventions play in unwritten constitutions?|They serve as binding fundamental rules and operational norms even though they are not codified in statutes|They act as temporary measures that expire immediately after a general election takes place|They function merely as informal suggestions that politicians can ignore without constitutional consequence|They represent the written enactments passed by the lower house of parliament during a crisis|Option A|Conventions are unwritten rules of constitutional practice that are binding and essential to the functioning of governance, particularly in unwritten systems.
5.1|What is the primary danger associated with an excessively rigid written constitution?|It invites frequent military coups due to the absence of any written legal framework|It can hinder necessary adaptation to modern socio-political realities due to cumbersome amendment hurdles|It invariably leads to the complete abolition of the legislative branch by the executive branch|It forces the state to rely exclusively on unwritten conventions rather than written statutes|Option B|Excessive rigidity makes a constitution difficult to amend, potentially stalling necessary legal adaptation to evolving societal needs and modern crises.

7.1|In the framework of constitutional governance, what does the system of checks and balances primarily achieve?|It completely eliminates friction between government branches|It allows each branch to monitor and limit the powers of the other branches|It centralizes all executive and judicial authority into the legislature|It prevents the judiciary from ever overturning an unconstitutional law|Option B|Checks and balances provide overlapping powers so that each branch can constrain potential abuses of power by the others.
7.1|Which of the following is a classic legislative check over the executive branch?|Judicial review of administrative decrees|Veto override and impeachment proceedings|Executive appointment of cabinet ministers|Promulgation of executive orders|Option B|The legislature can check executive overreach through the power of impeachment and by overriding an executive veto with the required majority.
7.1|Which constitutional mechanism allows the judiciary to check both the legislature and the executive?|Budget appropriation|Executive veto|Judicial review|Vote of no confidence|Option C|Judicial review empowers the courts to invalidate legislative statutes and executive actions that violate the constitution.
7.1|How does the executive branch typically exercise a check on the legislative branch's lawmaking power?|By dissolving the judiciary at will|Through the power of legislative veto|By directly amending the constitution without approval|Through lifetime appointment of lawmakers|Option B|The executive veto allows the executive branch to reject bills passed by the legislature, forcing them to reconsider or muster enough votes to override it.
7.1|Why is the budget approval process considered a vital component of legislative oversight over the executive?|It ensures the judiciary maintains control over taxation|It prevents the executive from spending public funds without legislative authorization|It allows the executive to dictate judicial salaries without interference|It completely strips the executive of any financial planning role|Option B|By controlling the purse strings, the legislature ensures that executive agencies cannot spend money outside of legally appropriated funds.
7.1|What would likely happen in a pure separation of powers model if one organ of government amassed all three functions?|Democratic accountability would be significantly enhanced|It would create a balanced system of reciprocal limitations|It would result in absolute power and institutional tyranny|It would automatically establish a decentralized federal state|Option C|Concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial authority in a single entity destroys institutional checks and inevitably leads to tyranny.
7.1|In the context of the separation of powers, what distinguishes adjudication from legislation and execution?|Adjudication involves drafting new public policies and statutes|Adjudication focuses on interpreting laws and applying them to specific legal disputes|Adjudication centers on implementing administrative programs and managing state resources|Adjudication relates strictly to mobilizing military defense and conducting foreign diplomacy|Option B|While legislation creates laws and execution implements them, adjudication is the judicial function of interpreting laws and resolving conflicts.

6.1|Which chapter of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution houses the Fundamental Rights enforceable by the courts?|Chapter II|Chapter III|Chapter IV|Chapter V|Option C|Chapter IV of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution contains the fundamental human rights provisions, ranging from the right to life to freedom of movement.|

6.1|Which of the following rights falls strictly under the category of socio-economic and political protections or civil liberties guaranteed in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution?|Right to Fair Hearing|Right to Free Universal Healthcare|Right to Free Tertiary Education|Right to Guaranteed Minimum Wage|Option A|The right to fair hearing is a core judicial protection explicitly codified within Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, unlike directive principles found elsewhere.|

6.1|Which constitutional category covers a person who acquires Nigerian citizenship because at least one of their parents was a citizen of Nigeria at the time of their birth inside the country?|Citizenship by Birth|Citizenship by Registration|Citizenship by Naturalisation|Citizenship by Investiture|Option A|Section 25(1)(a) stipulates that every person born in Nigeria after the date of independence, either of whose parents or grandparents is a citizen of Nigeria, belongs to citizenship by birth.|
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, which of the following best describes the first principle of the rule of law?|Absolute supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power|Predominance of executive decrees over legislative enactments|Immunity of public officials from ordinary legal processes|Supremacy of military tribunals in times of civil unrest|Option A|Dicey's first principle establishes that the regular law is supreme and absolute, rejecting arbitrary power, prerogative, or wide discretionary authority by the government.
8.1|How did A.V. Dicey define his second principle of the rule of law regarding equality?|Equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law administered by ordinary law courts|Exemption of government ministers from civil litigation while in office|Differentiation of legal standards based on social and political status|Subjection of citizens exclusively to specialized administrative tribunals|Option A|Dicey's second principle emphasizes equality before the law, meaning no person is above the law and all classes are subject to ordinary courts.
8.1|What constitutes A.V. Dicey's third formulation of the rule of law?|The constitution is a consequence of the rights of individuals as defined and enforced by the courts|Constitutional rights are granted and can be arbitrarily withdrawn by legislative fiat|Fundamental rights exist only when codified in an explicit state charter or bill of rights|Individual liberties are secondary to the collective economic goals of the state|Option A|Dicey argued that individual rights are part of the British constitution because they are secured through judicial decisions rather than abstract declarations.
8.1|Which specific provision in the Nigerian Constitution serves as a major limitation to A.V. Dicey's principle of equality before the law?|Section 308 granting executive immunity to the President and Governors|Section 36 guaranteeing the right to a fair hearing in civil and criminal trials|Section 12 outlining the procedure for domesticating international treaties|Section 45 allowing for the restriction of fundamental rights during emergencies|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants temporary immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to certain executive office holders, restricting Dicey's equality principle.
8.1|In the context of the limitations of the rule of law in Nigeria, what is an ouster clause?|A legislative or decree provision that strips courts of jurisdiction to review certain actions|A constitutional guarantee protecting citizens from unlawful arrest and detention|An executive order mandating the immediate release of political prisoners|A judicial precedent establishing the supremacy of common law over customary law|Option A|Military ouster clauses explicitly prohibit courts from entertaining challenges against decrees or edicts, thereby undermining regular judicial oversight.
8.1|How does delegated legislation pose a challenge to A.V. Dicey's traditional concept of the rule of law?|It empowers non-elected administrative bodies to create laws with wide discretionary powers|It forces the legislature to debate every minute detail of public policy before implementation|It completely abolishes the existence of ordinary law courts in favor of tribunals|It ensures that all rules are created through transparent public referendums|Option A|Delegated legislation transfers law-making authority to the executive branch, introducing broad discretionary powers that conflict with Dicey's anti-discretion stance.
8.1|Which scenario best illustrates a direct suspension of regular legal processes as a limitation to the rule of law in Nigeria?|Declaration of a state of emergency under constitutional provisions|Enactment of a private member bill by the National Assembly|Filing a civil suit against a multinational corporation for environmental damage|Appointing a new Chief Justice of the Federation by the executive branch|Option A|A state of emergency allows the state to suspend certain constitutional rights and expand executive powers, serving as a classic structural limitation to the rule of law.
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey strongly oppose the French droit administratif system of his time?|Because it subjected government officials to special administrative courts rather than ordinary courts|Because it failed to protect any individual rights whatsoever against state intrusion|Because it gave the legislature absolute power to alter the constitution without judicial review|Because it merged executive and judicial powers into a single unaccountable office|Option A|Dicey criticized droit administratif because it shielded state officials from ordinary courts, violating his principle of equality before ordinary law.
8.1|Which of the following elements represents a key institutional requirement for Dicey's second principle to function effectively?|An independent judiciary free from political interference by the executive or legislature|A bicameral legislature with veto power over judicial appointments|An executive branch with unlimited discretionary authority during crises|A centralized bureaucracy that controls all legal education and training|Option A|An independent judiciary is vital to ensure that ordinary courts can impartially hold all citizens and government officials accountable under ordinary law.
8.1|What is a primary criticism of A.V. Dicey's strict formulation of the rule of law in modern governance?|It fails to account for the modern necessity of administrative discretion and regulatory agencies|It places too much emphasis on socio-economic rights rather than civil liberties|It assumes that written constitutions are superior to unwritten common law traditions|It completely ignores the existence of criminal law in favor of civil law disputes|Option A|Modern legal scholars note that Dicey's rejection of administrative discretion is impractical in contemporary welfare states where specialized agencies manage complex public sectors.
9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly through a constitutional amendment process|Rules and regulations made by executive ministers or administrative agencies under legislative authority|Judicial rulings handed down by the Supreme Court to interpret ambiguous statutes|Executive decrees issued unilaterally by the president without any legislative backing|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers, departments, or agencies under powers specifically delegated to them by the legislature through an Enabling Act.
9.1|What is the primary function of an Enabling Act or Parent Act in relation to delegated legislation?|It establishes the judicial framework used by courts to review executive corruption|It provides the constitutional authorization and limits for administrative bodies to make subsidiary laws|It mandates the immediate dissolution of parliament whenever an administrative rule is challenged|It replaces the constitution as the supreme law governing federal territories|Option B|An Enabling Act (or Parent Act) is passed by the legislature to grant specific rule-making powers to an executive body and define the scope within which subsidiary legislation can be made.
9.1|What legal consequence follows if an administrative agency enacts a subsidiary law that exceeds the powers granted by its Parent Act?|The law is automatically ratified by a joint session of the national legislature|The agency head faces immediate criminal prosecution for treasonable felony|The rule is declared null and void under the Doctrine of Ultra Vires|The legislation becomes a permanent constitutional amendment|Option C|Under the Doctrine of Ultra Vires, any administrative rule or regulation that goes beyond the authority granted in the Enabling Act is struck down by the courts as illegal and void.
9.1|Which of the following institutions exercises the power of judicial review to strike down unauthorized delegated legislation in Nigeria?|The Federal Executive Council|The court system|The civil service commission|The legislative committee on statutory instruments|Option B|Courts exercise judicial review to evaluate subsidiary legislation and invalidate any rules that violate the Doctrine of Ultra Vires or breach the limits set by the Parent Act.
9.1|Why is delegated legislation considered necessary in modern governance according to political scientists?|It completely eliminates the need for any legislative oversight or parliamentary involvement|It allows technical and complex regulations to be handled swiftly by experts without overburdening the legislature|It ensures that the judiciary has absolute control over the administrative policy-making process|It prevents any form of public participation in the creation of national economic policies|Option B|Delegated legislation saves parliamentary time and taps into administrative expertise, allowing technical and rapid rule-making suited for complex modern governance.
9.1|Which of the following is a standard mechanism used by the legislature to control delegated legislation?|Parliamentary review and scrutiny of statutory instruments|Direct executive veto of court injunctions|Compulsory public referendums for every administrative circular|Total privatization of government parastatals|Option A|Parliamentary review allows the legislature to monitor, scrutinize, and sometimes annul subsidiary legislation to ensure that executive agencies do not abuse their rule-making powers.
9.1|What role does publication in the official government gazette play regarding delegated legislation?|It serves as a formal legal requirement to give public notice and legal effect to the subsidiary laws|It acts as an informal suggestion that executive ministers can choose to ignore at will|It transfers the legislative power permanently back to local government councils|It prevents the judiciary from ever reviewing the validity of the administrative rule|Option A|Official publication in the gazette is a mandatory procedural step that brings subsidiary laws to the attention of the public and gives them binding legal force.
9.1|When an administrative agency acts beyond its legal capacity while issuing a rule, this legal violation is formally termed what?|Delegated sovereignty|Ultra vires|Stare decisis|Ultra modernism|Option B|Ultra vires is a Latin term meaning beyond powers, which describes the legal defect when an administrative agency exceeds the jurisdiction granted by its Enabling Act.
9.1|Which branch of government holds the original constitutional authority to delegate legislative powers to executive agencies?|The judiciary through appellate jurisdiction|The legislature through an Act of Parliament|The military high command through decree boards|The civil service union through collective bargaining|Option B|The legislature holds the primary law-making authority and can choose to delegate subsidiary rule-making powers to executive agencies through a statutory Enabling Act.
9.1|How does judicial review differ fundamentally from parliamentary review in the context of delegated legislation?|Judicial review invalidates ultra vires laws through court litigation, whereas parliamentary review involves legislative oversight of rules|Judicial review is conducted exclusively by foreign tribunals, whereas parliamentary review is internal|Judicial review creates new enabling acts, whereas parliamentary review dissolves the executive branch|Judicial review applies only to customary laws, whereas parliamentary review applies only to international treaties|Option A|Judicial review is a court-based legal challenge that strikes down unauthorized rules, while parliamentary review is a political and legislative oversight mechanism to monitor subsidiary laws.
11.1|Which of the following best characterizes the executive branch in a presidential system of government?|Fusion of legislative and executive powers|Strict separation of powers and fixed tenure|Collective responsibility to the legislature|Primus inter pares executive leadership|Option B|A presidential system is defined by a clear separation of powers between the executive and the legislature, complemented by a fixed tenure for the president.
11.1|In a parliamentary system of government, the executive is primarily accountable to which of the following?|The military high command|The supreme court judiciary|The parliament or legislature directly|The regional sub-national governors|Option C|In parliamentary democracies, the executive branch is drawn from and fused with the legislature, making it directly accountable to parliament through mechanisms like a vote of no confidence.
11.1|What is the direct consequence when a parliamentary government loses a vote of no confidence?|The legislature is dissolved and early elections are usually triggered|The prime minister assumes absolute presidential executive powers|The judiciary takes over temporary administrative control of the state|The military suspends the constitution and issues authoritarian decrees|Option A|A vote of no confidence forces the government of the day to fall, typically resulting in the resignation of the cabinet and the calling of new parliamentary elections.
11.1|Which concept is fundamentally absent from the structural design of a presidential system?|Fixed executive tenure|Separation of powers|Collective responsibility of the cabinet|Checks and balances|Option C|Collective responsibility is a core feature of parliamentary systems where cabinet ministers jointly share responsibility for government policies, unlike presidential systems where individual appointees answer solely to the president.
11.1|What title is typically ascribed to the head of government in a parliamentary system, highlighting their status as first among equals?|Commander-in-Chief|Primus Inter Pares|Supreme Dictator|Executive President|Option B|The prime minister is styled as Primus Inter Pares because they lead the cabinet while theoretically remaining politically equal with their ministerial colleagues.
11.1|How does a military regime typically govern a state upon seizing power, based on the study notes?|By upholding strict parliamentary consensus and coalition building|Through the enforcement of authoritarian decrees and a suspended constitution|By maintaining the absolute independence of the judiciary and legislature|Through regularized plebiscites and collective cabinet accountability|Option C|Military regimes govern outside normal constitutional frameworks by suspending the foundational laws of the land and ruling through arbitrary, authoritarian decrees.
11.1|Which system of government is characterized by a complete fusion of executive and legislative powers?|Presidential system|Federal democratic system|Parliamentary system|Confederal system|Option C|The parliamentary model merges the executive and legislative branches, as members of the cabinet are simultaneously sitting members of parliament.
11.1|What distinguishes the tenure of a president in a presidential system from that of a prime minister in a parliamentary system?|A president serves a fixed term whereas a prime minister's tenure depends on legislative confidence|A president can be removed instantly by a simple parliamentary vote of no confidence|A prime minister enjoys a constitutionally rigid and unalterable term length|A president lacks any fixed timeline and serves purely at the pleasure of the legislature|Option A|Presidents enjoy fixed constitutional terms that are independent of legislative survival, whereas prime ministers serve only as long as they maintain a parliamentary majority.
11.1|Which structural feature is most prominent during a military administration?|Separation of state powers into distinct branches|Fusion of powers enforced through authoritarian command structures|Collective ministerial responsibility to an elected parliament|Primus inter pares executive power distribution|Option B|Military governments concentrate all governmental authority into the hands of military rulers, resulting in a complete fusion of powers without democratic checks.
11.1|Which of the following is a direct institutional outcome of the separation of powers in a presidential democracy?|The executive branch automatically dictates legislative timelines|The executive branch cannot be easily unseated by a legislative vote of no confidence|Ministers must concurrently serve as elected members of the legislature|The prime minister must maintain party consensus to stay in office|Option B|Because executive and legislative branches are institutionally distinct and possess fixed tenures, a presidential executive does not rely on parliamentary confidence to survive.
12.1|Which of the following fundamental characteristics primarily distinguishes a pressure group from a political party in a democratic system?|Pressure groups seek to influence public policy directly without contesting formal elections|Pressure groups are legally prohibited from engaging in any form of public lobbying or advocacy|Political parties focus exclusively on economic wage negotiations rather than governance|Political parties operate entirely outside the constitutional framework unlike registered pressure groups|Option A|Pressure groups focus on influencing government decisions and public policy from the outside without seeking to win elective political office themselves.
12.1|The Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) and the Nigerian Labour Congress (NLC) are prime examples of which category of interest groups?|Sectional or protective groups representing specific occupational and material interests|Promotional groups dedicated entirely to altruistic global human rights causes|Anomic groups characterized by sudden, spontaneous, and unorganized civil unrest|Revolutionary syndicates aiming to violently overthrow the existing constitutional order|Option A|Sectional or protective groups like ASUU and NLC are formed primarily to protect and advance the specific economic, professional, and social interests of their members.
12.1|A civil society coalition organizing a campaign to abolish the death penalty or protect global environmental standards best exemplifies which type of association?|Promotional or cause group driven by abstract principles rather than material self-interest|Sectional pressure group focused exclusively on securing higher wages for industrial workers|Anomic interest group emerging spontaneously out of sudden public frustration and riots|Bureaucratic agency established by the legislature to formulate national economic policy|Option A|Promotional or cause groups advocate for ideological, moral, or altruistic causes that benefit society at large rather than the narrow material interests of their members.
12.1|When public frustration erupts into sudden, unorganized, and spontaneous street riots following an unpopular government policy, political scientists classify this as which group type?|Anomic pressure group manifesting as erratic and leaderless collective behavior|Protective sectional association engaging in routine collective bargaining processes|Institutional interest group operating formally within government administrative structures|Promotional cause group executing a well-planned public awareness media campaign|Option A|Anomic groups are spontaneous, unstructured, and often violent reactions to sudden political or economic stress, lacking formal organization or permanent leadership.
12.1|Which of the following techniques is most characteristic of sectional economic unions like the Nigerian Labour Congress when routine negotiations with employers or government fail?|Executing organized strikes and industrial picketing to exert economic pressure|Contesting general elections to capture legislative majority seats directly|Dissolving the organization permanently to form a registered political party|Issuing judicial injunctions to compel compliance from executive branch ministers|Option A|Strikes and picketing are core industrial action techniques deployed by labor unions to disrupt productivity and force concessions from the government or employers.
12.1|A professional body such as the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) primarily utilizes which strategy to influence judicial appointments and legal reforms?|Lobbying policymakers and submitting formal legal memoranda on public bills|Engaging in uncoordinated, spontaneous street riots during economic crises|Boycotting all judicial proceedings indefinitely without any stated political objective|Creating armed wings to forcefully occupy legislative chambers during budget sessions|Option A|Professional bodies like the NBA rely heavily on institutional lobbying, expert legal commentary, and direct engagement with lawmakers to shape legislation.
12.1|What is the defining operational difference between a protective interest group and a promotional interest group regarding their membership scope?|Protective groups have restricted membership tied to specific trades or professions while promotional groups are open to any citizen supporting the cause|Protective groups operate exclusively in secret underground cells while promotional groups require state legislative registration|Promotional groups restrict membership strictly to wealthy corporate executives while protective groups only admit students|Protective groups are funded entirely by foreign donors whereas promotional groups rely exclusively on statutory state grants|Option A|Protective groups limit membership to specific occupations or social strata to safeguard their interests, whereas promotional groups welcome anyone who shares their advocacy goals.
12.1|During a fuel price hike, civil rights activists refuse to purchase petroleum products or patronize transport companies, representing which pressure group tactic?|A consumer boycott designed to inflict financial loss and force policy reversal|An anomic riot characterized by chaotic, leaderless destruction of public property|A legislative lobbying campaign aimed at drafting private member bills in parliament|A sectional wage negotiation strategy restricted to registered trade union members|Option A|A boycott involves concerted refusal to buy goods or services to pressure targeted entities or governments into altering unpopular economic decisions.
12.1|Why are anomic groups generally considered unstable and difficult for political analysts to study systematically within a democratic framework?|They lack permanent institutional structures, defined leadership hierarchies, and predictable operational rules|They are legally recognized corporations mandated to submit annual financial audit reports to the legislature|They function exclusively as registered political parties participating in every national election cycle|They rely strictly on long-term collective bargaining agreements signed with the federal ministry of labor|Option A|Anomic groups lack formal organization, continuity, and permanent leaders, making their emergence unpredictable and their actions volatile.
12.1|Which combination accurately pairs Nigerian pressure groups with their correct analytical classifications based on standard political science typology?|ASUU as a sectional group and Amnesty International as a promotional group|NLC as an anomic group and ASUU as a promotional cause group|NBA as an anomic group and spontaneous rioters as sectional groups|Amnesty International as a protective group and NLC as a promotional group|Option A|ASUU protects specific academic staff interests (sectional), while Amnesty International advocates for universal human rights principles (promotional).
13.1|What is the foundational objective that primarily distinguishes political parties from other interest groups or civil society organizations?|To contest elections with the ultimate goal of capturing and exercising state power|To lobby legislative bodies exclusively on behalf of specific economic sectors|To provide social welfare benefits without engaging in formal electoral competition|To monitor governmental policies and ensure bureaucratic accountability from outside government|Option A|Political parties are uniquely defined by their core objective to contest elections and win governmental power, whereas interest groups seek to influence policy rather than govern.
13.1|Which of the following functions performed by political parties involves selecting and presenting candidates for elective public offices?|Political socialization|Political recruitment|Interest aggregation|Policy legitimation|Option B|Political recruitment refers to the process by which political parties identify, select, and present candidates to run for public office and staff government institutions.
