13.1|What fundamental role do political parties play in bridging the gap between the governed and the government?|They act as a crucial link by communicating citizen preferences to policymakers while mobilizing public support for state policies|They replace the civil service entirely with partisan loyalists who manage technical administrative tasks|They function strictly as private clubs with no institutional connection to the formal machinery of the state|They prevent public participation in governance by centralizing all decision-making within judicial committees|Option A|Parties serve as vital intermediaries between citizens and the state, translating public demands into political action and mobilizing the electorate behind governance programs.
14.1|Which electoral system awards a legislative seat to the candidate who secures the highest number of votes cast in a single-member constituency, even without an absolute majority?|Proportional Representation system|Absolute Majority runoff system|First-Past-The-Post system|Alternative vote ranking system|Option C|First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) is a plurality system where the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they cross the 50% threshold.
14.1|What is the primary distinguishing feature of an Absolute Majority electoral system compared to First-Past-The-Post?|It requires a candidate to secure more than 50 percent of the total valid votes cast to win|It allocates seats strictly according to the total percentage of votes a political party receives nationally|It automatically forces the two leading parties to form a coalition government after every election|It restricts political participation to only two major dominant political parties in the state|Option A|An absolute majority system mandates that a winning candidate must secure over 50 percent of the votes, often triggering a runoff election if the threshold is not met initially.
14.1|How does Proportional Representation fundamentally differ from majoritarian electoral systems?|It eliminates the need for any form of voter registration or independent electoral commissions|It translates a political party's share of the national popular vote directly into a corresponding share of legislative seats|It restricts legislative representation strictly to independent candidates rather than political parties|It mandates that every constituency must be represented by exactly one legislative member|Option B|Proportional Representation ensures that legislative seats are distributed in proportion to the votes received by each political party, enhancing minority representation.
14.1|Which of the following bodies is constitutionally empowered by the Nigerian state to organize, undertake, and supervise federal elections?|The National Orientation Agency|The Independent National Electoral Commission|The Directorate of Democratic Governance|The Supreme Judicial Electoral Council|Option B|INEC is the statutory, independent body established to manage the electoral process, conduct voter registration, and supervise elections in Nigeria.
14.1|Beyond conducting elections, which administrative function is a core responsibility of INEC during the electoral process?|Drafting the national constitution and amending legislative bills|Formulating fiscal monetary policies for the ruling government|Screening political candidates and maintaining the official voter register|Appointing judicial officers to election petition tribunals|Option C|INEC is legally mandated to oversee voter registration and thoroughly screen political candidates to ensure they meet eligibility criteria before contesting elections.
14.1|Why might a multi-party democracy adopt a First-Past-The-Post system despite its tendency to produce disproportionate legislative outcomes?|It guarantees that every minority party secures proportional parliamentary representation|It is relatively simple to administer and often produces clear legislative majorities for stable governance|It prevents the formation of coalition governments under all circumstances|It requires candidates to achieve absolute consensus across all geopolitical zones|Option B|FPTP is valued for its simplicity and its tendency to create decisive single-party majorities, avoiding the complexities of coalition-building.

7.1|What is the primary rationale behind Montesquieu's advocacy for the separation of powers?|To promote economic efficiency and industrial growth|To prevent the concentration of absolute power and tyranny|To ensure the military remains superior to civil authority|To streamline the legislative drafting process for rapid execution|Option B|Separation of powers ensures that no single body controls all arms of government, thereby checking authority and preventing tyrannical rule.
7.1|Which governmental branch is primarily responsible for the adjudication function according to the study notes?|The executive branch|The legislative branch|The judicial branch|The bureaucratic civil service|Option C|Adjudication involves interpreting laws and administering justice, which is the core constitutional responsibility of the judicial branch.
7.1|In a system of checks and balances, which mechanism allows the executive branch to reject a bill passed by the legislature?|Judicial review|Veto power|Impeachment|Budget approval|Option B|The veto is a constitutional power held by the executive to reject legislation passed by the law-making body, forming part of the checks and balances system.
7.1|Which check and balance mechanism empowers the legislature to remove an erring executive or judicial officer?|Veto|Budget approval|Impeachment|Judicial review|Option C|Impeachment is a legislative check that allows parliament to formally charge and remove high-ranking officials for constitutional misconduct or abuse of power.
7.1|What purpose do the mechanisms of checks and balances serve when integrated with the separation of powers?|They completely eliminate the need for an independent judiciary|They allow each branch to monitor and restrain the powers of the other branches|They consolidate all authority under a single supreme leader during emergencies|They abolish the legislature in favor of executive decrees|Option B|Checks and balances provide constitutional means for each branch to oversee and limit the actions of the other branches, ensuring a balance of power.
7.1|Which institutional body typically exercises the power of the purse and budget approval within a constitutional framework?|The judiciary|The executive cabinet|The legislature|The armed forces council|Option C|Budget approval is a fundamental legislative check that grants parliament control over state finances and government expenditure.
7.1|What role does judicial review play in the framework of checks and balances?|It allows courts to declare legislative or executive actions unconstitutional|It enables the judiciary to draft emergency legislation during a crisis|It gives judges the authority to veto executive budget proposals directly|It permits judges to appoint members of the legislature|Option A|Judicial review empowers the courts to examine laws and executive acts to ensure they conform to the constitution, checking potential overreach.
7.1|If the three distinct functions of government were concentrated in a single body, what would be the most likely consequence according to Montesquieu?|Enhanced administrative speed|Total democratic stability|The rise of tyranny|Economic prosperity|Option B|Montesquieu argued that uniting legislative, executive, and judicial powers in the same hands inevitably leads to the abuse of power and tyranny.
9.1|What is the primary constitutional function of an Enabling or Parent Act in the context of delegated legislation?|To grant limited law-making authority from the legislature to executive bodies or ministers|To allow the judiciary to completely rewrite administrative statutes at will|To permanently strip the legislature of all supreme legislative powers|To replace the constitution with ministerial decrees and emergency ordinances|Option A|The Enabling Act serves as the legal foundation passed by the legislature that delegates specific rule-making authority to executive agencies or ministers.
9.1|Which legal doctrine is primarily applied by the courts to invalidate executive rules that exceed the powers granted in a parent statute?|Doctrine of Ultra Vires|Doctrine of Sovereign Immunity|Doctrine of Separation of Powers|Doctrine of Judicial Review of Elections|Option A|The doctrine of ultra vires is used by courts to strike down delegated legislation that goes beyond the authority granted by the enabling act.
9.1|Which of the following bodies is constitutionally responsible for passing the initial Enabling Act that permits delegated legislation?|The National Legislature or Parliament|The Supreme Court of Nigeria|The Federal Executive Council|The Civil Service Commission|Option A|Only the legislature possesses the primary law-making power required to enact a parent or enabling act that delegates authority to others.
9.1|What is a primary justification for the widespread use of delegated legislation in modern governance?|The need for technical expertise and speed in handling complex socio-economic matters|To completely bypass the court system and prevent any judicial scrutiny|To abolish the need for a bicameral legislature permanently|To ensure that executive ministers hold lifetime legislative positions|Option A|Delegated legislation allows subject-matter experts within executive agencies to swiftly create detailed rules without burdening the legislature.
9.1|Which of the following constitutes a standard legislative or administrative control measure over delegated legislation?|Publication in the official gazette and parliamentary review|Immediate ratification by a public referendum in every state|A mandatory unanimous vote by all state governors|Approval by international human rights tribunals|Option A|Publication in the official gazette ensures public notice, while parliamentary review enables legislative oversight of delegated instruments.
9.1|If an executive minister issues a statutory instrument that directly contradicts a provision of the Parent Act, what legal status does that instrument hold?|It is considered null and void under the doctrine of ultra vires|It automatically amends the Parent Act by implication|It remains fully enforceable until a new election is held|It becomes a supreme constitutional document|Option A|Any delegated legislation that contradicts or exceeds the scope of the parent act is ultra vires and legally void.
9.1|How does delegated legislation differ fundamentally from primary legislation?|Delegated legislation is created by executive authorities under delegated powers rather than directly by parliament|Delegated legislation cannot be challenged in any court of law under any circumstances|Delegated legislation requires a two-thirds majority of all citizens to be valid|Delegated legislation is only used for military appointments and nothing else|Option A|Primary legislation is enacted directly by parliament, whereas delegated legislation is created by executive bodies using authority granted by parliament.
9.1|What role does judicial review play regarding delegated legislation?|It empowers courts to examine rules and strike down those exceeding statutory authority|It allows judges to draft alternative economic policies for the cabinet|It requires judges to pass new enabling acts during court sessions|It restricts courts from ever reviewing executive actions|Option A|Judicial review allows the judiciary to check executive power by striking down rules that violate the scope of the enabling act.
9.1|Which term describes the administrative instruments, rules, and orders created by executive agencies pursuant to legislative delegation?|Delegated legislation|Judicial precedent|Executive veto|Constitutional amendment|Option A|Rules and orders made by executive authorities under powers granted by an enabling act are collectively known as delegated legislation.
9.1|Why is parliamentary review considered an essential safeguard against the misuse of delegated legislation?|It allows the legislature to monitor, scrutinize, and check the rule-making power it delegated|It transfers all judicial authority directly to legislative committees|It prevents executive agencies from hiring civil servants|It ensures that ministers receive life tenure for their administrative decisions|Option A|Parliamentary review provides a mechanism for the legislature to oversee how executive agencies exercise the law-making powers entrusted to them.
8.1|Which political theorist is most famously credited with formalizing the classical doctrine of the Rule of Law through his three core principles?|Max Weber|A.V. Dicey|Karl Marx|Thomas Hobbes|Option B|A.V. Dicey formally articulated the classical tripartite doctrine of the Rule of Law in his seminal 1885 study on the law of the constitution.|
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey's first principle, what does the supremacy of regular law mean in a democratic state?|The legislature can pass any law without constitutional limits|Arbitrary power and wide discretionary authority by the government are rejected|Customary laws supersede statutory enactments in all circumstances|Judicial pronouncements carry more weight than constitutional provisions|Option B|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law reigns supreme and protects citizens against arbitrary, wide, or discretionary government power.|
8.1|How does A.V. Dicey define the second principle of the Rule of Law regarding equality before the law?|All citizens including government officials are subject to the same ordinary laws administered by ordinary courts|Political leaders enjoy judicial immunity to ensure smooth governance|Specialized military tribunals have jurisdiction over civilian offenses during crises|Judges are legally immune from public criticism or civil liability|Option A|Dicey's second principle emphasizes that no person is above the law and everyone regardless of rank is subject to ordinary laws in ordinary courts.|
8.1|Which of the following best captures A.V. Dicey's third principle concerning the protection of individual rights?|Rights are granted exclusively through executive decrees and temporary proclamations|Individual rights are derived from judicial decisions and constitutional court interpretations rather than abstract declarations|Constitutional bills of rights are necessary prerequisites for any functioning democracy|Human rights can be suspended indefinitely during national emergencies|Option B|Dicey argued that individual rights in the British constitution flow organically from judicial decisions and remedies rather than abstract constitutional declarations.|
8.1|Which constitutional provision in Nigeria serves as a major practical limitation to A.V. Dicey's second principle of equality before the law?|Section 308 granting executive immunity to the President and Governors|Section 36 guaranteeing the right to a fair hearing|Section 45 allowing restriction of fundamental rights during emergencies|Section 6 of the 1999 Constitution vesting judicial powers|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants temporary immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to certain executive office holders, limiting strict legal equality.|
8.1|How does delegated legislation pose a challenge to A.V. Dicey's conception of the Rule of Law?|It transfers primary lawmaking powers to the executive branch, increasing wide discretionary authority|It forces the judiciary to surrender its power of judicial review to local governments|It forces citizens to undergo military trials without legal representation|It eliminates the need for written constitutions altogether|Option A|Delegated legislation empowers executive bodies to make rules, which Dicey viewed cautiously because extensive executive discretion can undermine regular law supremacy.|
8.1|What are military ouster clauses in Nigerian constitutional history, and how do they relate to the Rule of Law?|Provisions inserted into decrees by military regimes to bar courts from reviewing their actions, violating Dicey's principles|Provisions that force military personnel to resign before contesting elections|Judicial orders that compel the military to return to their barracks immediately|Clauses that require international human rights watchdogs to monitor military budgets|Option A|Military ouster clauses explicitly strip courts of jurisdiction to question executive or military decrees, directly undermining the supremacy of regular law and judicial protection.|
8.1|In the context of the Nigerian legal and political framework, when is a state of emergency legally invoked to limit rights?|During grave public crises or emergencies where normal governance is threatened, subject to constitutional safeguards|Whenever the ruling political party faces defeat in local elections|Whenever the legislature disagrees with the executive budget proposal|Automatically at the end of every civilian presidential term|Option A|A state of emergency allows the state to lawfully restrict certain individual rights and expand executive powers during existential national crises.|
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey place heavy emphasis on ordinary courts of law rather than specialized administrative tribunals?|Ordinary courts ensure uniform application of the law and protect citizens from arbitrary state bureaucracy|Administrative tribunals are always staffed by military generals and intelligence officers|Ordinary courts are cheaper and faster to operate than specialized tribunals|Administrative tribunals lack the authority to enforce criminal penalties|Option A|Dicey believed that ordinary courts safeguard individual liberties better because they treat all state officials and citizens under the same uniform legal system.|
8.1|Which critique is most commonly leveled against A.V. Dicey's strict adherence to the Rule of Law in modern constitutional states?|It fails to account for the modern necessity of delegated legislation and administrative discretion required in a welfare state|It relies too heavily on communist ideology and central economic planning|It grants absolute and unchecked powers to the judicial branch over all other arms of government|It completely abolishes the need for a written constitution or parliament|Option A|Modern critics argue that Dicey's rigid nineteenth-century model is impractical today because contemporary governance requires specialized administrative agencies and delegated powers.|
10.1|Which of the following best characterizes a federal political administrative system?|Constitutional division of powers between a central government and autonomous federating units|Absolute concentration of all sovereign authority within a single central government|A loose alliance of fully sovereign states delegating limited powers to a weak central authority|Complete political decentralization where regional units possess unilateral rights to secede at will|Option A|A federal system relies on a constitutional division of powers that legally guarantees autonomy to both the central government and the federating units.
10.1|What is the defining structural feature of a unitary system of government?|Power is shared equally through concurrent legislative lists between regions and the center|All constitutional authority and administrative power are concentrated in a central government|Federating units hold residual powers while the central government handles foreign affairs only|Sovereign states maintain independent military forces while sharing a common currency union|Option B|In a unitary system, constitutional authority is centralized, and any regional administrative bodies derive their power entirely from the center.
10.1|Which of the following nations is traditionally cited as a classic example of a unitary administrative system?|Nigeria and the United States|Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates|The United Kingdom and France|Canada and Australia|Option C|Countries like the United Kingdom and France operate under unitary systems where the central legislature holds supreme constitutional authority.
10.1|How does a confederal system fundamentally differ from a federal system?|Confederal systems concentrate absolute power in the executive branch while federal systems use a parliament|Confederal units retain absolute sovereignty and the right to secede, whereas federal units are constitutionally bound|Federal systems have weak central governments while confederal systems have absolute centralized authority|Confederal governments are created by judicial decree whereas federal systems are established by military rule|Option B|A confederation is a loose association of sovereign states that delegate restricted powers to a weak center, keeping the right of secession.
10.1|In the context of political administrative systems, what does the right of secession typically signify?|The legal authority of a central government to unilaterally dissolve regional state parliaments|The constitutional mechanism used by local governments to collect internal revenue taxes|The inherent right of member states in a confederation to formally withdraw from the union|The diplomatic process through which a unitary state grants local autonomy to provinces|Option C|The right to secede is a defining characteristic of confederal arrangements, reflecting the ongoing sovereign independence of member states.
10.1|Which administrative system is most susceptible to severe central dominance and the potential erosion of local autonomy?|A confederal system because the center has overwhelming financial leverage|A federal system because the judiciary always sides with regional governors|A unitary system because all constitutional authority is concentrated at the center|A decentralized confederation because member states lack executive leadership|Option C|Because a unitary system concentrates all constitutional authority at the center, local units operate entirely at the discretion of the central government.
10.1|What primary mechanism legally safeguards the division of powers in a federal political system?|An entrenched constitution that neither level of government can unilaterally alter|Executive decrees issued by the head of state during a national emergency|Bilateral treaties signed annually between regional governors and the prime minister|Unanimous consent votes cast by traditional rulers and civil service commissioners|Option A|Federal systems require a rigid or entrenched constitution to legally protect the autonomous powers of both the central and regional governments.
10.1|Why are confederal systems historically unstable or short-lived in practice?|Because they lack a central judicial system to settle border disputes between citizens|Because the central government is usually too weak to enforce policies or collect taxes effectively against defiant members|Because regional units are constitutionally prohibited from maintaining local police forces|Because the central authority invariably transforms into an absolute monarchy over time|Option B|Confederal systems grant limited powers to a weak center, making it difficult to enforce collective decisions or maintain long-term cohesion.
10.1|Which political administrative system best describes a scenario where regional governments exist merely as administrative agents of the central authority?|Federal system|Confederal system|Unitary system|Dual-sovereignty system|Option C|In a unitary system, regional or local bodies do not possess independent constitutional powers but act as administrative extensions of the center.
10.1|Which of the following best defines the federating units in a true federal administrative structure?|Autonomous sub-national entities whose powers are guaranteed by the constitution rather than granted by the center|Temporary administrative zones created by executive fiat to improve tax collection efficiency|Autonomous sovereign nations that retain the constitutional right to unilaterally secede at any moment|Sub-national municipal councils responsible exclusively for local sanitation and road maintenance|Option A|Federating units in a federal system possess constitutional autonomy, meaning their existence and powers cannot be arbitrarily revoked by the central government.

7.1|How does the system of checks and balances modify pure separation of powers?|It completely eliminates any interaction between the three branches of government|It allows each branch to exercise partial oversight and restraint over the actions of the other branches|It grants supreme and unchecked authority to the legislative branch over all others|It merges the executive and judicial branches into a single administrative unit|Option B|Checks and balances introduce overlapping constitutional powers so that no single branch can act without accountability or potential resistance from the others.
7.1|Which of the following constitutional mechanisms serves as a legislative check on the executive branch?|Judicial review of administrative regulations|Executive orders bypassing parliament|Legislative impeachment and budget approval|Line-item veto by the judiciary|Option C|Parliament exercises direct checks over the executive through tools like budget approval, legislative oversight, and the power of impeachment.

7.1|Which of the following represents the primary mechanism through which the judiciary exercises a check on the other branches?|Executive pardons|Legislative censure|Judicial review|Budget appropriation|Option C|Judicial review empowers the courts to invalidate legislative and executive actions that violate the constitution, acting as a vital check.
7.1|What was the primary theoretical motivation behind Montesquieu's advocacy for the separation of powers in 1748?|To maximize economic efficiency and industrial output|To prevent the rise of tyranny through the concentration of political power|To establish a hereditary monarchy with absolute divine rights|To eliminate the need for a constitution or written laws|Option B|Montesquieu observed that when legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body, tyrannical abuse of power inevitably follows.
7.1|In a robust system of checks and balances, what is the consequence of one branch attempting to overstep its constitutional boundaries?|Automatic dissolution of the entire government|Intervention and corrective restraint by the other branches|Transfer of absolute power to the armed forces|Suspension of all civil rights and liberties|Option B|The design of checks and balances ensures that any overreach by one branch triggers constitutional counter-measures by the other branches.

9.1|What is the legal consequence if an executive agency issues a regulation that contradicts the provisions of its parent act?|The regulation remains valid until the president issues an executive override|The regulation is deemed unconstitutional and struck down under the doctrine of ultra vires|The parent act is automatically amended to reflect the new agency regulation|The regulation becomes a binding constitutional convention over time|Option B|When a rule exceeds or violates the boundaries set by the parent statute, it is ultra vires (beyond powers) and will be declared null and void by the courts.

2.1|What is the primary function of the Committee Stage during the passage of a bill into law?|Conducting a detailed, clause-by-clause technical scrutiny and amendment of the bill|Performing the final ceremonial vote before submitting the document to the judiciary|Announcing the official title of the legislation to the general public for awareness|Securing immediate executive assent from the head of state before legislative review|Option A|The Committee Stage provides an opportunity for specialized panels to carefully examine, scrutinize, and propose amendments to the bill clause by clause.
2.1|What is the primary purpose of the Report Stage in the legislative workflow?|To allow the whole house to consider the amendments and findings submitted by the committee|To conduct public hearings and gather petitions from interest groups and civil society|To grant final legislative approval through an unalterable signature by the presiding officer|To forward the draft legislation directly to international legal experts for ratification|Option A|The Report Stage brings the committee's findings and recommended amendments back to the entire house for review and adoption.
2.1|What characterizes the Third Reading stage of a bill before it is sent for executive approval?|Extensive public lobbying and introduction of entirely new amendments|Final reading and voting on the bill in its final perfected form with little debate|Preliminary reading where the clerk reads the short title for administrative records|Immediate referral of the bill to the supreme court for constitutional validation|Option B|The Third Reading is the final review stage where members vote on the perfected bill as a whole, typically without major amendments.

5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A constitution that cannot be altered under any circumstances by the legislature|A codified document containing the fundamental laws and organizational framework of a state|A collection of uncodified historical conventions and judicial precedents|A temporary decree issued by the executive branch during a state of emergency|Option B|A written constitution is a single, codified document that formally sets out the fundamental laws, powers, and structural framework of a state.
5.1|What is the defining characteristic of an unwritten constitution?|It exists entirely in oral traditions without any legal statutes|It lacks any form of fundamental law or limitation on power|It is not contained in a single codified document but derived from various statutes and conventions|It can only be amended through a violent revolution or total state collapse|Option C|An unwritten constitution is characterized by the absence of a single codified text, drawing instead from unwritten conventions, parliamentary statutes, and judicial rulings.
5.1|How is a rigid constitution fundamentally distinguished from a flexible one?|It requires a special, more difficult amendment procedure than ordinary legislation|It can be suspended at will by the head of state during a political crisis|It is permanent and completely immune to any legal modifications over time|It applies exclusively to military regimes rather than democratic systems|Option A|A rigid constitution mandates a special, complex amendment process that differs from the passage of ordinary laws to safeguard its fundamental provisions.
5.1|What is the core philosophical tenet of constitutionalism?|The belief that the judiciary should hold absolute power over the other branches of government|The requirement that all citizens must memorize the constitution to vote|The principle that government powers are legally limited by a fundamental law to protect liberties|The doctrine that the executive branch should have unchecked authority during national emergencies|Option C|Constitutionalism is the political philosophy asserting that government power must be legally limited by a fundamental law to safeguard individual rights.
5.1|Which classification best describes a constitution that can be amended through the same process as ordinary laws?|A codified constitution|A rigid constitution|A flexible constitution|An unwritten constitution|Option C|A flexible constitution does not require a special amendment procedure and can be altered by the legislature using the standard lawmaking process.
5.1|Why are written constitutions typically associated with being rigid?|Because they are printed on durable parchment that prevents physical alterations|Because they generally outline strict, specialized procedures for any future modifications|Because they prohibit the legislature from passing any new laws whatsoever|Because they are interpreted solely by the military rather than civilian courts|Option B|Written constitutions are usually designed to be rigid to prevent arbitrary or hasty changes by transient political majorities through standard legislative procedures.
5.1|Which of the following represents a primary source of an unwritten constitution like that of the United Kingdom?|Secret military decrees and presidential executive orders|Constitutional conventions, historical charters, and judicial decisions|Referendums held exclusively during national elections|Direct directives issued by international bodies like the United Nations|Option B|Unwritten constitutions rely heavily on accumulated historical customs, parliamentary statutes, judicial precedents, and constitutional conventions.
5.1|In the context of Nigerian government and politics, what is the primary function of constitutionalism?|To maximize the discretionary powers of the president over regional governments|To ensure that the ruling party remains in power indefinitely without opposition|To act as a bulwark against tyranny by legally restraining state actors and protecting rights|To replace traditional customary laws with uniform international codes|Option C|Constitutionalism serves to prevent authoritarian overreach by imposing legal limits on government institutions and safeguarding citizens' fundamental liberties.
5.1|What is a major advantage of having a codified written constitution?|It completely eliminates all forms of political corruption within the state|It provides clarity, certainty, and an accessible reference point for the limits of power|It allows the executive branch to bypass legislative hurdles during economic crises|It ensures that the constitution never needs to be amended or updated|Option B|A codified written constitution provides clear, accessible documentation of governmental powers and citizen rights, reducing ambiguity.
5.1|Which scenario best illustrates the practical failure of constitutionalism?|A legislature using a special majority vote to amend a clause in the constitution|A supreme court striking down an unconstitutional act passed by the parliament|An executive branch routinely ignoring court orders and arresting political opponents|Citizens peacefully protesting government policies within the bounds of the law|Option C|Constitutionalism fails in practice when those in power disregard legal limitations, bypass fundamental laws, and violate individual liberties with impunity.
9.1|What is delegated legislation primarily defined as in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly during plenary sessions|Executive orders and rules made by ministers or agencies under legislative authority|Judicial rulings handed down by the Supreme Court to interpret constitutional provisions|Customary laws recognized and enforced by traditional local councils|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to rules, orders, and regulations made by executive ministers or agencies using powers specifically granted to them by the legislature through an enabling act.
9.1|Which specific piece of legislation serves as the foundational legal authority that empowers an executive body or minister to create delegated legislation?|An Appropriation Act passed during the annual budgetary process|An Enabling or Parent Act enacted by the legislature|A Constitutional Amendment ratified by state houses of assembly|A Judicial Precedent established by the appellate court|Option B|An enabling or parent act is the primary statute passed by the legislature that delegates rule-making authority to an executive agency or minister.
9.1|What is the primary function of the doctrine of ultra vires in relation to delegated legislation?|To expedite the legislative drafting process within committee rooms|To ensure that executive agencies receive adequate funding for enforcement|To strike down rules or orders made by agencies that exceed the powers granted in the parent act|To mandate automatic parliamentary approval for all statutory instruments without debate|Option C|The doctrine of ultra vires empowers the judiciary to declare null and void any delegated legislation that goes beyond the powers authorized by the enabling act.
9.1|Which control mechanism involves the formal examination of delegated legislation by the legislature after it has been promulgated?|Judicial review conducted by the high court|Parliamentary review and scrutiny|Executive veto by the president or governor|Public referendum coordinated by the electoral commission|Option B|Parliamentary review allows the legislature to oversee, scrutinize, and potentially annul subsidiary laws created by executive bodies to ensure they align with legislative intent.
9.1|Why is official publication in a government gazette considered a crucial requirement for delegated legislation?|It guarantees that the executive agency receives financial grants from the treasury|It ensures legal notice and public awareness so that citizens are informed of binding rules|It automatically converts a subsidiary law into a rigid constitutional amendment|It prevents the judiciary from exercising the doctrine of ultra vires|Option B|Publication in a gazette gives formal legal notice to the public, ensuring that citizens are aware of regulations they are expected to obey before enforcement.
9.1|If an executive minister creates a subsidiary regulation that contradicts a provision in the parent act, what legal status does that regulation hold?|It automatically supersedes the parent act due to executive expertise|It remains valid until the president issues an executive pardon|It is ultra vires and can be struck down by a court of law|It becomes a binding custom after a period of twelve months|Option C|Any subsidiary regulation that contradicts or exceeds the scope of the parent act is ultra vires, meaning it is unauthorized and legally void.
9.1|Which branch of government holds the ultimate constitutional power to delegate rule-making authority to executive agencies?|The Judiciary through court directives|The Legislature through statutory enactment|The Civil Service through bureaucratic fiat|The Electoral Commission through guideline formulation|Option B|The legislature holds the constitutional power to make laws and can choose to delegate specific rule-making functions to executive bodies via enabling acts.
9.1|What is the main rationale behind the practice of delegating legislative powers to executive ministers and specialized agencies?|To bypass the judiciary and weaken the principle of separation of powers|To allow experts to handle technical details quickly without clogging parliamentary time|To permanently transfer supreme legislative sovereignty to the executive branch|To eliminate the need for any form of judicial or parliamentary oversight|Option B|Delegated legislation saves parliamentary time and utilizes the specialized expertise of executive agencies to handle complex, technical details of governance.
9.1|What terminology describes a situation where an administrative agency exercises delegated power improperly or for an unauthorized purpose?|Intra vires compliance|Delegated sovereignty|Abuse of discretion or acting ultra vires|Legislative supremacy|Option C|Acting outside the authorized scope or for an improper purpose constitutes acting ultra vires, making the administrative action legally challengeable.
9.1|Which of the following represents a classic institutional check exercised by the courts against the abuse of delegated legislation?|Withholding budgetary allocations from the erring ministry|Issuing a vote of no confidence against the cabinet minister|Conducting judicial review based on the ultra vires doctrine|Dissolving the parliament to call for fresh general elections|Option C|Judicial review is the mechanism through which courts examine subsidiary legislation and strike down any provisions that violate the limits set by the parent act.

12.1|How do pressure groups primarily distinguish themselves from political parties in a democratic political system?|They seek to directly capture and control state power through democratic elections.|They attempt to influence public policy and government decision-making without seeking elective office.|They operate exclusively within the judicial branch of government to challenge unconstitutional laws.|They rely entirely on violent and unconstitutional methods to force governmental legislative action.|Option B|Unlike political parties which aim to acquire political power through contesting elections, pressure groups focus solely on influencing government decisions and policy without seeking political office.
12.1|Which of the following best characterizes a sectional or protective interest group within a modern state?|It advocates for broad societal causes that do not directly benefit its registered membership.|It represents and defends the specific socioeconomic and professional interests of a defined membership group.|It operates spontaneously without formal structure or defined long-term objectives.|It functions as an official organ of the ruling government party to implement state development policy.|Option B|Sectional or protective groups, such as trade unions and professional associations, exist primarily to safeguard and promote the occupational or material interests of their specific members.
12.1|The Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) and the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) are classified as sectional groups because they|promote abstract moral causes that apply universally across the entire population.|organize temporary violent protests to disrupt civil order during political crises.|defend the specific material, professional, and welfare interests of their respective professions.|sponsor political candidates to win legislative seats in federal elections.|Option C|ASUU and the NBA are classic examples of sectional or protective groups because their primary mandate is protecting the welfare and professional interests of university lecturers and legal practitioners.
12.1|An organization campaigning globally for human rights protection, such as Amnesty International, exemplifies a promotional group because it|protects the exclusive economic interests of its corporate members.|advances a cause or principle intended to benefit society rather than specific members.|participates directly in electoral politics by endorsing parliamentary candidates.|emerges spontaneously in response to short-term societal crises without structure.|Option B|Promotional or cause groups advocate for broad values, principles, or social changes that benefit the general public or victimized groups rather than securing selective benefits for members.
12.1|How do anomic pressure groups differ structurally from sectional and promotional pressure groups?|Anomic groups possess highly organized bureaucratic structures and formal constitutional charters.|Anomic groups emerge spontaneously as unorganized, short-lived, and often violent collective reactions.|Anomic groups rely exclusively on professional lobbying in legislative committees.|Anomic groups represent formal corporate partnerships established by economic institutions.|Option B|Anomic groups are characterized by a lack of formal structure, spontaneous formation during intense emotion or frustration, and short-lived actions such as sudden riots or civil disturbances.
12.1|Which pressure group technique involves direct persuasive engagement with legislators, policymakers, and government administrators to shape legislation?|Picketing|Boycotting|Lobbying|Strike action|Option C|Lobbying is the direct process through which interest groups communicate with government officials to influence legislative drafts, policy decisions, and regulatory frameworks.

12.1|Picketing as a technique employed by organized labor unions involves|posting union members outside workplace entrances to inform the public and deter non-striking workers.|refusing to pay government taxes until specific labor legislation is passed into law.|mobilizing formal diplomatic sanctions against multinational corporations operating in the country.|contesting election results in tribunal courts following flawed democratic processes.|Option A|Picketing involves stationing group members outside business or government premises to draw public attention, express grievances, and dissuade others from entering during a dispute.

7.1|How does budget approval function as a check and balance within government systems?|It allows the judiciary to rewrite fiscal policies|It enables the legislature to control public funds and limit executive spending|It gives the executive absolute control over tax collection|It empowers the military to oversee fiscal legislation|Option B|By holding the power of the purse the legislature can approve or deny funding thereby checking the financial initiatives of the executive branch.|
7.1|What is the primary consequence if all three government functions are concentrated in a single body or individual?|Democratic consolidation|Increased administrative efficiency|Tyranny and absolute rule|Enhanced judicial independence|Option C|Montesquieu warned that combining legislative executive and judicial powers in the same hands inevitably leads to tyranny and oppression.|
7.1|Which of the following best captures the relationship between the separation of powers and the system of checks and balances?|They are contradictory concepts where one destroys the other|Checks and balances complement separation of powers by providing interactive controls to prevent abuse|Checks and balances replace the need for separate government branches|Separation of powers applies only to parliamentary systems while checks and balances apply to presidential systems|Option B|While separation of powers divides authority checks and balances introduce strategic overlaps and control mechanisms to ensure mutual accountability.|
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, what is the core meaning of the first principle of the Rule of Law?|The absolute supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power|The exclusive right of the legislature to make executive decrees|The subordination of parliament to judicial review|The absolute immunity of public officials from prosecution|Option A|Dicey's first principle establishes that regular law is supreme and excludes the existence of arbitrariness or broad discretionary power by the government.
8.1|Which of the following best captures A.V. Dicey's second principle of the Rule of Law?|Equality before the ordinary courts and equal subjection of all classes to the law|Special military tribunals trying civilian offenses without appeal|Immunity of government ministers from ordinary civil suits|Different legal systems for the ruling elite versus ordinary citizens|Option A|The second principle asserts that all persons, regardless of rank or status, are subject to the same ordinary law administered by ordinary courts.
8.1|How did A.V. Dicey frame the origin of individual rights under the British constitution?|As a product of ordinary judicial decisions defining the remedies of individuals|As temporary privileges granted at the discretion of the head of state|As abstract declarations enshrined in an entrenched written constitution|As entitlements derived purely from international human rights treaties|Option A|Dicey argued that individual rights in Britain are not the source of a constitution, but rather the result of judicial decisions protecting personal freedom through ordinary law.
8.1|Which provision in the Nigerian Constitution serves as a major limitation to the Rule of Law by granting immunity from prosecution to certain executive officeholders?|Section 308|Section 45|Section 68|Section 33|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants temporary immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to specific executive officers while in office.
8.1|What is delegated legislation, and why is it considered a challenge to Dicey's pure doctrine of the Rule of Law?|The power given to executive bodies to make laws, which introduces wide administrative discretion|The total absence of any legal framework governing civil servants|The direct creation of statutes exclusively by elected local government councils|The complete dissolution of regular courts in favor of tribal arbitration|Option A|Delegated legislation allows non-legislative bodies to create laws, increasing discretionary administrative powers that Dicey sought to limit.
8.1|How do military ouster clauses function as a limitation to the Rule of Law in a polity?|They explicitly strip regular courts of jurisdiction to review certain government actions or decrees|They mandate that all criminal cases be tried by civilian judges before military review|They guarantee absolute judicial independence over military tribunals|They abolish all forms of executive immunity during periods of emergency|Option A|Ouster clauses legally bar the judiciary from inquiring into the validity of specific state actions, directly undermining judicial supremacy and oversight.
8.1|During a legally declared state of emergency, what typically happens to certain fundamental rights in relation to the Rule of Law?|They can be lawfully restricted or derogated from within constitutional boundaries to restore public order|They are permanently abrogated without any possibility of future legal restoration|They become completely absolute and immune to any legislative modification|They are transferred entirely to the jurisdiction of foreign human rights courts|Option A|A state of emergency allows for authorized constitutional derogations or limitations on certain rights to address severe national crises.
8.1|Which thinker is most famous for systematically formulating the classical doctrine of the Rule of Law in the 19th century?|A.V. Dicey|Thomas Hobbes|Karl Marx|Max Weber|Option A|A.V. Dicey famously articulated the classical concept of the Rule of Law in his 1885 work 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution'.
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey strongly oppose wide discretionary authority for government officials?|Because wide discretion easily paves the way for arbitrariness and despotism|Because it makes the legal system entirely too cheap and accessible|Because it requires all administrative decisions to be ratified by popular referendum|Because it prevents the judiciary from ever interpreting a statute|Option A|Dicey maintained that wherever there is discretion, there is room for arbitrariness, which threatens individual liberty under the law.
8.1|Under Dicey's formulation, how are legal rights and constitutional liberties best secured in a state?|Through judicial remedies and the ordinary courts rather than abstract declarations|Through strict executive orders issued during political crises|Through the unilateral power of the head of state to grant pardons|Through legislative resolutions passed without judicial scrutiny|Option A|Dicey emphasized that effective remedies provided by ordinary courts are far superior for protecting rights than theoretical statements in written constitutions.
5.1|Which of the following best defines constitutionalism in the study of political science?|The absolute supremacy of the legislature over all other arms of government|The philosophy and practice that government powers are legally limited by fundamental law|The process by which a country drafts its very first independence constitution|The legal mechanism of amending unwritten codes through ordinary parliamentary acts|Option B|Constitutionalism is the political philosophy asserting that government authority is strictly limited by fundamental laws to safeguard individual liberties against tyranny.
5.1|What is the primary characteristic that distinguishes a written constitution from an unwritten constitution?|A written constitution cannot be amended under any circumstances|A written constitution is contained in a single codified document|An unwritten constitution is entirely based on religious decrees and customs|An unwritten constitution lacks any legal validity or judicial enforcement|Option B|A written constitution is codified and formally compiled into a single document, whereas an unwritten constitution is scattered across multiple statutes, conventions, and judicial precedents.
5.1|Why are written constitutions typically associated with being rigid?|They require a special, more complex amendment procedure than ordinary legislation|They can only be altered by the unanimous vote of all citizens in a referendum|They are permanent legal frameworks that forbid any form of political adaptation|They are drafted exclusively by foreign colonial masters who prohibit modifications|Option A|Written constitutions are usually rigid because changing them requires a special, demanding legislative procedure rather than the simple majority used for ordinary laws.
5.1|Which of the following is a classic example of a country operating primarily under an unwritten constitution?|The Federal Republic of Nigeria|The United States of America|The United Kingdom of Great Britain|The French Fifth Republic|Option C|The United Kingdom operates on an unwritten constitution, meaning its fundamental political rules are derived from a mix of statutes, court judgments, and constitutional conventions.
5.1|What is the primary purpose of incorporating fundamental human rights into a written constitution?|To grant absolute dictatorial power to the executive branch during crises|To establish the official state religion and suppress ideological pluralism|To legally restrict government overreach and protect individual liberties|To determine the exact annual fiscal budget of the federal government|Option C|Constitutionalism utilizes fundamental laws and bills of rights specifically to protect individual liberties from arbitrary state interference and government overreach.
5.1|Which of the following best describes constitutional conventions within an unwritten constitutional framework?|Unwritten rules and political practices that are considered binding by those in government|Permanent judicial punishments handed down to politicians who violate the law|Formal statutory enactments passed by a two-thirds majority in parliament|International treaties signed between sovereign nations regarding trade tariffs|Option A|Constitutional conventions are unwritten political customs, norms, and practices that are widely accepted as obligatory and binding upon state actors.
5.1|What is the primary constitutional consequence of a rigid constitution?|It prevents hasty, emotional, or arbitrary changes to the supreme law of the land|It makes governance completely stagnant and incapable of responding to emergencies|It allows the executive president to alter laws by mere executive proclamation|It completely eliminates the need for an independent judiciary or court system|Option A|The requirement of a difficult or special amendment procedure ensures stability by protecting the fundamental law from impulsive legislative changes driven by transient political majorities.
5.1|In the context of constitutionalism, what does the supremacy of a fundamental law imply?|All governmental institutions and officials derive their powers from and are subordinate to the constitution|The military holds ultimate veto power over all civilian laws and judicial rulings|Traditional rulers possess the legal authority to overrule the national parliament|Political parties are legally superior to the constitution that created them|Option A|Constitutionalism demands that all actions of the executive, legislature, and judiciary must conform to the fundamental law, ensuring that no branch of government is above the law.
5.1|Which of the following documents or sources would typically form part of an unwritten constitution?|A single comprehensive book ratified by a constituent assembly in 1960|Historical statutes, judicial precedents, and established political customs|Secret executive decrees issued without parliamentary knowledge or debate|International declarations that have never been recognized by domestic courts|Option B|An unwritten constitution is an aggregate of various sources, including parliamentary statutes, judicial rulings, common law, and unwritten political conventions.
5.1|How does a flexible constitution differ fundamentally from a rigid constitution?|It can be amended through the same simple legislative process used for ordinary laws|It can only be modified through a violent revolution or a national civil war|It applies exclusively to local government councils and municipal bylaws|It is never written down and exists entirely in the minds of traditional leaders|Option A|A flexible constitution does not require a special or arduous amendment procedure, meaning it can be easily amended by the legislature passing ordinary laws.
9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly through a constitutional amendment process|Rules and orders made by executive ministers or agencies using authority granted by a parent act|Judicial precedents established by the Supreme Court during constitutional interpretation|Resolutions passed by local government councils regarding customary land tenure systems|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive bodies or ministers under specific powers delegated to them by the legislature through an enabling act.
9.1|What is the primary legal instrument through which the legislature transfers law-making powers to an executive agency?|An enabling or parent act|A presidential executive order|A judicial writ of mandamus|A constitutional convention|Option A|An enabling or parent act is the foundational statute passed by the legislature that grants subordinate bodies the authority to make delegated legislation.
9.1|What is the primary function of the doctrine of ultra vires in relation to delegated legislation?|To expedite the legislative drafting process in the National Assembly|To ensure executive rules do not conflict with international treaties|To strike down subordinate rules made outside the powers granted by the enabling act|To compel civil servants to publish government policies in the national gazette|Option C|The doctrine of ultra vires empowers the judiciary to invalidate any delegated legislation that exceeds the scope or authority granted by the enabling parent act.
9.1|Which of the following is a recognized mechanism for controlling delegated legislation in Nigeria?|Internal audits by the Ministry of Finance|Parliamentary review and judicial review|Direct referendum by the electorate|Disciplinary action by the civil service commission|Option B|Control mechanisms over delegated legislation primarily include legislative oversight through parliamentary review and judicial oversight through courts applying the ultra vires doctrine.
9.1|Why is delegated legislation considered a necessity in modern governance systems like Nigeria?|It completely eliminates the need for bicameral legislatures in lawmaking|It allows experts and ministers to quickly address complex technical details without bogging down the legislature|It prevents the judiciary from ever challenging executive actions|It ensures that all laws originate exclusively from traditional rulers and local councils|Option B|Delegated legislation saves legislative time and utilizes executive expertise to handle technical and rapid details of governance.
9.1|What is a mandatory procedural requirement for most delegated legislation to ensure public awareness and legal validity in Nigeria?|Broadcasting on national television during prime time|Publication in the official government gazette|Approval by a panel of traditional monarchs|Ratification by the state governors forum|Option B|Official publication in the government gazette is a standard requirement that gives public notice and legal effect to delegated legislation.
9.1|If an administrative agency passes a regulation that directly contradicts a provision of its parent enabling act, how is that regulation classified?|Intra vires and legally binding|Ultra vires and legally void|Constitutional and supreme|Customary and unwritten|Option B|Any subordinate rule or regulation that violates or exceeds the provisions of its parent act is considered ultra vires and therefore null and void.
9.1|Which branch of government exercises the power of judicial review to strike down unauthorized delegated legislation?|The executive branch through the Federal Executive Council|The legislative branch through a special joint committee|The judicial branch through courts of law|The electoral branch through the Independent National Electoral Commission|Option C|The judiciary possesses the constitutional power of judicial review to examine delegated legislation and invalidate rules that violate the ultra vires doctrine.
9.1|What role does the legislature play after delegating its law-making powers to an executive minister?|It loses all oversight capability over that subject matter|It retains the power of parliamentary review and can amend or repeal the parent act|It acts as an appellate court for citizens complaints|It takes over the daily drafting of minor administrative circulars|Option B|Delegation does not abdicate legislative sovereignty; the legislature retains ultimate control through parliamentary review, oversight, and the power to amend or revoke the enabling act.
9.1|In administrative law, what does the term parent act signify in relation to delegated legislation?|The original constitution drafted at independence|The primary statute enacted by the legislature that authorizes subordinate rule-making|The supreme court judgment that established the separation of powers|The internal rulebook of a specific ministry or department|Option B|The parent act is the primary legislation passed by parliament that serves as the legal foundation and boundary for any delegated legislation created underneath it.

10.1|Which of the following best characterizes a federal political administrative system?|All constitutional authority is concentrated exclusively in a single central government|Power is shared through a constitutional division of powers between a central government and autonomous federating units|A loose alliance of sovereign states delegates only limited authority to a weak central government|Administrative power is entirely devolved to local municipal councils without a central authority|Option B|A federal system is defined by a constitutional division of powers that establishes both a central government and autonomous federating units like states.
10.1|In a unitary political administrative system, where does ultimate constitutional authority reside?|Distributed equally among regional and provincial governments|Concentrated entirely within the central government|Vested primarily in a loose alliance of independent states|Divided equally between local authorities and traditional rulers|Option B|In a unitary system such as those in the UK or France, all constitutional authority is concentrated at the central level.
10.1|Which of the following is a primary structural characteristic of a confederal system of government?|A strong central government with absolute authority to override state laws|A permanent union where member states surrender all rights to secede|A loose alliance of sovereign states delegating limited power to a weak center with the right to secede|A rigid constitutional division of power enforced by an independent judiciary|Option C|A confederal system consists of a loose alliance of sovereign states that grant limited powers to a weak central authority while retaining the right to secede.

10.1|Which statement accurately compares a federal system with a confederal system?|A federal system features a strong center with autonomous units, whereas a confederal system features a weak center with sovereign states holding the right to secede|Both systems concentrate all constitutional authority entirely in the central government|A federal system is a loose alliance of sovereign states, whereas a confederal system is rigidly unified by a single constitution|Both systems deny federating units or member states any legal autonomy|Option A|Federal systems empower a central government alongside autonomous units via constitutional division, while confederations keep ultimate sovereignty with the member states who maintain the right to secede.
10.1|Why might political entities choose a confederal arrangement over a federal one?|To maximize central government control over local taxation and defense|To maintain individual state sovereignty while cooperating loosely on matters of mutual concern without risking centralized dominance|To eliminate regional differences and establish a single uniform legal code|To centralize all administrative authority into a single branch of government|Option B|States choose confederation to collaborate on specific common interests while safeguarding their individual sovereignty and avoiding a powerful central government.
10.1|Which of the following administrative systems represents the polar opposite of a unitary system regarding the concentration of power?|A parliamentary republic|A confederal system where power is heavily decentralized to sovereign member states with secession rights|A presidential democracy with a bicameral legislature|A constitutional monarchy with a unitary framework|Option B|While a unitary system concentrates all power centrally, a confederal system disperses sovereignty among independent states that delegate minimal power to a weak center.
14.1|Which electoral system awards a legislative seat to the candidate who secures the highest number of votes cast in a single-member constituency regardless of whether they achieve an absolute majority?|First-Past-The-Post system|Proportional Representation system|Absolute Majority runoff system|List-system of voting|Option A|First-Past-The-Post is a plurality system where the candidate with the most votes wins, even if it is less than 50 percent of the total votes.
14.1|What is the defining structural characteristic of an Absolute Majority electoral system?|It requires a candidate to secure more than 50 percent of the total valid votes cast to win outright|It allocates seats in direct proportion to the total popular vote percentage won by each political party|It uses multi-member districts exclusively without any runoff provisions|It automatically disqualifies any independent candidate from participating in subsequent rounds|Option C|An absolute majority system requires a candidate to win an absolute majority (over 50 percent), frequently triggering a second-round runoff if the threshold is not met.
14.1|How does Proportional Representation fundamentally differ from First-Past-The-Post in translating voter preferences into legislative seats?|It links legislative seat allocation directly to the percentage of total votes won by each political party|It restricts participation strictly to two dominant political parties to guarantee stable governance|It completely eliminates the need for any form of voter registration or independent electoral commission|It relies entirely on individual candidate personalities rather than party manifestos|Option A|Proportional representation ensures that the share of seats a party wins reflects closely the proportion of total votes it received nationwide or regionally.

5.1|Which statement accurately describes the relationship between a constitution and constitutionalism?|A country with a written constitution automatically practices genuine constitutionalism|A constitution is the structural framework of government, whereas constitutionalism is the active philosophical commitment to limiting that government by law|Constitutionalism only exists in countries without any formal written legal documents|A constitution and constitutionalism are identical terms with no theoretical distinction|Option B|Having a constitution does not guarantee constitutionalism; constitutionalism requires the actual adherence to legal limitations and the protection of rights inscribed within that framework.

14.1|Which electoral system awards a legislative seat to the candidate who secures the highest number of votes cast in a single-member constituency, even without an absolute majority?|First-Past-The-Post|Proportional Representation|Absolute Majority|Alternative Vote|Option A|First-Past-The-Post is a plurality system where the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they cross the 50 percent threshold.
14.1|What is the primary defining feature of an Absolute Majority electoral system in presidential elections?|A candidate must win all votes cast across every polling unit nationwide|A candidate must secure more than 50 percent of total valid votes cast to avoid a runoff election|Seats are allocated strictly based on the percentage of popular votes won by political parties|Voters rank candidates in order of preference until a consensus is reached|Option B|Absolute majority systems require a candidate to obtain an outright majority of more than 50 percent of the votes to win outright.
14.1|How does Proportional Representation (PR) fundamentally impact party competition compared to First-Past-The-Post systems?|It eliminates the need for any independent regulatory electoral body|It ensures legislative seats are distributed to political parties roughly in proportion to their total share of the popular vote|It forces minor parties to merge with major parties before contesting elections|It restricts ballot access to only two dominant political parties|Option B|Proportional Representation allocates legislative seats according to the percentage of votes each party wins, preventing disproportionate outcomes.
14.1|What critical constitutional responsibility does the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) perform regarding candidates before an election?|Financially funding campaign headquarters for all registered political parties|Drafting and passing legislative bills governing electoral offences|Screening and clearing candidates to ensure they meet legal qualifications to contest|Appointing judicial panels to adjudicate legislative disputes|Option C|INEC is statutorily mandated to screen candidates to verify that they satisfy all constitutional and electoral requirements.
14.1|Which of the following functions falls directly under the administrative mandate of INEC during the electoral process?|Compiling, maintaining, and updating the national register of voters|Delimiting international boundaries between sovereign states|Adjudicating criminal offences committed during political campaigns|Formulating macroeconomic policies to stabilize the national currency|Option A|Voter registration and the continuous revision of the voter register are core administrative duties of INEC.
14.1|In a Two-Round system utilizing the Absolute Majority rule, what happens if no candidate achieves the required threshold in the first ballot?|A fresh election is scheduled featuring an entirely new set of candidates nominated by the judiciary|A runoff election is held between the top two leading candidates from the initial ballot|All political parties are automatically merged into a coalition government|The candidate with the plurality of votes is immediately declared the winner|Option B|When an absolute majority is not met in the first round, a runoff or second ballot is conducted between the top two contenders.
14.1|Why is the First-Past-The-Post system often criticized in heterogeneous societies like Nigeria?|It guarantees that every minority ethnic group secures legislative representation|It can lead to manufactured majorities where a party wins substantial legislative control with a minority of overall popular votes|It requires complex mathematical formulas that confuse illiterate voters|It makes the establishment of independent electoral commissions legally impossible|Option B|First-Past-The-Post often produces disproportional legislative outcomes where seat distribution does not match vote shares.

14.1|What is a major advantage frequently associated with Proportional Representation systems?|They foster high levels of political inclusion and representation for minority parties and diverse interests|They completely eradicate political corruption within legislative assemblies|They prevent the formation of coalition governments and ensure single-party stability|They eliminate the financial costs associated with conducting elections|Option A|Proportional representation ensures that diverse political groupings gain representation relative to their electoral support.
