2.1|Which of the following legislative structures is primarily characterized by having only a single chamber for law-making?|Bicameral legislature|Unicameral legislature|Plural executive legislature|Federalist legislature|Option B|A unicameral legislature consists of only one legislative chamber or house, unlike a bicameral system which features two distinct chambers.
2.1|Countries such as Nigeria and the United States operate which type of legislative structure?|Unicameral legislature|Pluralistic legislature|Bicameral legislature|Unitary legislature|Option C|Nigeria and the United States both utilize a bicameral legislative structure featuring two separate chambers, typically a Senate and a House of Representatives.
2.1|What is a primary functional advantage commonly associated with a bicameral legislative system?|Faster passage of emergency bills|Lower operational and financial costs|Enhanced institutional checks on the executive branch|Elimination of all legislative deadlocks|Option C|A key rationale for a bicameral structure is that the two chambers provide robust checks and balances on executive power and accommodate diverse societal interests.
2.1|Which of the following nations is cited as an example of a unicameral legislative system?|United States|United Kingdom|Nigeria|Israel|Option D|Israel operates a unicameral legislature known as the Knesset, consisting of a single legislative assembly rather than two separate houses.
2.1|What is the chief argument often raised in favor of a unicameral legislature over a bicameral one?|It provides deeper representation for ethnic minorities|It is typically faster and more cost-effective in passing laws|It guarantees absolute judicial review of statutes|It entirely prevents the dominance of major political parties|Option B|Unicameral systems are generally praised for being faster in decision-making and cheaper to maintain due to the absence of a second chamber.
2.1|During which stage of the law-making process is a bill formally presented to the legislature for the very first time without debate?|Second Reading|Committee Stage|First Reading|Third Reading|Option C|The First Reading involves the formal introduction and presentation of the bill to the house without any debate or detailed scrutiny.
2.1|In which legislative stage do members engage in a comprehensive debate regarding the core principles, merits, and general policy of a bill?|First Reading|Second Reading|Report Stage|Presidential Assent|Option B|The Second Reading is the critical stage where legislators debate the general principles and policy direction of the proposed bill.
2.1|Where does a bill undergo the most rigorous clause-by-clause scrutiny, technical amendment, and detailed examination?|First Reading|Third Reading|Committee Stage|Presidential Assent|Option C|The Committee Stage is dedicated to detailed, clause-by-clause examination and technical amendment of the bill by a specialized group of legislators.
2.1|What action marks the final formal step that transforms a successfully passed legislative bill into an official act of law?|Committee review|Report stage adoption|Presidential assent|Third reading vote|Option C|Presidential assent is the final constitutional requirement where the executive head signs the bill into law, completing the legislative process.
2.1|Which stage of the legislative process immediately precedes the final third reading and involves presenting the committee's amendments back to the whole house?|First Reading|Report Stage|Executive Veto|Public Hearing|Option B|The Report Stage occurs after committee scrutiny, where the committee reports its findings and proposed amendments back to the full house for consideration before the final vote.
1.1|Which of the following best defines government from an institutional perspective within the study of Nigerian politics?|The physical territory defined by fixed international borders and permanent populations|A temporary political agent responsible for formulating and executing the collective will of the state|An abstract corporate legal person possessing supreme and absolute sovereignty over a given geographical space|The total sum of all cultural norms and informal institutions that shape political behavior in a society|Option B|From an institutional standpoint, government functions as the temporary political machinery or agent created to formulate and execute the collective will of the state.
1.1|How does the concept of the state fundamentally differ from that of the government in political science?|The state is temporary and changes with every election cycle whereas the government is permanent and unchanging|The state represents a permanent sovereign entity encompassing all citizens and institutions whereas government is its transient political operator|The state is merely an executive committee of the ruling class while the government possesses absolute legal sovereignty|The state exists only in democratic systems whereas government is unique to authoritarian regimes|Option B|The state is a permanent, sovereign institutional entity, whereas the government acts as its temporary political agent or machinery.
1.1|When government is viewed as an academic discipline or field of study in political science, what is its primary focus?|Analyzing the economic output and market capitalization of private multinational corporations|Examining the processes, structures, institutions, and behavioral dynamics through which political power is exercised|Studying the ancient religious texts and cultural mythologies of pre-colonial African societies|Predicting meteorological shifts and environmental resource allocations across national boundaries|Option B|As an academic discipline, government refers to the systematic study of political structures, institutions, processes, and the exercise of power.
1.1|In the context of the art and process of governing, what does government primarily entail?|The spontaneous and unorganized social interactions of individuals in a stateless community|The deliberate practice of ruling, managing public affairs, and steering societal direction through policy implementation|The complete abolition of all legal frameworks to achieve absolute individual liberty|The exclusive accumulation of private capital by political elites without public accountability|Option B|Government as an art and process involves the practical skills, mechanisms, and activities of ruling and managing public affairs.
1.1|According to classical social contract theory, particularly associated with Thomas Hobbes, what is the primary justification for establishing a government?|To maximize individual economic profits through aggressive market competition and deregulation|To escape the chaotic, violent, and insecure conditions of the state of nature where life is solitary and brutish|To ensure the total elimination of social classes and establish a stateless communist utopia|To facilitate foreign colonial conquest and secure external territorial expansion for the ruling elite|Option B|Hobbes argued that government is necessary to lift humanity out of the chaotic and dangerous state of nature by establishing order and security.
1.1|Which of the following characteristics is unique to the state rather than the government?|Temporary tenure dependent on electoral outcomes or successful political coups|Permanent institutional existence and continuous sovereignty over a defined territory|Immediate vulnerability to dissolution during a standard legislative vote of no confidence|Subjectivity to frequent ideological restructuring and cabinet reshuffling by political parties|Option B|Unlike governments, which come and go through elections or crises, the state is a permanent and continuous sovereign entity.
1.1|What role does the government play regarding the collective will of the people within a sovereign state?|It actively suppresses the collective will to maintain absolute monarchical dominance over citizens|It formulates and executes the collective will of the state through laws, policies, and administrative agencies|It completely ignores public sentiment in favor of external international directives|It delegates all lawmaking powers directly to private corporate entities without state oversight|Option B|The core institutional function of a government is to articulate, formulate, and execute the collective will and public policies of the state.
1.1|Why is government classified as a temporary political agent relative to the state?|Because governments can be replaced through elections, revolutions, or reforms while the underlying state apparatus persists|Because government officials only work part-time hours during legislative sessions and retire permanently afterward|Because the state legally dissolves every four years requiring a completely new geographical territory to be founded|Because governments have no physical offices or bureaucratic structures and exist solely as philosophical ideas|Option A|Governments are temporary because political leaders and administrations change over time, whereas the permanent state endures.
1.1|What foundational problem of human coexistence does the Hobbesian justification for government directly attempt to resolve?|The inefficiencies caused by a lack of advanced digital technology in ancient agrarian economies|The security dilemma and perpetual state of conflict inherent in an unregulated state of nature|The bureaucratic delays experienced in modern parliamentary committee hearings|The high taxation rates imposed by decentralized federal financial institutions|Option B|The Hobbesian justification addresses the war of all against all in the state of nature, solving it through political authority and social order.
1.1|In the analysis of POL 122, when government is described as an institution, what is being emphasized?|The permanent physical boundaries that separate one nation from its neighboring countries|The concrete organizational structures, offices, and apparatuses through which public authority is exercised|The psychological mindset and political apathy of the general voting populace during elections|The historical evolution of tribal rituals prior to the introduction of modern constitutionalism|Option B|Viewing government as an institution focuses on the concrete structural framework of offices, agencies, and organs that exercise public power.

5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A document that cannot be altered under any circumstances|A codified fundamental law contained in a single authoritative document|A collection of unwritten judicial precedents and royal decrees|A set of political conventions enforced exclusively by moral pressure|Option B|A written constitution is a codified fundamental law systematically set out in a single formal document, making its provisions easily accessible and clear.
5.1|What is the defining characteristic of an unwritten constitution?|It is entirely illegal and unrecognized by international law|It exists purely as an oral tradition with no physical records|It is derived from a scattered accumulation of statutes conventions and judicial rulings|It lacks any mechanism for enforcement or judicial review|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not absent of text, but rather uncodified, drawing its authority from a mix of historical statutes, judicial decisions, and political conventions.
5.1|How does a rigid constitution differ fundamentally from a flexible constitution?|It requires a special, more difficult legislative procedure or referendum for amendment|It can never be amended or revised by any branch of government|It can be amended through the same simple majority process as ordinary laws|It applies only to military dictatorships and authoritarian regimes|Option A|A rigid constitution establishes a special, cumbersome amendment process to safeguard its core principles against hasty political changes.
5.1|What is the core philosophical focus of constitutionalism?|Ensuring absolute supremacy of the executive branch over the legislature|Limiting governmental power through a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|Centralizing all state powers in a single sovereign authority to maintain order|Prioritizing economic development over civil and political rights|Option B|Constitutionalism is fundamentally the political philosophy that government powers must be legally limited by a fundamental law to safeguard citizens' rights.
5.1|Which term describes a constitution that can be amended by the same simple legislative process used for ordinary statutes?|Rigid constitution|Codified constitution|Flexible constitution|Dogmatic constitution|Option C|A flexible constitution allows for easy amendments because it does not require special legislative majorities or referendums distinct from ordinary lawmaking.

5.1|In the context of Nigerian constitutional development, what does constitutionalism primarily seek to prevent?|Economic inflation and international trade imbalances|Arbitrary exercise of power and the abuse of governmental authority|The establishment of a bicameral legislature|Frequent changes in the national currency and tax policies|Option B|Constitutionalism seeks to prevent arbitrary governance and the abuse of state power by enforcing adherence to legal limitations.
5.1|Which term describes a constitution that is difficult to amend because it requires special legislative majorities or referendums?|An unwritten constitution|A flexible constitution|A rigid constitution|A unitary constitution|Option C|A rigid constitution is explicitly designed to be difficult to amend, protecting core principles from transient political pressures.

5.1|Why are written constitutions typically codified into a single formal document?|To ensure transparency, accessibility, and clarity regarding the structure of government and citizen rights|To prevent citizens from ever reading or understanding the laws of the land|To make future amendments entirely impossible under any circumstances|To eliminate the need for an independent judiciary or court system|Option A|Codifying a constitution into a single document ensures clarity, accessibility, and a clear point of reference for the limits of governmental power.
5.1|Which relationship best describes the connection between a constitution and constitutionalism?|They are exact synonyms representing the physical text of a legal document|A constitution is the foundational legal document, whereas constitutionalism is the active political philosophy ensuring those laws effectively limit government power|Constitutionalism is merely a historical term with no relevance to modern written constitutions|A constitution applies only to monarchies while constitutionalism applies only to republics|Option B|While a constitution is the formal legal instrument, constitutionalism represents the living ethos and practice of limiting state power through that law.

1.1|Which of the following best captures the dual nature of government as both an institution and a process?|It is a permanent sovereign legal entity and a temporary policy agency|It is a set of ruling structures and the continuous art of governing society|It is an academic discipline and a purely physical geographical territory|It is a domestic economic system and an international diplomatic treaty|Option B|Government functions structurally as an institution of the state and dynamically as the art or process of governing.
1.1|What fundamental conceptual distinction exists between the state and the government in political science?|The state is temporary and mortal while the government is permanent and immortal|The state represents the physical citizenry whereas the government represents foreign entities|The state is a permanent sovereign entity while the government is a temporary political agent|The state is an academic field of study while the government is a legalistic myth|Option C|The state is a permanent, sovereign corporate entity, whereas governments change over time as temporary agents.
1.1|From a theoretical perspective, what is the primary function of government within an organized society?|To formulate and execute the collective will of the political community|To eliminate all forms of social stratification and establish economic equality|To abolish all legal statutes and return individuals to a state of nature|To operate exclusively as a commercial enterprise for profit generation|Option A|Government exists primarily to formulate and execute the collective will and public policies of the state.
1.1|In the context of political science, how is government viewed when studied as a discipline?|As a physical infrastructure built by the ruling class|As an academic field focused on analyzing political power and statecraft|As a bureaucratic hurdle designed to restrict individual liberty entirely|As a temporary contract that expires annually without renewal|Option B|Government as a discipline refers to the academic study of political institutions, power dynamics, and governance.
1.1|Which classical philosophical concept is most closely associated with the Hobbesian justification for establishing a government?|The divine right of absolute monarchs to rule unconditionally|The absolute necessity to escape the chaotic violence of the state of nature|The complete elimination of laws to maximize personal autonomy|The inevitability of a classless communist utopia through revolution|Option B|Thomas Hobbes argued that government is necessary to escape the brutish and chaotic state of nature.
1.1|When government is conceptualized as an 'art', what does this specifically imply?|The mechanical manufacturing of public infrastructure and civil roads|The practical skill, craft, and process of managing public affairs and governing|The abstract painting of political portraits by historical figures|The aesthetic evaluation of constitutional documents in literature|Option B|Viewing government as an art highlights the practical skills, processes, and techniques involved in governing.
1.1|Why is the state considered permanent while a government is regarded as transient?|Governments can be dissolved or replaced through elections or coups without destroying the sovereign state|States are built with indestructible physical materials while governments use paper laws|States only exist during periods of war whereas governments function only during peace|Governments are eternal legal entities while states are merely temporary administrative districts|Option A|A government can change or fall through political transitions, but the underlying sovereign state persists.
1.1|Which of the following options accurately describes the role of government as an institutional framework?|It provides the formal machinery and structures through which state power is exercised|It serves as an informal social club for elite politicians to network privately|It acts as a private corporation trading goods on international stock exchanges|It operates strictly as a religious hierarchy enforcing moral doctrines exclusively|Option A|Government as an institution provides the formal structures, offices, and agencies through which state power is exercised.
1.1|According to the foundational theories of political organization, why did humans transition away from a state of nature?|To secure social order, protection, and predictability through a sovereign authority|To establish nomadic tribes that avoid permanent settlements entirely|To maximize tax collection for foreign imperial powers|To abolish all forms of rules and collective responsibilities|Option A|The transition from a state of nature to an organized government was driven by the need for security, order, and cooperation.
1.1|How does the study of government as a branch of knowledge differ from government as an institution?|As a branch of knowledge it focuses on empirical and theoretical analysis rather than wielding executive power directly|As a branch of knowledge it possesses the legal monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force|As a branch of knowledge it collects taxes and constructs public highways directly|As a branch of knowledge it consists exclusively of elected presidents and prime ministers|Option A|Studying government as a discipline involves analytical inquiry and scholarship,
2.1|Which of the following represents a primary structural justification for adopting a bicameral legislature in a federal state like Nigeria?|It eliminates the need for presidential assent in passing executive bills|It accommodates diverse interest groups and regional differences through equitable representation|It accelerates the legislative process by reducing parliamentary debate time|It reduces administrative costs by maintaining a smaller legislative assembly|Option B|Bicameralism in federal nations like Nigeria ensures that sub-national units and minority groups receive balanced representation, thereby safeguarding diversity.
2.1|What is a major administrative advantage of a unicameral legislative system over a bicameral system?|It provides a stronger system of institutional checks on executive dominance|It guarantees equal political representation for all federating units|It eliminates legislative deadlocks and reduces the financial cost of governance|It ensures more rigorous clause-by-clause scrutiny of complex bills|Option C|Unicameral legislatures feature a single chamber, making the law-making process cheaper to maintain and faster due to the absence of inter-chamber conflict.
2.1|Which pair of countries operates a unicameral legislative system as highlighted in comparative government studies?|Nigeria and United States|United Kingdom and Nigeria|United States and Ghana|Ghana and Israel|Option D|Both Ghana and Israel utilize a single-chamber parliament to streamline their legislative processes.
2.1|What key activity characterizes the First Reading stage of a bill in the legislature?|The formal presentation and introduction of the bill title without general debate|A detailed clause-by-clause scrutiny of the bill by a standing committee|A comprehensive parliamentary debate on the core principles and merits of the bill|The signing of the bill into law by the head of state|Option A|During the First Reading, the short title of the bill is formally presented to the chamber without any floor debate.
2.1|At which stage of the law-making process do legislators debate the general principles and fundamental policy objectives of a bill?|First Reading stage|Second Reading stage|Committee Stage|Report Stage|Option B|The Second Reading is dedicated to analyzing and debating the overarching principles, policy justification, and necessity of the proposed bill.
2.1|What primary function is performed during the Committee Stage of law-making?|Formal introduction of the bill to the presiding officer of the house|Final passage vote by the whole chamber before executive submission|Detailed clause-by-clause examination, expert scrutiny, and proposed amendments|Public proclamation of the bill as an active act of parliament|Option C|The Committee Stage involves specialized legislative committees conducting thorough technical examinations and proposing clause-specific modifications.
2.1|What occurs during the Report Stage of the legislative process?|The executive branch reports back to parliament on the feasibility of the proposed bill|The bill is formally read by title for the very first time on the floor of the house|Judicial review of the bill prior to final voting|The standing committee submits its findings and recommended amendments to the entire house|Option D|At the Report Stage, the committee presents its finalized findings and proposed amendments to the full house for consideration and adoption.
2.1|What is the main purpose of the Third Reading stage in the life cycle of a bill?|Final review and formal voting on the passage of the bill by the chamber|Initial introduction of the bill to the clerk of the national assembly|Detailed line-by-line review of committee recommendations|Submission of the bill to judicial officers for constitutional approval|Option A|The Third Reading allows the legislative chamber to review the bill in its final revised form and take a final vote on its enactment.
2.1|What final constitutional requirement converts a passed legislative bill into an enforceable law?|Gazetting by the Ministry of Justice|Presidential Assent|Judicial ratification by the Supreme Court|Approval by the Council of State|Option B|A bill passed by the legislative arm becomes law only when the President signs it into law or the legislature overrides a presidential veto.
2.1|How does a bicameral legislature enhance the principle of checks and balances within the state?|It centralizes law-making authority strictly within the executive cabinet|It prevents judicial review of legislative enactments|It acts as a legislative check against hasty law-making and executive overreach|It limits parliamentary debates to emergency executive decrees|Option C|A second chamber provides second thoughts on legislation, preventing hasty law-making and serving as a counterweight against potential executive dominance.

5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A constitution derived entirely from unwritten judicial precedents and historical customs|A single codified legal document enacted by a constituent assembly or legislature|A supreme body of uncodified statutes passed over centuries by royal decree|A fluid collection of conventions and traditional norms lacking any formal legal text|Option B|A written constitution is a formal, codified document containing the fundamental laws and principles of a state, usually enacted at a specific historical moment.
5.1|What is the defining characteristic of constitutionalism?|The absolute supremacy of the legislature over all executive decisions|The concentration of state power in the hands of a single autocratic ruler|The principle that governmental power is legally limited by a fundamental law|The total absence of any written legal framework within a sovereign state|Option C|Constitutionalism is the philosophical and political principle that government powers must be strictly limited by fundamental law to safeguard individual liberties.
5.1|How does an unwritten constitution primarily derive its authority and rules?|Through a single comprehensive foundational document ratified by citizens|From uncodified statutes, judicial decisions, historical conventions, and recognized traditions|Exclusively through emergency decrees issued by the head of state during a crisis|By direct international treaties signed with neighboring sovereign nations|Option B|An unwritten constitution is not codified into a single document, instead drawing its framework from a mix of statutes, judicial precedents, and historical conventions.
5.1|Which constitutional category is typically associated with a high degree of rigidity?|A written and codified constitution that requires a special, complex amendment procedure|An unwritten constitution that adapts fluidly through ordinary legislative acts|A flexible constitution that can be altered by a simple majority vote anytime|A customary constitution governed entirely by unwritten tribal practices|Option A|Written constitutions are frequently designed to be rigid, meaning they mandate special, arduous amendment procedures to protect fundamental laws from fleeting political shifts.
5.1|What is the primary purpose of limiting governmental power through a fundamental law?|To maximize state revenue extraction through arbitrary taxation policies|To protect individual liberties and prevent the abuse of state authority|To eliminate the need for any legislative branch in the governance process|To ensure the executive branch holds permanent emergency powers indefinitely|Option B|Constitutionalism establishes legal boundaries on government action specifically to shield individual rights and liberties from arbitrary state interference or tyranny.
5.1|Which of the following best describes the structural nature of an unwritten constitution?|It is entirely nonexistent and leaves the state without any legal governance framework|It is completely rigid and impossible to modify under any political circumstance|It is flexible because its core principles are found across multiple statutes and conventions|It is restricted solely to military dictatorships and absolute monarchies|Option C|Unwritten constitutions are generally flexible, allowing the political system to evolve organically through ordinary legislation and changing constitutional conventions.
5.1|Why are codified constitutions often described as rigid?|Because they prohibit all future generations from enacting any new laws whatsoever|Because they require extraordinary legislative majorities or referendums to amend|Because they are permanently sealed and can never be updated or interpreted|Because they are enforced exclusively by military tribunals rather than courts|Option B|Rigidity in a written constitution means that changing its text requires more than a simple legislative majority, often demanding supermajorities or special constituent procedures.
5.1|Which concept focuses specifically on the limitation of political power rather than just the existence of a state document?|Statutory administration|Constitutionalism|Legislative supremacy|Executive centralization|Option B|Constitutionalism goes beyond merely having a constitution, representing the active political philosophy that state power must be legally restrained.
5.1|Which of the following elements is most central to the concept of constitutionalism?|Unchecked executive discretion during peacetime|Arbitrary rule by executive decree without judicial review|The supremacy of fundamental law over ordinary government actions|The complete merging of legislative and judicial functions into one office|Option C|Constitutionalism requires the supremacy of fundamental law, ensuring that ordinary laws and government actions remain subordinate to constitutional limits.
5.1|In the context of constitutional design, what distinguishes a codified constitution from an uncodified one?|The presence of a single, systematically arranged document containing the supreme laws|The complete absence of any written rules or judicial interpretations in the state|The reliance entirely on oral traditions passed down through generations|The restriction of fundamental rights to members of the ruling political party|Option A|A codified constitution is distinct because its fundamental laws are compiled and organized into a single, authoritative written document.
7.1|Which political theorist is most famously credited with formalizing the doctrine of the separation of powers in his 1748 publication?|John Locke|Baron de Montesquieu|Thomas Hobbes|Jean-Jacques Rousseau|Option B|Baron de Montesquieu articulated the classic tripartite division of governmental powers in his 1748 work to prevent tyranny and safeguard political liberty.
7.1|According to the doctrine of the separation of powers, how many distinct functions of government are primarily identified?|Two functions|Three functions|Four functions|Five functions|Option B|The framework divides state authority into three distinct functions: legislation, execution, and adjudication, each to be exercised by separate bodies.
7.1|What is the fundamental institutional rationale for implementing a strict separation of powers within a constitutional democracy?|To increase administrative efficiency and speed up policy implementation|To prevent the concentration of absolute power and the rise of tyranny|To eliminate the need for a bicameral legislature|To ensure the judiciary controls the budget|Option B|Separating governmental functions ensures that no single body holds unchecked authority, thereby protecting citizens from tyrannical rule.
7.1|In the context of governance, which body is constitutionally entrusted with the function of adjudication?|The Executive branch|The Legislature|The Judiciary|The Bureaucracy|Option C|Adjudication refers to the interpretation and application of laws, a primary function exclusively assigned to the judicial branch.
7.1|Which governmental function is primarily responsible for formulating, debating, and passing laws?|Legislation|Execution|Adjudication|Administration|Option A|Legislation involves the formal creation, amendment, and enactment of statutory laws by a representative lawmaking body.
7.1|What mechanism allows the executive branch to reject a bill passed by the legislative branch?|Judicial review|Impeachment|Veto power|Budget approval|Option C|The executive veto is a classic check and balance tool enabling the executive to halt or send back legislation passed by lawmakers.
7.1|Which constitutional tool empowers the legislature to remove high-ranking executive or judicial officials for grave misconduct?|Veto|Impeachment|Judicial review|Budget appropriation|Option B|Impeachment serves as a legislative check on executive and judicial powers, allowing for formal charges and potential removal from office.
7.1|How does the system of checks and balances interact with the separation of powers?|It completely eliminates the boundaries between the three branches|It allows each branch to monitor and restrain the powers of the other branches|It centralizes all authority within the legislative branch|It subordinates the judiciary entirely to the executive branch|Option C|While separation of powers divides functions, checks and balances provide overlapping powers so each branch can constrain the others, preventing abuse.
7.1|Which of the following represents a judicial check on the other branches of government?|Vetoing a legislative bill|Declaring a legislative act or executive action unconstitutional|Approving executive cabinet appointments|Withholding financial appropriations|Option B|Judicial review gives courts the authority to evaluate actions by the executive and legislative branches and invalidate those that violate the constitution.
7.1|Why is legislative approval of the national budget considered an essential check and balance?|It allows the legislature to control government spending and hold the executive financially accountable|It grants the executive total autonomy over public funds|It transfers judicial authority to lawmakers|It prevents the judiciary from interpreting the law|Option A|Controlling the purse strings gives the legislature vital leverage to monitor, restrain, and shape the policy priorities of the executive branch.
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, what does the principle of the supremacy of regular law entail in a constitutional democracy?|The absolute predominance of regular law over arbitrary power and the exclusion of wide discretionary authority by the government|The legal authority of the military to override civilian legislation during a national crisis|The absolute power of the legislature to pass retroactive criminal statutes without judicial review|The supremacy of international human rights conventions over domestic constitutional provisions|Option A|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law reigns supreme and protects citizens from arbitrary, wide discretionary power exercised by rulers.
8.1|Which of the following best describes Dicey's second principle of the rule of law regarding equality before the law?|All citizens including government officials are subject to the same ordinary laws administered by ordinary courts|Government officials enjoy complete immunity from civil suits while performing official state duties|Specialized administrative tribunals must handle all disputes involving government ministries independently|Traditional rulers possess sovereign immunity that exempts them from criminal prosecution in magistrate courts|Option A|Dicey argued that no individual is above the law and everyone regardless of rank is subject to the ordinary law of the land before ordinary courts.
8.1|How does Dicey's third principle conceptualize the protection of individual rights within the British constitution?|Rights are primarily derived from and protected by judicial decisions and the remedies of ordinary common law rather than abstract declarations|Rights are solely granted through temporary legislative decrees that can be suspended at executive will|Rights are exclusively secured by embedding them in an entrenched, written constitutional bill of rights|Rights are secondary privileges subordinate to national security directives issued by the prime minister|Option A|Dicey maintained that individual rights in Britain are secured through the enforcement of common law remedies by the judiciary rather than abstract constitutional codes.
8.1|Which specific provision in the Nigerian Constitution serves as a major constitutional limitation on the rule of law by granting immunity from prosecution to certain executive officeholders?|Section 308|Section 36|Section 12|Section 45|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants absolute immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to the President Vice President Governors and Deputy Governors while in office.
8.1|How does delegated legislation pose a conceptual challenge to A.V. Dicey's strict interpretation of the rule of law?|It empowers the executive branch to create rules with the force of law bypassing direct parliamentary scrutiny and increasing discretionary power|It mandates that all judicial rulings must be approved by the legislature before enforcement|It eliminates the jurisdiction of ordinary courts over administrative regulatory bodies completely|It guarantees that citizens have absolute participation in drafting administrative guidelines|Option A|Delegated legislation transfers lawmaking power to executive bodies which expands administrative discretion and challenges Dicey's aversion to arbitrary rule-making.
8.1|What effect do military ouster clauses have on the application of the rule of law in a political system?|They explicitly strip courts of jurisdiction to review certain legislative or executive actions undermining judicial oversight|They empower ordinary magistrates to nullify unconstitutional decrees issued by military juntas automatically|They strengthen the supremacy of regular law by compelling the executive to respect fundamental freedoms|They ensure absolute equality before ordinary courts for all citizens without exception|Option A|Ouster clauses legally block courts from inquiring into the validity of specific state actions thereby restricting judicial review and weakening the rule of law.
8.1|In the context of Nigerian constitutional law, a legally declared state of emergency primarily affects the rule of law by enabling what action?|The temporary suspension or restriction of certain fundamental human rights and the expansion of executive powers|The complete abolition of the judiciary and the transfer of all judicial powers to traditional rulers|The permanent amendment of the constitution without legislative ratification or public referendum|The dissolution of all sub-national state governments and the permanent annexation of their territories|Option A|A state of emergency allows for lawful derogations from specific fundamental rights and grants broader powers to manage crises which acts as a practical limitation on the rule of law.
8.1|Which of the following represents a fundamental critique of A.V. Dicey's principle of equality before the law in modern administrative states?|Modern governments rely on specialized tribunals and discretionary administrative powers that treat public officials and regulatory agencies differently|Ordinary courts have been completely replaced by executive committees in contemporary democratic states|Administrative law systems in countries like France violate human rights by upholding absolute legal equality|Wealthy citizens are routinely executed under criminal codes while poor citizens face civil fines exclusively|Option A|Critics note that Dicey underestimated the necessity of administrative law and specialized tribunals which handle state regulatory matters outside ordinary courts.
8.1|A major criticism of Dicey's view on individual rights is that unwritten conventions and common law remedies are inadequate compared to which of the following?|An entrenched written bill of rights that explicitly guarantees fundamental liberties against legislative encroachment|A military decree system that enforces public morality through swift executive punishment|A system of administrative fiat where rights are granted solely based on economic productivity|An absolute monarchy where rights are derived from royal proclamations and religious edicts|Option A|Scholars argue that an entrenched written bill of rights provides clearer and more reliable protection for individual liberties than common law principles alone.
8.1|When evaluating the limitations of the rule of law in Nigeria, executive immunity under Section 308 is frequently debated because it can result in which situation?|Impunity and temporary shielding of key executive leaders from accountability for corruption or criminal offenses while in office|The permanent revocation of all judicial appointments made during a democratic civilian administration|The automatic transfer of legislative powers from the National Assembly to the Supreme Court|The complete elimination of federalism and the establishment of a unitary administrative structure|Option A|Section 308 prevents victims or anti-corruption agencies from prosecuting covered executive officials until they leave office which can delay accountability.
9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly through constitutional amendment|Rules and orders made by executive ministers or agencies under powers granted by a legislative act|Judicial precedents established by the Supreme Court during constitutional interpretation|Executive directives issued solely by the president without any legislative backing|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers, departments, or agencies under specific powers delegated to them by the legislature through a parent act.
9.1|What is the legislative statute known as that grants executive bodies the authority to make delegated legislation|The Enabling Act or Parent Act|The Appropriation Act and Finance Bill|The Constitution Amendment Decree|The Supreme Court Jurisdictional Statute|Option A|The Enabling Act, also referred to as the Parent Act, is the primary statute passed by the legislature that delegates rule-making authority to an executive body.
9.1|What legal doctrine allows the judiciary to strike down administrative rules that exceed the powers granted by the legislature|The Doctrine of Separation of Powers|The Doctrine of Ultra Vires|The Doctrine of Ministerial Responsibility|The Doctrine of Collective Cabinet Responsibility|Option B|The Doctrine of Ultra Vires is the legal principle used by courts to declare rules made under delegated legislation null and void if they exceed the powers authorized by the enabling act.
9.1|Which of the following is a primary mechanism for controlling delegated legislation to ensure administrative accountability|Direct impeachment of executive ministers by the electorate|Parliamentary review and publication in the official government gazette|Mandatory referendum before any ministerial rule takes effect|Abolition of the civil service after every legislative session|Option B|Control over delegated legislation is maintained through institutional safeguards such as parliamentary review of the rules and mandatory publication in the official gazette.
9.1|When an executive agency creates a rule that directly contradicts the provisions of its parent act what happens to that rule under the doctrine of ultra vires|It remains fully enforceable until the legislature explicitly amends the constitution|It is automatically suspended until the president grants executive assent|It is struck down or declared null and void by the judiciary as unauthorized|It supersedes the parent act because administrative agencies possess delegated sovereignty|Option C|Under the doctrine of ultra vires, any administrative rule that goes beyond or contradicts the boundaries set by the enabling act is illegal and will be struck down by the courts.
9.1|Why is delegated legislation considered a practical necessity for modern legislative systems like Nigeria|Because the legislature lacks the time and technical expertise to handle every minute detail of governance|Because the executive branch holds absolute sovereignty over all lawmaking processes in a democracy|Because judicial review prevents the legislature from enacting any primary laws whatsoever|Because the constitution prohibits the National Assembly from drafting laws directly|Option A|Delegated legislation allows the legislature to focus on broad policy matters while delegating technical and voluminous rule-making to specialized executive agencies due to time and expertise constraints.
9.1|What role does the official government gazette play in the administration of delegated legislation|It serves as the official public registry where new rules and orders must be published to take legal effect|It grants absolute judicial immunity to ministers who draft controversial policies|It replaces the enabling act whenever parliament is dissolved for elections|It functions as a tax collection ledger for executive administrative agencies|Option A|Publication in the official gazette is a vital control and publicity mechanism that ensures the public and affected parties are formally notified of new delegated laws.
9.1|In the hierarchical structure of laws governing delegated legislation which legal instrument holds superior authority|The administrative circular issued by the permanent secretary|The delegated rule or order created by the minister|The Enabling Act or Parent Act passed by the legislature|The internal memo of the government department|Option C|The Enabling Act holds superior legal authority because delegated legislation derives its validity entirely from the powers granted within that parent statute.
9.1|Which organ of government exercises the power of judicial review over delegated legislation in Nigeria|The National Assembly through legislative committees|The Federal Executive Council during cabinet meetings|The Judiciary through the courts|The Independent National Electoral Commission|Option C|The judiciary exercises the power of judicial review, examining delegated legislation to ensure that executive agencies do not exceed the authority granted by the legislature.
9.1|What is the primary consequence if an executive agency issues a subsidiary legislation without any statutory backing from a parent act|The rule is legally invalid and ultra vires because executive bodies cannot legislate out of thin air|The rule automatically becomes a primary constitutional provision after thirty days|The National Assembly is forced to retroactively adopt the rule as a constitutional amendment|The judiciary must enforce the rule to maintain administrative efficiency|Option A|Executive agencies possess no inherent lawmaking powers and must trace every piece of delegated legislation back to a valid enabling act, otherwise the rule is ultra vires and void.
10.1|What distinguishes a federal system of government from a unitary system regarding political power?|Powers are constitutionally divided between a central government and autonomous federating units|All authority is concentrated in a single central government with no regional devolution|Power is exclusively held by a loose alliance of sovereign states with a weak center|Sovereignty is fully retained by local municipal councils rather than a national authority|Option A|A federal system is defined by a constitutional division of powers between the central government and autonomous regional units, unlike a unitary system.
10.1|Which of the following countries is cited as a classic example of a unitary system of government?|United Kingdom and France|Nigeria and the United States|Switzerland and early historical confederations|Various federations across modern Latin America|Option A|The United Kingdom and France are well-known examples of unitary systems where constitutional authority is concentrated centrally.

10.1|Which governmental system concentrates all constitutional authority and power within a central governing body?|Unitary system|Federal system|Confederal system|Dual-mandate system|Option A|A unitary system concentrates all constitutional authority in the central government rather than dividing it among regional units.
10.1|When comparing federalism and confederalism, what is a primary difference concerning the central authority?|A federal center holds direct authority over citizens and constitutional autonomy, whereas a confederal center is weak and relies on member states|A confederal center has supreme legislative dominance over regional units unlike a federal center|A federal center depends entirely on the goodwill of states to execute laws unlike a confederal center|A confederal center possesses a monopoly on military force while federal centers do not|Option A|Federal systems create a dual citizenship and direct governance relationship, whereas confederal centers are intentionally weak and dependent on sovereign states.
10.1|Which administrative system is most susceptible to severe centrifugal pressures or complete dissolution due to the legal right of secession?|Confederal system|Unitary system|Federal system|Monarchical system|Option A|Confederal systems are inherently fragile because member states maintain sovereignty and the right to secede, leading to potential dissolution.
10.1|Under which system of government do regional or state governments derive their legitimacy and authority directly from a supreme constitution rather than central legislative grace?|Federal system|Unitary system|Autocratic system|Delegated municipal system|Option A|In a federal system, state legitimacy and power stem from the constitution, protecting them from arbitrary abolition by the center.
10.1|What is the core structural implication of establishing a unitary administrative system?|National uniformity in policy implementation and centralized legislative supremacy|Complete political independence of regional provincial assemblies|Equitable distribution of sovereign authority among equal provincial partners|A weak central administration coordinating autonomous regional units|Option A|Unitary systems prioritize centralized legislative supremacy, leading to uniform national policies across all administrative regions.

11.1|Which institutional feature ensures that a presidential executive cannot unilaterally dissolve the legislature?|The strict principle of separation of powers and checks and balances|The convention of collective responsibility among executive branch members|The absolute supremacy of parliamentary sovereignty over executive actions|The subordination of the executive branch to judicial decree and review|Option A|Separation of powers ensures that the executive and legislative branches operate independently with fixed mandates, preventing the executive from dissolving parliament.

1.1|Which of the following best defines government when viewed as an institution of the state?|The continuous academic discipline studying political systems|The permanent sovereign entity possessing a monopoly on legitimate violence|The machinery responsible for formulating and executing the collective will of the society|The informal network of citizens participating in mass civil disobedience|Option C|As an institutional framework, government refers to the organized apparatus and agencies tasked with creating, interpreting, and implementing public policies for the state.
1.1|What fundamental characteristic distinguishes the state from the government in political science?|The state is a permanent and sovereign entity while the government is a temporary political agent|The state is subject to frequent electoral turnover whereas the government lasts indefinitely|The government holds ultimate supreme authority while the state acts merely as its administrative branch|The state is composed solely of elected officials while the government encompasses the entire population|Option A|The state represents a permanent, institutionalized political community, whereas governments are transient administrations that exercise power on behalf of the state.
1.1|In the context of the conceptual dimensions of government, what does government-as-an-art refer to?|The theoretical models taught within academic political science departments|The practical process, skills, and techniques of governing and managing public affairs|The physical architecture and bureaucratic structures housing state ministries|The legal documentation defining the fundamental boundaries of territorial jurisdiction|Option B|Viewing government as an art highlights the dynamic skills, methods, and practical craftsmanship involved in the day-to-day art of ruling and steering public policy.
1.1|How is government understood when approached as an academic discipline?|As the physical infrastructure utilized by public servants to execute laws|As the historical evolution of monarchs and hereditary dynasties over time|As a systematic field of study encompassing political science, public administration, and governance|As the philosophical justification for absolute monarchy in pre-modern societies|Option C|As a discipline, government serves as an academic field dedicated to analyzing political institutions, behaviors, and administrative theories.
1.1|According to classical political philosophy, what primary condition does the institution of government seek to prevent by escaping the state of nature?|Economic inflation and unequal distribution of private capital assets|A condition of perpetual insecurity, chaos, and a war of all against all|Excessive bureaucratic red tape and over-regulation of private commerce|The complete collapse of international trade agreements and foreign relations|Option B|Thomas Hobbes argued that government is necessary to escape the brutish, chaotic state of nature where life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.

1.1|When government is defined as the machinery for formulating and executing the collective will, what is its primary societal function?|Translating societal demands and public interests into binding authoritative policies and actions|Eliminating all forms of political opposition to ensure complete ideological uniformity|Privatizing all public infrastructure to maximize corporate efficiency and profit margins|Dissolving national borders to promote a decentralized global anarchist collective|Option A|The core function of government as an institution is to articulate, aggregate, and implement the collective goals and laws binding a political community.
1.1|What role does sovereignty play in distinguishing the state from the government?|Sovereignty is an attribute exclusively possessed by the government, never the state|Sovereignty resides permanently in the state as supreme legal authority, exercised temporarily by the government|Sovereignty is shared equally among all citizens without institutional mediation|Sovereignty is a temporary privilege granted exclusively to the ruling political party during its tenure|Option B|Sovereignty belongs to the state as the supreme, independent power, which the government is merely authorized to wield on its behalf.

1.1|Which perspective emphasizes government as a dynamic process of decision-making, policy formulation, and conflict resolution?|Government as an academic curriculum|Government as a static territorial map|Government as an art or process of governing|Government as a permanent geographical feature|Option C|Viewing government as an art or process underscores the active, ongoing mechanics of managing conflict, negotiating interests, and directing public affairs.

5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A constitution that is enacted by a military dictator rather than elected representatives|A single codified document containing the fundamental laws and organizational framework of a state|A political document that cannot be amended under any circumstances regardless of public consensus|An uncodified collection of historical conventions statutes and judicial precedents without a supreme text|Option B|A written or codified constitution consolidates the core laws rules and institutional frameworks of a government into a single authoritative document.
5.1|What is a primary characteristic that distinguishes an unwritten constitution from a written one?|It is entirely immune to judicial interpretation and constitutional amendments|It is permanently fixed and cannot evolve through legislative statutes or conventions|It lacks a single codified foundational document and relies on conventions statutes and precedents|It can only be modified through a nationwide referendum involving all registered voters|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not contained in a single codified document but rather derives its authority from a mix of statutes judicial rulings and political customs.
5.1|Which of the following best describes the core philosophical essence of constitutionalism?|The total concentration of absolute legislative and executive power in a single supreme officeholder|The belief that governmental powers must be legally limited by a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|The practice of drafting lengthy legal documents that grant unlimited discretionary powers to the executive branch|The suppression of minority rights through majority rule to ensure unhindered state development|Option B|Constitutionalism is fundamentally about the limitation of governmental power through a supreme fundamental law designed to safeguard citizen liberties against arbitrary rule.
5.1|Why are written constitutions frequently associated with rigidity?|Because they require special, more difficult amendment procedures compared to ordinary legislation|Because they are permanently frozen upon drafting and can never undergo any form of modification|Because they are exclusively drafted by the executive branch without parliamentary oversight|Because they prohibit courts from interpreting legislative statutes or executive actions|Option A|Written constitutions are often rigid because their fundamental nature requires special, stringent amendment procedures distinct from ordinary lawmaking to prevent casual alterations.
5.1|Which concept refers to unwritten rules of political behavior that are considered binding by those in government despite not being codified in law?|Constitutional conventions|Executive decrees|Legislative ordinances|Judicial mandates|Option A|Constitutional conventions are unwritten political customs and practices that regulate the conduct of government officials and are widely accepted as binding.
5.1|In the context of Nigerian constitutional development, what is a primary legal advantage of a written constitution?|It eliminates the possibility of political conflict and executive overreach entirely|It provides clarity, certainty, and a definitive legal reference point for checking government actions|It automatically ensures that all citizens participate directly in the amendment process|It prevents any form of judicial review by supreme courts or tribunals|Option B|A written constitution offers clarity and transparency by serving as a clear standard against which the legality of government actions can be measured.
5.1|What does the concept of constitutionalism actively seek to prevent?|The establishment of an independent judiciary with judicial review powers|The tyranny of arbitrary power and the infringement of fundamental human rights by the state|The enactment of ordinary legislative statutes by elected parliamentary representatives|The decentralization of administrative authority to local and regional governments|Option B|Constitutionalism serves as a direct philosophical and legal check against arbitrary rule and the abuse of state power, ensuring human rights protection.
5.1|How do statutes contribute to what is classified as an unwritten constitution?|By serving as the sole source of law while completely ignoring historical conventions|By supplementing constitutional principles through ordinary legislation that lacks a single codified supreme charter|By automatically replacing all judicial precedents whenever a new government is elected|By providing temporary emergency powers that override fundamental human rights permanently|Option C|Unwritten constitutions rely heavily on ordinary legislative statutes alongside conventions and case law, since there is no single overarching foundational document.
5.1|Which of the following statements accurately contrasts written and unwritten constitutions?|Written constitutions are exclusive to monarchies whereas unwritten constitutions are unique to republics|Written constitutions are consolidated in a formal document whereas unwritten constitutions are spread across multiple sources|Written constitutions cannot be amended whereas unwritten constitutions are amended daily by citizens|Written constitutions have no legal force whereas unwritten constitutions represent supreme law|Option B|The key structural difference is that written constitutions are compiled into a single formal document, whereas unwritten constitutions draw from a decentralized body of statutes, conventions, and judicial rulings.
5.1|Which scenario best illustrates the practical application of constitutionalism within a democratic state?|The executive branch unilaterally suspending parliament to expedite urgent economic reforms|A supreme court declaring a popular legislative act null and void because it violates fundamental rights|The military taking over government functions to restore public order during a national crisis|The ruling political party abolishing opposition parties to maintain permanent electoral dominance|Option B|Constitutionalism is demonstrated when an independent judiciary uses fundamental law to check government overreach and protect individual liberties against legislative or executive violations.

8.1|Who is the renowned British constitutional theorist credited with formulating the classical doctrine of the Rule of Law?|Thomas Hobbes|A.V. Dicey|John Locke|Max Weber|Option B|A.V. Dicey popularized the formal concept of the Rule of Law in his 1885 work introducing its three core constitutional tenets.
8.1|Which of the following best describes Dicey's first principle of the Rule of Law?|Supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power|Primacy of military decrees over civil statutes|Absolute sovereignty of the executive branch|Supremacy of unwritten cultural traditions|Option A|Dicey's first principle dictates that regular law is supreme and absolute, rejecting arbitrary power, prerogative, or wide discretionary authority by the government.
8.1|Dicey's second principle of the Rule of Law emphasizes which of the following concepts?|Special tribunals for government officials|Equality before ordinary courts and law|Immunity of public servants from litigation|Different legal systems for the elite and commoners|Option B|The second principle asserts that all persons, regardless of rank or status, are subject to the ordinary law of the land administered by ordinary courts.
8.1|How does Dicey's third principle characterize the protection of individual rights in the British constitution?|Rights originate from specific constitutional enactments|Rights are granted at the discretion of the legislature|Rights are the result of judicial decisions defining individual liberties|Rights are temporary privileges subject to executive revocation|Option C|Unlike many countries with codified bills of rights, Dicey argued that English individual rights are secured through the ordinary judicial remedies and decisions of courts.
8.1|Which specific provision in the Nigerian Constitution serves as a primary limitation on the Rule of Law by granting blanket legal immunity to certain executive officeholders?|Section 308|Section 45|Section 36|Section 12|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to the President, Vice President, Governors, and Deputy Governors while in office.
8.1|How does delegated legislation challenge the absolute application of A.V. Dicey's principles?|It forces Parliament to debate every single minor rule|It allows the executive or administrative bodies to create laws with minimal direct parliamentary oversight|It mandates that all laws must originate from ordinary courts|It eliminates the need for judicial review entirely|Option B|Delegated legislation empowers non-legislative bodies to make rules and regulations, which can conflict with Dicey's view of strict parliamentary supremacy and regular law.
8.1|What effect do military ouster clauses have on the implementation of the Rule of Law?|They strengthen the jurisdiction of ordinary courts|They reinforce fundamental human rights protections|They legally bar the judiciary from reviewing specific government actions or decrees|They mandate strict equality before ordinary tribunals|Option C|Ouster clauses are legislative instruments used by military or authoritarian regimes to strip courts of their power to review executive or legislative actions.
8.1|In the context of limitations to the Rule of Law, what is a primary constitutional justification for declaring a state of emergency?|To permanently replace the legislature with the judiciary|To temporarily suspend or restrict certain fundamental rights in response to a grave national crisis|To grant lifetime tenure to executive officeholders|To abolish all forms of delegated legislation nationwide|Option B|A state of emergency allows the government to lawfully limit certain constitutional rights to preserve public safety and restore order during critical threats.
8.1|Which of the following scenarios directly violates Dicey's concept of equality before the law?|A police officer being prosecuted in an ordinary magistrate court for theft|A citizen suing a government ministry for breach of contract in a high court|A political official receiving total exemption from criminal prosecution while holding office due to statutory immunity|A judge interpreting a statute passed by the legislature|Option C|Statutory immunity prevents officials from being held accountable in ordinary courts, running contrary to Dicey's ideal of universal legal equality.
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey place strong emphasis on the role of ordinary courts rather than administrative tribunals?|Ordinary courts are believed to provide impartial protection of individual rights without favoring state authority|Administrative tribunals are historically controlled by the military|Ordinary courts have the exclusive power to write the constitution|Administrative tribunals lack judges entirely|Option A|Dicey distrusted continental administrative law systems because he believed specialized tribunals favored state bureaucrats over ordinary citizens' rights.
9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly during emergency sessions|Executive orders issued by the president without any legislative backing|Rules and orders made by executive ministers or agencies under powers granted by a parent statute|Judicial interpretations of constitutional provisions handed down by the Supreme Court|Option C|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers, departments, or agencies utilizing powers expressly delegated to them by the legislature through an enabling or parent act.
9.1|What is the primary constitutional or legal instrument that empowers executive bodies to enact delegated legislation|The National Gazette publication|The Enabling or Parent Act passed by the legislature|The executive directive of the sitting president|The judicial review mandate of the Supreme Court|Option B|An enabling or parent act is the foundational statute passed by the legislature that grants secondary rule-making authority to an executive agency or minister.
9.1|What legal doctrine is applied by the judiciary to strike down delegated legislation that exceeds the powers granted by the parent act|The Doctrine of Separation of Powers|The Doctrine of Ultra Vires|The Doctrine of Collective Responsibility|The Doctrine of Ministerial Implied Immunity|Option B|The doctrine of ultra vires empowers the courts to declare any delegated legislation null and void if the rule-making body exceeds the authority granted to it by the parent act.
9.1|Which of the following is a primary mechanism used by the legislature to control delegated legislation|Direct dismissal of executive ministers who draft poor rules|Parliamentary review and oversight of rules made by agencies|Immediate executive veto of judicial rulings on statutory interpretation|Mandatory annual public referendums on minor administrative rules|Option B|Parliamentary review serves as a crucial legislative control mechanism ensuring that executive agencies do not abuse or overstep the law-making authority delegated to them.
9.1|Why is the publication of delegated legislation in the official gazette considered an essential control mechanism|It allows the executive branch to alter the parent act secretly if needed|It provides public notice and transparency so citizens know the law they are expected to obey|It automatically transfers legislative power back to the judiciary|It prevents the application of the doctrine of ultra vires in lower courts|Option B|Publication in the gazette ensures public awareness and legal transparency, preventing secret administrative laws from being enforced against unsuspecting citizens.
9.1|If an administrative agency passes a regulation that directly contradicts a provision of its enabling act how will the courts typically treat that regulation|The courts will uphold it as a legitimate exercise of administrative discretion|The courts will refer it to the president for constitutional amendment|The courts will strike it down as ultra vires and unauthorized|The courts will demand a monetary fine from the drafting minister|Option C|Any administrative rule or regulation that violates or exceeds the boundaries set by the parent statute is considered ultra vires and will be invalidated by the judiciary.

9.1|What is the primary reason modern legislatures delegate law-making powers to executive agencies and ministers|To bypass public consultation and fast-track controversial policies completely|To reduce the legislative workload and allow experts to handle complex technical details|To weaken the power of the judiciary in interpreting commercial contracts|To ensure that executive branch officials can permanently amend the constitution|Option B|Delegated legislation allows legislatures to manage heavy workloads and lets specialized executive departments handle intricate technical regulations efficiently.
9.1|In the context of Nigerian administrative law what does the term ultra vires literally translate to or signify in practice|Beyond powers or outside the scope of legal authority|Within the strict boundaries of legislative approval|Under direct supervision of the executive cabinet|Subject to immediate parliamentary ratification|Option A|The Latin term ultra vires means beyond powers, signifying that an administrative agency has acted outside the legal boundaries established by its parent act.
9.1|Which of the following best illustrates a failure of administrative control over delegated legislation|An agency enacting a rule without the required publication in the official gazette and parliamentary review|A minister consulting heavily with industry stakeholders before drafting technical standards|The Supreme Court striking down a regulation that clearly violated the parent act|The legislature explicitly revoking a delegated power through a subsequent amendment act|Option A|Failing to publish rules in the gazette or submit them for parliamentary review undermines transparency and legal accountability, representing a breakdown in procedural controls.

2.1|At which stage of the law-making process do legislators primarily debate the general principles, policy merits, and philosophy of a proposed bill?|Committee Stage|First Reading|Second Reading|Report Stage|Option C|The Second Reading is the critical juncture where members debate the broader policy direction, principles, and general merits of the bill rather than getting bogged down in clause-by-clause details.
2.1|What is the core function of the Committee Stage during the legislative passage of a bill?|Conducting the final ceremonial vote for constitutional validation|Thorough scrutiny, detailed investigation, and possible amendment of individual clauses|Presenting the bill for the first time to the entire chamber floor|Obtaining the mandatory executive assent from the president|Option B|The Committee Stage involves intensive examination, expert input, and clause-by-clause analysis to refine the technical aspects of the bill before it returns to the main floor.
2.1|Which stage directly follows the Committee Stage in the standard progression of a bill becoming law?|Third Reading|Presidential Assent|Report Stage|First Reading|Option C|After the committee finishes its rigorous examination and amendments, the bill moves to the Report Stage where the house reviews the committee's findings and recommended changes.
2.1|What characterizes the Third Reading stage of a bill in the legislature?|The formal introduction of a brand new legislative proposal|The final debate and voting on the bill in its refined form before final passage|The assignment of the bill to a specialized ad-hoc investigatory panel|The initial public hearing involving civil society organizations and interest groups|Option B|The Third Reading represents the final review and definitive vote on the bill as a complete package, confirming whether it clears the legislative assembly for executive action.
2.1|What is the final constitutional requirement for a successfully passed bill from the legislature to officially become operational law in Nigeria?|Judicial ratification by the Supreme Court|Referendum approval by a simple majority of citizens|Presidential Assent or override of a veto|Gazetting by the international diplomatic council|Option C|A bill passed by the legislature only attains the full force of law after receiving Presidential Assent, unless the legislature constitutionally overrides a presidential veto.
2.1|Why is a bicameral structure considered particularly valuable in federal states like Nigeria and the United States?|It completely removes the need for an independent judiciary or executive branch|It ensures that law-making is restricted exclusively to traditional rulers and elites|It provides an institutional framework to accommodate regional diversity and check executive overreach|It speeds up legislative business by avoiding redundant debates between houses|Option C|Federal systems use bicameralism to balance population-based representation with equal regional representation, simultaneously creating institutional checks against executive concentration of power.
