5.1|Which of the following best defines a written constitution?|A document that cannot be altered under any circumstances by the legislature|A constitution whose provisions are entirely derived from unwritten historical customs|A formal, codified document containing the fundamental laws and institutional frameworks of a state|An uncompiled collection of judicial rulings and parliamentary statutes only|Option C|A written constitution is a single, codified document that deliberately outlines the fundamental laws, powers, and structural frameworks of government.
5.1|What distinguishes an unwritten constitution from a written one?|It lacks any legal framework entirely and relies solely on the whims of current rulers|It is composed of a collection of statutes, judicial precedents, and constitutional conventions rather than a single codified document|It can only be amended through a violent revolution rather than legislative processes|It prohibits citizens from exercising basic democratic rights and freedoms|Option B|An unwritten constitution is not codified into a single document but is instead found across various statutes, judicial decisions, and entrenched political conventions.
5.1|Which type of constitution typically requires a special, complex legislative procedure for amendment?|A flexible constitution|An unwritten constitution|A rigid constitution|A unitary constitution|Option C|A rigid constitution demands special, rigorous amendment procedures—such as supermajorities or referendums—to safeguard its fundamental provisions from hasty changes.
5.1|What is the core philosophical meaning of constitutionalism?|The absolute supremacy of the monarch over all state institutions|The principle that government powers are legally limited by a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|The complete concentration of executive and legislative authority in a single office|The subordination of the judiciary to the executive branch during national emergencies|Option B|Constitutionalism is the political philosophy asserting that government power must be legally bounded and restrained by a supreme law to safeguard citizens' rights.
5.1|In the context of constitutional design, what is a primary characteristic of a flexible constitution?|It can be amended through the same simple majority process used for ordinary laws|It can never be altered once it is enacted by the founding fathers|It requires the approval of all regional states before any single word can change|It exists purely as a set of unwritten moral guidelines without legal force|Option A|A flexible constitution does not require special amendment hurdles and can be modified through the standard legislative process for ordinary statutes.
5.1|Which element is least likely to form part of an unwritten constitution?|Parliamentary statutes|Judicial precedents|Constitutional conventions|A single comprehensive foundational charter text|Option D|A single comprehensive foundational charter text defines a written or codified constitution, whereas unwritten constitutions are piecemeal and uncodified.
5.1|Why do modern democratic states often prefer a rigid, written constitution?|To ensure that executive leaders can alter fundamental laws overnight during crises|To provide legal certainty and prevent arbitrary exercises of power by temporary majorities|To eliminate the need for an independent judiciary or courts of law|To guarantee that political parties never alternate in power through elections|Option B|A rigid, written constitution provides stability and clear legal boundaries, preventing fleeting political majorities from easily eroding fundamental rights.
5.1|How do constitutional conventions function within the framework of an unwritten constitution?|They are legally enforceable rules written directly into penal codes|They are binding political customs and practices that are widely accepted and observed despite lacking formal codification|They are temporary executive decrees issued during economic depressions|They are foreign treaties that override domestic legislation automatically|Option B|Constitutional conventions are unwritten political rules and traditions that carry normative weight and regulate governmental behavior effectively.

5.1|What is the primary legal consequence of having a codified constitution?|All citizens are automatically granted lifetime immunity from criminal prosecution|The fundamental laws of the land are clearly ascertainable in a single authoritative document, minimizing ambiguity|The legislature becomes permanently supreme over both the executive and the judiciary|Parliament is relieved of the duty to pass any new laws ever again|Option C|Codification ensures that constitutional provisions are explicitly written down in a master document, providing clear benchmarks for judicial review and governance.

7.1|Why did Montesquieu emphasize that the legislative and executive powers should never be concentrated in the same person or body?|Because combined powers inevitably destroy political liberty and lead to arbitrary laws|Because it causes administrative delays in the execution of emergency decrees|Because it reduces the state tax revenue collection efficiency|Because it prevents the judiciary from issuing injunctions against corporations|Option A|Montesquieu maintained that if legislative and executive powers are united, there can be no political liberty because tyrannical laws could be enacted and executed arbitrarily.

8.1|Dicey's first principle of the Rule of Law refers to which of the following concepts?|Absolute supremacy of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary or wide discretionary power|The complete elimination of parliament's power to make laws|The total subordination of the judiciary to executive decrees|The supremacy of military tribunals over civil courts|Option A|The first principle establishes that law rules supreme and protects citizens against the exercise of arbitrary, wide, or discretionary executive power.|
8.1|What does A.V. 9.1|What is the primary function of an enabling or parent act in the creation of delegated legislation|To repeal existing constitutional clauses that restrict executive rulemaking powers|To grant specific legal authority and guidelines to executive agencies or ministers to make subsidiary laws|To allow the judiciary to bypass legislative review of emergency executive proclamations|To mandate local governments to collect taxes without legislative oversight from the National Assembly|Option B|An enabling or parent act is the foundational statute passed by the legislature that grants and defines the legal boundaries of power for executive rule-making.

9.1|Why is official publication in a government gazette legally significant for delegated legislation|It transfers ownership of the executive agency to the legislature for auditing purposes|It ensures that subsidiary laws are publicly known and accessible before they can affect citizens' rights|It automatically amends the national constitution to reflect the new executive policy|It exempts the implementing agency from any form of future judicial review|Option B|Publication in the government gazette provides formal legal notice to the public, ensuring transparency and that citizens are aware of the binding rules.

9.1|Which of the following bodies is primarily responsible for drafting delegated legislation in day-to-day governance|The Supreme Court of Nigeria during appellate sessions|Executive ministries, departments, agencies, and specialized ministers|State governors acting without legislative authorization or executive councils|Private legal practitioners registered with the Nigerian Bar Association|Option B|Delegated legislation is formulated by executive branch entities such as ministries and agencies because the legislature lacks the time and technical expertise for detailed rulemaking.
9.1|What is a major justification for the widespread use of delegated legislation in modern democratic governance|It completely eliminates the need for parliamentary elections and legislative sessions|It saves parliamentary time and allows experts to handle technical details of complex public policies|It prevents courts from ever interfering in executive policymaking or financial budgets|It ensures that all laws are permanent and can never be repealed or modified by future administrations|Option B|Delegated legislation relieves the legislature of heavy workloads and utilizes administrative expertise for technical and fast-moving policy areas.

1.1|Why is the Hobbesian state of nature considered undesirable by political theorists?|It guarantees excessive taxation without political representation|It leads to perpetual conflict and insecurity where life is solitary and brutish|It creates an overbearing bureaucracy that stifles individual economic freedom|It forces citizens into compulsory military service for foreign expansion|Option B|Hobbes characterized the state of nature as a condition of constant war and insecurity, making the establishment of government necessary for survival.
1.1|Which of the following captures the dual nature of government as both a structure and an activity?|A permanent territory and a temporary population|An institutional framework and the process of ruling|An academic syllabus and a legislative chamber|A sovereign entity and a subordinate municipality|Option B|Government encompasses both the structural institutions that exist and the active processes and arts of ruling a political community.
1.1|What primary role does institutionalized government play regarding the collective will of society?|It suppresses public opinion to maintain complete bureaucratic autonomy|It formulates and executes that collective will into enforceable public policy|It completely replaces the need for any formal constitution or laws|It restricts political participation exclusively to academic researchers|Option B|Government serves as the primary mechanism through which the collective will of the society is formally articulated and executed.
2.1|Which stage of the law-making process in a parliament is primarily dedicated to debating the general principles and broad philosophy of a bill rather than its specific clauses?|First Reading|Second Reading|Committee Stage|Third Reading|Option B|The Second Reading is the stage where lawmakers engage in general debate regarding the overarching principles, aims, and merits of a proposed bill.
2.1|A major comparative advantage of a bicameral legislature over a unicameral legislature in a federal state like Nigeria is that it|eliminates the financial costs of running a parliament|prevents executive dominance while providing representation for diverse sub-national groups|accelerates the speed of passing urgent socio-economic bills|ensures single-chamber supremacy over judicial appointments|Option B|Bicameralism accommodates societal diversity by offering equal regional or state representation in the upper chamber while acting as an institutional check on executive power.
2.1|In which phase of the legislative process is a bill subjected to detailed, line-by-line scrutiny, expert evaluation, and potential clause amendments?|First Reading|Report Stage|Committee Stage|Presidential Assent|Option C|During the Committee Stage, legislative committees thoroughly analyze the specific details, technicalities, and clauses of a bill, often inviting expert testimony and recommending amendments.
2.1|What key institutional characteristic distinguishes a unicameral legislative system, such as that found in Ghana, from a bicameral system?|It operates with two equal law-making chambers|It consists of a single legislative assembly responsible for all law-making|It transfers all legislative functions to the judiciary|It automatically bypasses the need for executive assent|Option B|Unicameralism is characterized by a single-chamber legislative body that performs all law-making and supervisory functions without an upper house.
2.1|The formal introduction of a bill into the legislature, involving the reading of its short title by the clerk without general debate, occurs at the|First Reading|Report Stage|Third Reading|Committee Stage|Option A|The First Reading is a purely procedural stage where the title of the bill is read aloud to formally introduce it to the legislative house.
2.1|Why might a nation with limited financial resources and an urgent need for swift policy execution choose a unicameral legislative structure over bicameralism?|Unicameral systems are less costly to run and process legislation faster by avoiding inter-chamber deadlocks|Unicameral systems give state governments veto power over national law-making|Unicameral systems guarantee that every ethnic group receives equal representation|Unicameral systems remove the requirement for presidential assent on money bills|Option A|Unicameral legislatures reduce operational expenses by maintaining only one chamber and streamline the legislative process by eliminating delays caused by dual-chamber debates.
2.1|At the Report Stage of the law-making process, what is the primary activity of the legislative chamber?|The initial formal presentation of the bill's short title by the clerk|The deliberation on amendments and recommendations submitted by the committee|The final voting on the entire bill without any further debates|The signing of the bill into law by the head of state|Option B|During the Report Stage, the committee submits its findings and proposed amendments back to the whole house for consideration and legislative approval.
2.1|A key argument often raised by political theorists against unicameralism is that a single legislative chamber|lacks the structural safeguards to prevent hasty legislation and tyranny of the majority|is inherently incapable of enacting public policy during national emergencies|always requires approval from an un-elected upper house before passing laws|creates constitutional deadlocks with the judiciary on constitutional interpretation|Option A|Without an upper house to review and delay proposed measures, unicameral legislatures risk passing rash, unconsidered laws driven by temporary majority sentiments.
2.1|What final procedural step is required for a bill passed by both legislative chambers in Nigeria to officially become an enforceable act of parliament?|Judicial Review|Presidential Assent|Gazetting by the First Reading Committee|Approval by the Council of State|Option B|Presidential Assent is the final stage where the executive head signs the passed bill, formally enacting it into a valid law.
2.1|During the Third Reading of a bill in parliament, the legislative chamber focuses primarily on|introducing major structural revisions and new amendments|debating the detailed provisions inside committee rooms|performing a final review and voting on the definitive text of the bill|soliciting public petitions and external legal opinions|Option C|The Third Reading is the final legislative stage where lawmakers perform a ultimate review of the finalized bill and vote on its passage into law without introducing major amendments.

3.1|Which of the following best defines the core structural difference between presidential and parliamentary executives?|The fusion versus separation of executive and legislative powers and the nature of the executive office|The total absence of laws in parliamentary systems compared to presidential systems|The complete subordination of the judiciary to the executive in single systems|The restriction of military command to the legislature in dual systems|Option A|Presidential systems feature a single executive with a separation of powers, whereas parliamentary systems feature a dual executive with a fusion of powers.

3.1|Which executive function involves negotiating treaties, appointing ambassadors, and representing the state internationally?|Conducting diplomacy|Commanding the military|Exercising the prerogative of mercy|Enforcing domestic criminal codes|Option A|Conducting diplomacy is an essential executive power concerning foreign relations, treaty-making, and international representation.
3.1|What is a primary vulnerability or criticism often leveled against a single executive system?|It risks leading to authoritarianism or political deadlock due to concentrated power|It completely eliminates any form of checks and balances from the judiciary|It prevents the executive from ever commanding the armed forces|It dissolves the distinction between domestic and foreign policy|Option A|Concentrating both Head of State and Head of Government roles in a single person can sometimes lead to excessive personal power or severe gridlock with the legislature.

3.1|Which of the following is classified strictly as a routine executive function rather than a judicial or legislative one?|Executing and enforcing enacted laws|Drafting and finally passing primary statutes|Adjudicating constitutional disputes between states|Interpreting the statutory meaning of penal codes|Option A|The fundamental role of the executive branch is the execution, administration, and enforcement of laws passed by the legislature.
4.1|Which of the following best defines the primary constitutional role of the judiciary within the Nigerian state framework?|Enforcing executive policy directives and administering legislative budgets|Interpreting the constitution and laws alongside the adjudication of disputes|Drafting primary legislation and decreeing emergency administrative measures|Managing the internal revenue service and auditing federal accounts|Option B|The core constitutional mandate of the judiciary is to interpret the constitution and statutory laws while impartially adjudicating legal disputes between entities.
4.1|What institutional mechanism empowers the Nigerian judiciary to declare legislative acts or executive actions unconstitutional and void?|Judicial Review|Executive Veto|Legislative Oversight|Electoral Mandate|Option A|Judicial review is the specific constitutional power possessed by the courts to examine legislative and executive actions and declare them null if they violate the constitution.
4.1|Which of the following institutional provisions is primarily designed to guarantee the financial autonomy and independence of the Nigerian judiciary?|Consolidated revenue salaries|Direct presidential grants|Voluntary legislative donations|Annual executive appropriations based on performance|Option A|Consolidated revenue salaries ensure that judicial officers receive guaranteed remuneration directly from the public treasury, shielding them from executive financial manipulation.

4.1|What is the principal constitutional body responsible for insulating the appointment, discipline, and promotion of Nigerian judges from external political interference?|National Judicial Council|Federal Executive Council|National Assembly Committee on Justice|Nigerian Bar Association Directorate|Option A|The National Judicial Council (NJC) is constitutionally empowered to handle judicial appointments, promotions, and discipline to safeguard judicial independence.
4.1|When a court exercises the power of judicial review to invalidate an unconstitutional statute, what is the legal status of that statute?|It remains valid only for civil cases|It is rendered completely null and void|It is suspended pending legislative amendment|It requires a referendum to become completely inactive|Option B|An unconstitutional statute declared void through judicial review loses all legal force and cannot be enforced by any arm of government.
4.1|Which of the following poses the most direct structural threat to judicial independence in a presidential system?|Executive control over judicial appointments and capital budgeting|Judicial participation in alternative dispute resolution|Frequent citation of foreign case law by supreme court justices|Public scrutiny of judicial rulings by academic researchers|Option A|When the executive branch wields unchecked control over judicial appointments and funding budgets, the impartiality of the judiciary is severely compromised.
4.1|In the context of Nigerian constitutionalism, the adjudication of disputes involves which of the following processes?|Resolving legal conflicts between individuals or between government organs impartially|Arbitrating trade union disputes through compulsory binding arbitration only|Mediating international border conflicts without reference to domestic law|Issuing executive orders to settle political impasses between governors|Option A|Adjudication refers to the legal process where courts hear and settle disputes impartially between citizens, corporations, or levels of government based on law.
4.1|Why are consolidated revenue fund allocations considered superior to annual budgetary votes controlled by the executive for judicial funding?|They bypass executive discretion, preventing financial starvation as a tool of political control|They allow judges to invest public funds in private commercial enterprises|They automatically increase judicial salaries based on inflation rates without legislation|They permit courts to collect direct taxes from litigants to fund operations|Option A|Funding through consolidated revenue funds prevents the executive from using budget withholding or cuts as leverage to influence judicial decisions.
4.1|Which theoretical principle underpins the separation of powers and justifies an independent judiciary checking the legislative and executive arms?|Checks and balances|Democratic centralism|Administrative centralization|Unitary supremacy|Option A|The doctrine of checks and balances ensures that each branch of government has specific powers to limit the others, maintaining constitutional equilibrium and preventing tyranny.
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey, what does the first principle of the rule of law primarily entail?|Absolute supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power|The supremacy of military decrees over civilian legislation|Immunity of public officials from ordinary legal processes|Supremacy of delegated legislation over parliamentary statutes|Option A|Dicey's first principle establishes that regular law is supreme and excludes the existence of arbitrary or wide discretionary powers of government.|
8.1|Which concept is a core pillar of A.V. 8.1|How did A.V. Dicey frame the third principle concerning the protection of individual rights?|Rights are granted exclusively through executive policy statements|Constitutional rights are the result of judicial decisions defining individual liberties|Rights exist only when suspended during a state of emergency|Individual liberties are derived solely from international treaties|Option C|Dicey argued that in countries like Britain, individual rights are the result of judicial decisions rather than abstract constitutional declarations.|
8.1|Which Nigerian constitutional provision directly constitutes a limitation to the rule of law by granting immunity from prosecution to certain executive officeholders?|Section 308|Section 45|Section 36|Section 12|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants absolute immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to the President, Vice President, Governors, and Deputy Governors while in office.|
8.1|In the context of the limitations to the rule of law, what does a military ouster clause typically seek to achieve?|To expand the jurisdiction of ordinary courts over military decrees|To prevent the judiciary from reviewing actions taken by a military or authoritarian government|To protect individual fundamental human rights from legislative abridgement|To enforce strict adherence to Dicey's equality before the ordinary courts|Option B|Ouster clauses are legislative or decree provisions designed to strip courts of their jurisdiction to review specific executive or governmental actions.|
8.1|How does delegated legislation pose a potential challenge to A.V. Dicey's conception of the rule of law?|It eliminates the need for any legislative body entirely|It concentrates broad law-making power within the executive branch, risking arbitrary power|It ensures that all laws are debated openly in ordinary courts of law|It forces judges to draft legislation instead of resolving disputes|Option B|Delegated legislation transfers rule-making authority to administrative bodies, which Dicey viewed with caution due to the potential expansion of discretionary power.|
8.1|During a legally declared state of emergency in Nigeria, what typically happens to certain fundamental rights under the framework of rule of law limitations?|They become completely absolute and immune from any restriction|They can be lawfully restricted or derogated from in accordance with constitutional procedures|They are permanently abolished from the legal system|They are transferred entirely to the jurisdiction of traditional rulers|Option B|A state of emergency allows the state to lawfully derogate from specific fundamental human rights to address national security crises, serving as a legal limitation.|
8.1|Which of the following best describes A.V. Dicey's view on the relationship between ordinary law and executive discretion?|Executive discretion must be wide and unrestricted by judicial oversight|Arbitrary power and wide discretionary authority are antithetical to the supremacy of regular law|Discretionary power should always supersede statutory law in times of peace|Executive authority should have higher legal standing than judicial rulings|Option B|Dicey strictly opposed wide discretionary authority, maintaining that where there is discretion there is room for arbitrariness, which undermines the rule of law.|
8.1|Which arm of government is primarily responsible for upholding Dicey's principle of equality before ordinary courts?|The Executive branch|The Legislature|The Judiciary|The Civil Service|Option C|The judiciary acts as the impartial arbiter ensuring that both ordinary citizens and public officials are judged by the same ordinary courts under the same laws.|
8.1|Which scenario represents a direct violation of A.V. 9.1|What is delegated legislation primarily defined as|Laws enacted directly by the legislature during constitutional emergencies|Executive orders issued by the president without any legislative backing|Rules and orders made by executive ministers and agencies using powers delegated by the legislature|Judicial interpretations applied by courts to resolve constitutional disputes|Option C|Delegated legislation refers to laws, rules, and orders created by executive ministers or administrative agencies under specific powers granted to them by the legislature.
9.1|Which legal instrument serves as the fundamental foundation authorizing an executive agency to enact delegated legislation|An executive presidential decree|An Enabling or Parent Act passed by the legislature|A judicial precedent established by the Supreme Court|A constitutional amendment ratified through a national referendum|Option B|An Enabling or Parent Act is the legislative statute that delegates lawmaking authority to an executive body, defining the boundaries within which rules can be made.
9.1|What is the legal consequence when an executive agency enacts a delegated rule that exceeds the powers granted by its Parent Act|The rule is automatically adopted as a constitutional amendment|The rule undergoes mandatory legislative debate before taking effect|The rule is declared null and void by the judiciary under the doctrine of ultra vires|The executive agency is dissolved by legislative resolution|Option C|Under the doctrine of ultra vires, any delegated legislation that goes beyond the scope or authority granted by the Parent Act is deemed unauthorized and struck down by the courts.
9.1|Which control mechanism involves the formal scrutiny of delegated rules by the lawmaking body before or after they take effect|Judicial review|Parliamentary review|Executive vetting|Public referendum|Option B|Parliamentary review is the legislative oversight mechanism used to examine, approve, or annul rules made under delegated powers.

9.1|How does the doctrine of ultra vires function as a control mechanism over administrative agencies|It empowers the president to veto parliamentary statutes at will|It allows citizens to vote on administrative policies directly|It enables courts to strike down unauthorized or excess executive regulations|It requires all executive ministers to stand for regular legislative elections|Option C|The doctrine of ultra vires acts as a judicial check, ensuring executive agencies do not exceed the boundaries or authority conferred upon them by the legislature.

9.1|Which phrase best describes the nature of power exercised when a minister issues subsidiary regulations under a Parent Act|Absolute and unchallengeable executive sovereignty|Original legislative authority derived directly from the electorate|Derivative and conditional lawmaking authority subject to statutory limits|Temporary emergency power that supersedes the national constitution|Option C|Delegated powers are derivative and conditional because they stem entirely from the Parent Act and must remain strictly within its authorized limits.

10.1|What primary weakness is most commonly associated with a confederal system of government?|Excessive bureaucratic red tape and over-centralization of economic planning|An overly powerful central executive that easily overrides regional autonomy|A weak central government that struggles to enforce policies or maintain collective defense uniformly|Rigid constitutional amendments that prevent any form of intergovernmental cooperation|Option C|Confederal systems inherently feature a weak central authority because member states retain sovereignty, making centralized enforcement and collective action difficult.
10.1|Which governmental model is best designed to manage deep ethnic, linguistic, or geographic diversity within a single multinational state?|A unitary system with strict administrative uniformity|A confederal system restricted purely to economic tariffs|A federal system with constitutionally guaranteed autonomy for regional units|An absolute monarchy with centralized prefectures|Option C|Federal systems are specifically designed to accommodate diverse populations by allowing regional autonomy and self-governance over local matters.
10.1|Under which political system does the central government reserve the legal right to unilaterally create or abolish lower-level administrative divisions?|Federal system|Confederal system|Unitary system|Dual-sovereignty system|Option C|In a unitary system, local or regional governments exist entirely at the pleasure of the central government, which can create, alter, or abolish them at will.
10.1|Which feature distinguishes a confederation from a federation?|Federations feature a supreme central constitution dividing powers, whereas confederations are formed by treaties among sovereign states|Federations lack any form of centralized executive body altogether|Confederations possess superior military forces compared to federations|Federations allow unconditional secession at any moment by any member state|Option A|A federation is bound by a supreme constitution dividing power, while a confederation is typically established through a treaty among independent sovereign states.
10.1|If a regional state within a country attempts to secede and the central government invokes constitutional supremacy to legally block it, which system is most likely being practiced?|Confederal system|Federal system with strong central authority or a unitary system|Alliance system of independent nations|Purely international treaty organization|Option B|Federal and unitary systems uphold central legal authority and generally reject the unilateral right of secession, unlike confederations where member states retain that right.
10.1|Which structural descriptor best characterizes the distribution of power in the United Kingdom?|Confederal model with decentralized administrative units|Unitary model where parliament holds supreme authority over local governments|Federal model with entrenched constitutional powers for Scotland and Wales|Sovereign alliance model based on an international treaty|Option B|The United Kingdom operates as a unitary state where Parliament is supreme and can devolve or reclaim powers from regional bodies like the Scottish Parliament at any time.
9.1|Which of the following best defines delegated legislation in the context of Nigerian government and politics?|Laws enacted directly by the National Assembly during plenary sessions|Rules and orders made by executive bodies or ministers under legislative authorization|Judicial precedents established by the Supreme Court on constitutional matters|Decrees promulgated solely by military heads of state without civilian input|Option B|Delegated legislation refers to rules, regulations, and orders formulated by executive ministers or agencies using specific powers delegated to them by the legislature through an enabling act.
9.1|What is the legal instrument or statute passed by the legislature that grants executive agencies the authority to make delegated legislation?|An appropriation ordinance|An enabling or parent act|A judicial writ of mandamus|A presidential executive order|Option B|An enabling or parent act is the primary legislation passed by parliament that empowers executive bodies to create subordinate laws and regulations.
9.1|Under the doctrine of ultra vires, what happens when a delegated legislation exceeds the powers granted by the parent act?|It is automatically adopted as a constitutional amendment|It becomes a binding customary law after a grace period|It is declared null and void by the judiciary|It must be renegotiated through a referendum|Option C|The doctrine of ultra vires empowers the courts to strike down any subordinate rule or regulation that goes beyond the scope or authority conferred by the enabling act.
9.1|Which of the following control mechanisms ensures that the public and affected citizens are adequately notified of new delegated legislation?|Publication in the official government gazette|A mandatory public debate on national television|Direct ballot voting by the electorate|Endorsement by traditional traditional rulers|Option A|Official publication in the government gazette is a critical administrative control and requirement ensuring transparency and public notice of statutory instruments.
9.1|Which branch of government exercises ultimate oversight over delegated legislation by reviewing and potentially annulling unauthorized administrative rules?|The executive cabinet|The judiciary through judicial review|The civil service commission|The electoral commission|Option B|The judiciary exercises oversight through judicial review, applying doctrines like ultra vires to invalidate administrative actions or delegated laws that violate statutory limits.
9.1|Why do modern legislatures increasingly delegate lawmaking powers to executive ministries and specialized agencies?|To bypass the constitutional requirement for executive assent|To handle complex, technical issues and save parliamentary time|To permanently transfer supreme legislative sovereignty to bureaucrats|To eliminate the need for any judicial oversight in governance|Option B|Delegation allows specialized executive bodies to manage complex technical details efficiently, relieving the legislature from the burden of micromanaging every administrative rule.
9.1|If a minister issues a regulation that directly contradicts a provision in the parent act, that regulation is classified as what?|Intra vires and legally binding|Ultra vires and legally invalid|Constitutionally protected by executive privilege|A temporary emergency decree|Option B|Any rule or regulation that contradicts or exceeds the boundaries set by the parent statute is considered ultra vires beyond powers and is legally void.
9.1|What form of legislative control involves parliament retaining the power to scrutinize, modify, or reject statutory instruments made by the executive?|Parliamentary review and control|Legislative impeachment proceedings|Congressional budget sequestering|Executive veto override|Option A|Parliamentary review allows the legislature to maintain a check on executive rule-making by evaluating subordinate legislation to ensure it aligns with legislative intent.
9.1|In Nigerian administrative law, which concept primarily serves as the sword used by courts to invalidate unauthorized subsidiary legislation?|The separation of powers doctrine|The doctrine of ultra vires|The rule of collective responsibility|The federal character principle|Option B|The doctrine of ultra vires literally meaning beyond powers is the primary legal tool utilized by courts to strike down unauthorized delegated legislation.
9.1|Which of the following is an essential prerequisite for any valid piece of delegated legislation to take effect?|Prior ratification through a nationwide referendum|The existence of a valid parent or enabling act passed by the legislature|Unanimous approval by all state governors|Direct authorship by the Chief Justice of Nigeria|Option B|Delegated legislation cannot legally exist without a valid parent or enabling act enacted by the legislature, which serves as the sole source of its delegated authority.

11.1|What immediate constitutional consequence occurs when a parliamentary government loses a vote of no confidence?|The judiciary assumes temporary emergency executive powers|The Prime Minister dissolves the military council immediately|The government falls and triggers either resignation or new elections|The constitution is suspended indefinitely via executive decree|Option C|A parliamentary government is bound by legislative confidence and must resign or call fresh elections if it loses a vote of no confidence.
11.1|How does the tenure of a chief executive in a presidential system differ fundamentally from that in a parliamentary system?|It is strictly fixed by the constitution regardless of legislative support|It fluctuates entirely depending on majority votes in parliament|It terminates automatically whenever a cabinet minister resigns|It lasts only as long as military generals endorse the administration|Option A|Presidential systems feature a fixed tenure for the executive, insulating them from legislative votes of no confidence.
11.1|Which statement best characterizes the nature of executive-legislative relations in a parliamentary democracy?|The executive is entirely separate and independent from the legislature|The executive branch is fused directly with the parliamentary legislature|The legislature holds zero power over executive policy or survival|The parliament acts solely as an advisory body to an elected monarch|Option B|Parliamentary systems are characterized by a fusion of powers where the executive emerges from and is accountable to the legislature.
11.1|Which political mechanism is completely absent in a presidential system of government?|Executive veto power over legislative bills|Fixed tenure of office for the head of state|Collective cabinet responsibility to the legislature|Constitutional separation of government branches|Option C|Collective responsibility applies to parliamentary cabinets where ministers share blame or credit for government policies before parliament.
11.1|Which core feature typically distinguishes a military regime from civilian democratic governance models?|Adherence to strict separation of powers and judicial review|Rule through authoritarian decrees and suspension of foundational laws|Absolute dependence on popular parliamentary votes of confidence|Guaranteed lifelong tenure through periodic competitive elections|Option B|Military regimes typically consolidate power by suspending the constitution and ruling through authoritarian, unchallengeable decrees.
11.1|Why does a military government inherently lack a constitutional separation of powers?|Because legislative and executive functions are fused within the ruling junta|Because power is strictly decentralized among regional governors|Because the judiciary assumes absolute control over military budgeting|Because the legislature retains veto power over military commanders|Option A|Military administrations fuse executive and legislative powers together, concentrating authority within the military council or junta.
11.1|In the context of comparative government forms, what does the term primus inter pares signify for a Prime Minister?|Immunity from all forms of civil or criminal prosecution|Superior legal status above all other branches of government|Status as first among equals within the ruling cabinet structure|Exclusive control over judicial appointments and military promotions|Option C|The term primus inter pares describes the Prime Minister as the leader of the cabinet who shares collegiate responsibility with peers.
11.1|What happens to the constitution during a typical military takeover or military government regime?|It is strictly reinforced to protect fundamental human rights|It is suspended or abrogated to accommodate authoritarian rule|It is automatically amended to expand parliamentary authority|It is transformed into a presidential charter with fixed terms|Option B|Military regimes typically suspend or modify the constitution to eliminate constitutional checks and legitimize decree-based rule.
8.1|Who is the renowned British constitutional theorist credited with popularizing the classical doctrine of the Rule of Law?|A.V. Dicey|Thomas Hobbes|John Locke|Max Weber|Option A|A.V. Dicey formally articulated the classical doctrine and principles of the Rule of Law in his 1885 publication on the law of the constitution.|
8.1|Which of the following is the first core principle of the Rule of Law according to A.V. Dicey?|Supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power|Absolute legislative supremacy without judicial review|Supremacy of military decrees over civilian statutes|Primacy of international treaties over domestic legislation|Option A|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law is supreme and absolute, protecting individuals from arbitrary, wide, or discretionary executive power.|
8.1|Under A.V. Dicey's formulation, what does the principle of equality before the law mean in practice?|Equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law administered by ordinary courts|Universal suffrage for all adult citizens regardless of status|Immunity of political leaders from criminal prosecution|Exemption of public officials from civil liability in tort|Option A|Dicey argued that no person is above the law and that officials and private citizens alike are subject to the same ordinary laws of the land.|
8.1|Which component completes A.V. Dicey's triad of the Rule of Law regarding individual liberties?|Protection of individual rights as the result of judicial decisions|Granting of fundamental rights strictly through temporary executive decrees|Codification of rights exclusively within rigid written constitutions|Creation of special administrative tribunals to handle civil liberties|Option A|Dicey maintained that individual rights in the British constitution are secured through judicial decisions and the remedies provided by common law rather than abstract constitutional declarations.|
8.1|Which specific provision in the Nigerian Constitution grants executive immunity to the President, Vice President, Governors, and Deputy Governors?|Section 308|Section 162|Section 214|Section 36|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution provides temporary immunity from civil and criminal proceedings to certain executive officeholders while in office, serving as a limitation to the Rule of Law.|
8.1|How does delegated legislation pose a theoretical challenge to A.V. Dicey's pure concept of the Rule of Law?|It empowers administrative bodies to create laws with wide discretionary authority|It forces the judiciary to dissolve ordinary courts in favor of tribunals|It forces the executive branch to submit to direct popular referendums|It eliminates all forms of parliamentary oversight permanently|Option A|Delegated lawmaking grants wide discretionary powers to the executive and administrative agencies, which contrasts with Dicey's aversion to arbitrary official discretion.|
8.1|What is the legal effect of military ouster clauses on the administration of justice under constitutional governance?|They legally bar courts from reviewing specific executive or legislative actions|They automatically dissolve the judiciary and replace judges with military tribunals|They permanently enshrine fundamental human rights into the constitution|They compel the executive branch to hold immediate democratic elections|Option A|Ouster clauses specifically strip courts of jurisdiction to question or invalidate certain official actions, representing a severe structural limitation on the Rule of Law.|
8.1|During a declared state of emergency, what typically happens to certain fundamental rights in Nigeria?|They may be lawfully derogated or restricted in accordance with constitutional procedures|They are permanently abolished from the legal system without recourse|They are transferred entirely to the direct jurisdiction of local government councils|They become absolute and override all existing statutory legislation|Option A|A state of emergency allows for the constitutional restriction of certain rights to restore public order, acting as a recognized legal limitation on normal civil liberties.|
8.1|Why did A.V. Dicey strongly oppose the French droit administratif system of administrative courts during his time?|He believed separate administrative courts created a privileged class exempt from ordinary law|He argued that administrative courts were too weak to enforce executive orders|He felt that ordinary judges lacked sufficient technical expertise in civil law|He maintained that administrative courts violated the principle of strict bicameralism|Option A|Dicey viewed separate administrative courts as granting preferential treatment to government officials, violating his principle that everyone should be judged by ordinary courts.|
8.1|Which of the following best captures a modern critique of A.V. Dicey's classical doctrine of the Rule of Law?|It focuses excessively on formal legal procedures while ignoring socio-economic inequalities|It demands complete abolition of all forms of written constitutional documents|It requires all nations to adopt a presidential system modeled after the United States|It assumes that the judiciary should possess absolute authority to write legislation|Option A|Modern legal scholars criticize Dicey's classical model for being overly formalistic, arguing that formal legal equality means little without substantive socio-economic justice and equity.|

8.1|According to A.V. 5.1|What is the defining characteristic of an unwritten constitution?|It is completely undocumented and exists only in the memories of lawmakers|It derives its legitimacy exclusively from military decrees rather than statutes|It is composed of a collection of various statutes judicial precedents and historical conventions rather than a single codified document|It can only be altered through a violent revolution or civil war|Option C|An unwritten constitution is not codified in a single text; instead, it consists of a composite of parliamentary statutes, judicial rulings, and long-standing political conventions.

5.1|How does constitutionalism fundamentally limit the exercise of state power?|By subordinating all government organs to the arbitrary will of the executive president|By ensuring that government powers are legally restricted by a fundamental law to protect individual liberties|By eliminating the judiciary so that laws are interpreted solely by elected officials|By granting absolute sovereignty to local government councils over regional matters|Option B|Constitutionalism is the philosophical and legal doctrine that government power must be bound and limited by a fundamental law to prevent tyranny and protect rights.

5.1|Why are written constitutions frequently associated with rigidity?|Because they are carved into stone monuments that cannot be physically altered|Because their amendment processes typically require supermajorities or special referendums rather than simple legislative votes|Because they are written in archaic legal language that modern courts refuse to read|Because they prohibit any form of judicial review by lower courts|Option B|Written constitutions are often rigid because altering their text requires specialized, difficult legislative procedures to ensure stability.

5.1|What is a primary advantage often attributed to a written and codified constitution?|It prevents any form of political corruption or election rigging permanently|It provides clarity, accessibility, and a clear benchmark for citizens and courts to evaluate the legality of government actions|It allows the executive branch to alter fundamental rights during economic crises without judicial oversight|It completely eliminates the need for an independent judiciary or legislature|Option B|Codification offers clarity and transparency, making it easier for citizens and courts to reference fundamental rules and check government overreach.
8.1|Which political theorist is most famously credited with formalizing the classical doctrine of the Rule of Law through his three core principles?|A.V. Dicey|Max Weber|Thomas Hobbes|Karl Marx|Option A|A.V. Dicey formally articulated the classical tripartite doctrine of the Rule of Law in his 1885 study on the law of the constitution.
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey's formulation of the Rule of Law, what does the supremacy of regular law mean in practice?|Absolute predominance of regular law over arbitrary power or wide discretionary authority by the government|The total elimination of all forms of written legislative enactments in favor of customary norms|The absolute immunity of government officials from all forms of civil or criminal litigation|The supremacy of military decrees over civilian statutes during a declared state of emergency|Option A|Dicey's first principle asserts that regular law reigns supreme and protects citizens from arbitrary, wide discretionary power by authorities.
8.1|In the context of A.V. Dicey's principles, what does equality before the ordinary courts entail?|Equal subjection of all classes and individuals to the ordinary law administered by ordinary legal tribunals|Special tribunals trying government officials exclusively for offenses committed in office|The exemption of law enforcement agents from standard judicial processes during enforcement operations|The absolute jurisdiction of customary courts over constitutional interpretation matters|Option A|Dicey emphasized that no individual is above the law and that everyone, regardless of rank, is subject to the same ordinary courts.
8.1|How does A.V. Dicey’s third principle characterize the protection of individual rights within the constitutional framework?|Rights are secured as a consequence of judicial decisions determining private rights in concrete disputes rather than abstract declarations|Rights are granted temporarily at the whim of the executive branch through executive orders|Rights are fully guaranteed only when codified into an immutable, rigid written constitution|Rights exist strictly as privileges extended by the legislature and can be revoked without legal recourse|Option A|Dicey argued that under the British constitution, individual rights are the result of judicial remedies and court rulings rather than abstract constitutional guarantees.

8.1|How do legislative ouster clauses enacted by military or civil governments impact the principle of the Rule of Law?|They strip regular courts of jurisdiction to review specific executive or legislative actions, undermining legal supremacy|They automatically expand the fundamental human rights protections available to all citizens|They mandate that ordinary courts must strictly enforce all civil rights without exception|They abolish delegated legislation and restore supreme lawmaking powers directly to the judiciary|Option A|Ouster clauses expressly prohibit courts from questioning government actions, directly contradicting Dicey's principles of legal supremacy and judicial oversight.

4.1|What fundamental judicial mechanism empowers the courts to declare legislative enactments or executive actions unconstitutional, null, and void?|Executive fiat|Judicial review|Legislative oversight|Prerogative writ|Option B|Judicial review gives the courts the authority to examine executive and legislative acts and invalidate those that conflict with the supreme provisions of the constitution.
4.1|Which institutional body in Nigeria is primarily responsible for ensuring the insulation of the judiciary from external control and guaranteeing administrative independence?|Federal Ministry of Justice|National Assembly Committee on Judiciary|National Judicial Council|Nigeria Police Force Service Commission|Option C|The National Judicial Council (NJC) plays a vital role in safeguarding judicial autonomy by managing appointments, discipline, and independence from other arms of government.
4.1|How does the security of tenure for judicial officers fundamentally strengthen the independence of the judiciary in a democratic setting?|It allows judges to remain in office indefinitely without mandatory retirement ages|It protects judges from arbitrary removal or intimidation by the executive or legislature|It guarantees that judges can engage in private commercial businesses while on the bench|It enables judges to automatically inherit legislative seats upon retirement|Option B|Security of tenure ensures that judges can deliver impartial rulings based strictly on the law without fearing political victimization, demotion, or arbitrary dismissal by political actors.
4.1|Why are judicial salaries funded directly from the consolidated revenue fund rather than being subject to annual legislative appropriations?|To ensure financial autonomy and prevent political manipulation of judicial remuneration|To allow the executive branch to alter salaries based on macroeconomic performance|To enable judges to determine their own salary scales annually without oversight|To make judicial officers direct employees of the central bank rather than the judiciary|Option A|Charging judicial salaries directly to the consolidated revenue fund prevents the executive or legislature from using financial starvation or salary cuts as a weapon to influence judicial decisions.
4.1|Which of the following scenarios is a direct practical application of the power of judicial review in Nigeria?|A judge presiding over a routine criminal trial involving theft|The Supreme Court nullifying an unconstitutional law passed by the National Assembly|The President appointing a new Chief Justice of Nigeria from a shortlist|The Attorney-General advising the executive branch on international treaties|Option B|Nullifying an unconstitutional legislative act is the quintessential exercise of judicial review, where the court strikes down laws that contravene the grundnorm.
4.1|In the separation of powers doctrine applied to Nigerian government, what is the primary structural danger if the judiciary lacks independence from the executive?|The executive would be forced to interpret laws without legal training|The judiciary would become a rubber stamp for authoritarian policies and abuse of power|The legislature would lose its power to pass budget appropriations completely|Citizens would bypass local courts and rely entirely on traditional rulers|Option B|Without institutional independence, the judiciary risks losing its impartiality, effectively transforming into an instrument of executive control rather than a neutral arbiter.
4.1|What is the core function of the Nigerian judiciary when resolving conflicts between the federal government and component state governments?|Mediating partisan political disputes as a party caucus leader|Acting as a constitutional federal arbiter to maintain the federal balance|Dissolving the state legislature and calling for fresh regional elections|Revising the constitutional division of legislative powers at will|Option B|The judiciary serves as the federal arbiter, using constitutional interpretation to settle federal-state jurisdictional conflicts and preserve federalism.
4.1|Which structural measure is most critical for insulating judicial appointments from partisan political interference in Nigeria?|Subjecting all judicial appointments to direct popular referendums|Involving an independent, professional body like the National Judicial Council in the screening and recommendation process|Allowing the ruling political party to exclusively appoint judges to lower courts|Requiring prospective judges to win elective political office before appointment|Option B|Involving the National Judicial Council ensures that judicial appointments are based on professional merit, integrity, and competence rather than partisan political patronage.
4.1|Which of the following best captures the dual significance of the judiciary in maintaining constitutionalism and the rule of law?|It formulates annual national budgets and controls the armed forces|It protects fundamental human rights and ensures that government actions remain within legal bounds|It writes the initial drafts of all bills before they reach the legislature|It coordinates foreign policy and diplomatic missions abroad|Option B|The judiciary upholds constitutionalism and the rule of law by checking overreach by other branches and serving as the ultimate protector of citizens' fundamental rights.
8.1|Which political theorist is most famously credited with formalizing the classic doctrine of the Rule of Law through his three core principles?|Thomas Hobbes|A.V. Dicey|John Locke|Karl Marx|Option B|A.V. Dicey formally articulated the classic doctrine of the Rule of Law in his 1885 study highlighting supremacy, equality, and individual rights protection.|
8.1|According to A.V. Dicey's principles of the Rule of Law, what does the supremacy of regular law imply?|The complete absence of arbitrary power and punishment of citizens only for distinct breaches of established law established in ordinary legal manners|The absolute immunity of government officials from all forms of judicial scrutiny and public liability|The temporary suspension of constitutional rights whenever the legislature passes a majority vote|The subordination of the judiciary to executive directives during national emergencies|Option A|Dicey asserted that the supremacy of regular law means a person can only be punished for a distinct breach of law established before ordinary courts, ruling out arbitrary power.|
8.1|What is meant by Dicey's second principle of the Rule of Law regarding equality before the law?|All citizens and public officials are subject to the same ordinary laws administered by the ordinary courts of the land|Wealthy citizens are entitled to specialized private arbitration tribunals rather than public courts|Only members of the legislature possess immunity from criminal prosecution while in office|Foreign nationals are exempt from local criminal legislation and legal procedures|Option C|Dicey's second principle establishes that no person is above the law and that all officials and citizens are subject to ordinary law administered by ordinary courts.|
8.1|How does Dicey conceptualize the protection of individual rights in relation to the Rule of Law?|As rights explicitly granted and revocable at will by presidential executive orders|As the foundation of the constitution stemming from judicial decisions determining individual liberties through private litigation|As secondary privileges that can be abolished whenever parliament deems it expedient|As international treaties that hold no binding authority within domestic municipal courts|Option B|Dicey argued that individual rights in the British constitution are not derived from a written code but are secured through ordinary judicial decisions resolving disputes.|
8.1|Which constitutional provision in Nigeria directly serves as a major limitation to A.V. Dicey's concept of equality before the law by granting absolute immunity from prosecution while in office?|Section 308|Section 45|Section 33|Section 68|Option A|Section 308 of the Nigerian Constitution grants executive immunity to specific officials like the President, Vice President, Governors, and Deputy Governors, limiting equality before the law.|
8.1|How does delegated legislation act as a limitation or challenge to the strict application of A.V. Dicey's Rule of Law?|It empowers the legislature to directly execute judicial sentences without trial|It allows administrative bodies and the executive branch to make laws, potentially bypassing full parliamentary scrutiny and expanding discretionary power|It completely dismantles the regular court system in favor of military tribunals|It eliminates individual freedoms by codifying permanent states of emergency into ordinary statutes|Option B|Delegated legislation transfers lawmaking powers to administrative agencies, which can introduce wide executive discretion that challenges Dicey's ideal of regular law supremacy.|
8.1|What effect do military ouster clauses have on the classic operation of the Rule of Law in a polity?|They expand the jurisdiction of ordinary courts to review all executive and military decisions|They explicitly strip courts of their constitutional power to review certain decrees or administrative actions, undermining judicial oversight|They mandate equal treatment of military personnel and civilians under ordinary criminal law|They guarantee the immediate enforcement of individual fundamental rights during political crises|Option B|Military ouster clauses explicitly forbid courts from inquiring into the validity of specific laws or actions, directly undermining the supremacy of regular law and judicial protection.|
8.1|In the context of limitations to the Rule of Law, what is a state of emergency primarily designed to do constitutionally?|Permanently abolish the judiciary and transfer all judicial power to the armed forces|Temporarily suspend or derogate certain fundamental rights and expand executive powers to manage extraordinary national crises|Eliminate the legislature permanently and establish an absolute monarchy|Grant immunity to every single citizen regardless of criminal liability|Option B|A state of emergency allows governments to exercise extraordinary powers and lawfully restrict certain individual rights to restore public order during severe crises.|
8.1|Which of the following best captures a core criticism or limitation of Dicey's rigid formulation of the Rule of Law in modern governance?|It fails to account for modern administrative states that necessitate broad ministerial discretion and delegated rulemaking|It assumes that judges are elected directly by the electorate every four years|It exclusively focuses on economic distribution rather than judicial procedures|It requires every citizen to possess a formal legal degree before filing a lawsuit|Option A|Modern states require administrative agencies with wide discretion to regulate complex sectors, which clashes with Dicey's strict rejection of wide discretionary powers.|
8.1|Under A.V. Dicey's framework, if an executive official commits a tortious act or breaks an ordinary law, how should they be treated?|They should be tried before special administrative courts that are completely separate from ordinary citizens|They should face trial in the exact same ordinary courts that judge private citizens for similar offenses|They are entirely shielded from any civil or criminal liability due to their official governmental status|They can only be investigated after a unanimous vote of approval from the ruling political party|Option B|Dicey fiercely opposed special administrative courts (like the French droit administratif), insisting that officials must be judged by ordinary courts under ordinary law.|
10.1|Which of the following best defines a federal system of government?|A system where all constitutional authority is concentrated in a single central government|A constitutional division of powers between a central government and autonomous federating units|A loose alliance of fully sovereign states that delegate limited powers to a weak center|A system where regional governments hold supreme authority and can abolish the central government|Option B|A federal system features a constitutional division of powers between a central government and autonomous regional units like states, ensuring neither level is entirely subordinate to the other.
10.1|What is the defining structural characteristic of a unitary system of government?|Power is shared equally between national and sub-national parliaments|All constitutional authority and sovereignty are concentrated in a single central government|Regional units possess the absolute right to secede from the national union|The central government only exercises powers expressly delegated to it by independent provinces|Option B|In a unitary system, all constitutional authority is concentrated at the center, and any regional administrative divisions derive their powers entirely from the central government.
10.1|Which of the following countries is traditionally classified as operating a unitary system of government?|Nigeria|The United States|France|Switzerland|Option C|France is a classic example of a unitary state where administrative authority is centralized, unlike federal states like Nigeria, the US, or Switzerland.
10.1|Which political system is characterized as a loose alliance of sovereign states that delegate limited power to a weak center?|Unitary system|Federal system|Confederal system|Monarchical system|Option C|A confederal system consists of independent sovereign states that form a weak central framework primarily for specific common goals while retaining ultimate sovereignty.
10.1|What distinctive right is typically retained by constituent units within a confederal political arrangement?|The right to unilaterally veto any central legislation|The constitutional right to secede from the union|The exclusive authority to conduct all foreign military alliances|The power to override international treaties signed by the central body|Option B|Constituent units in a confederal system maintain their ultimate sovereignty, which inherently includes the legal and political right to secede from the loose alliance.
10.1|How does a federal system fundamentally differ from a confederal system regarding sovereignty?|Federal systems vest sovereignty in autonomous states while confederal systems vest it in the center|Federal systems divide sovereign powers constitutionally between center and units whereas confederal systems leave sovereignty primarily with the constituent states|Confederal systems prohibit secession while federal systems explicitly encourage it|Federal systems concentrate all power at the center unlike confederal systems|Option B|Federalism establishes a shared constitutional order dividing powers, whereas a confederation is formed by sovereign states that keep their ultimate sovereignty and grant only limited powers to the center.
10.1|Which of the following is a primary structural consequence of adopting a unitary system?|Frequent jurisdictional conflicts between state courts and federal courts|Uniform application of laws across the entire territory enacted by the central legislature|The necessity of a rigid written constitution to prevent central overreach|Guaranteed constitutional autonomy for local government councils|Option B|Because all authority rests in the central government, laws and policies in a unitary state are uniformly applied across the entire national territory without competing regional constitutions.
10.1|In the context of the constitutional distribution of authority, what is the status of federating units in a federal system?|They are completely subordinate administrative departments of the central executive|They are fully sovereign entities with the unilateral right to dissolve the center|They possess autonomous powers constitutionally guaranteed and protected from central encroachment|They operate purely at the discretion of the central legislature|Option C|Federating units in a federation hold autonomous powers defined and protected by a supreme constitution, shielding them from arbitrary elimination or interference by the central government.
10.1|Which structural arrangement best describes a scenario where independent states create a central governing body solely for defense and foreign trade while retaining domestic sovereignty?|A unitary state|A federal republic|A confederal system|A centralized autocracy|Option C|Delegating limited functional powers to a weak central authority while preserving state sovereignty is the textbook definition of a confederal arrangement.
10.1|What is a primary vulnerability or structural weakness associated with a confederal system of government?|An inherent tendency for the central government to become overly authoritarian and tyrannical|The weakness of the central center making it difficult to enforce compliance or collect taxes effectively from member states|The complete absence of local administrative units or grassroots governance|Rigid constitutional rigidity that prevents any form of cooperation among states|Option B|Because power is decentralized to a weak center, confederal governments often struggle with enforcing uniform policies, collecting revenues, or maintaining authority over member states.
9.1|What is delegated legislation primarily defined as|Laws enacted directly by the legislature during emergency sessions|Rules and orders made by executive ministers and agencies using powers delegated by the legislature|Constitutional amendments ratified by a referendum of citizens|Judicial rulings delivered by the Supreme Court interpreting statutory ambiguity|Option B|Delegated legislation consists of laws, rules, or orders created by executive ministers or agencies under specific powers granted to them by the legislature through an Enabling Act.
9.1|Which specific statute serves as the legal foundation that empowers an executive agency to issue delegated legislation|The Independence Constitution|The Enabling or Parent Act|The Electoral Act|The Supreme Court Practice Direction|Option B|An Enabling Act or Parent Act is the foundational legislation passed by parliament that grants administrative bodies or ministers the legal authority to make subsidiary laws.
9.1|What is the legal implication of the doctrine of ultra vires in the context of delegated legislation|It mandates that all subsidiary legislation must be published in the national newspaper before enforcement|It protects executive agencies from parliamentary investigation or scrutiny|It empowers the legislature to veto executive appointments to independent commissions|It strikes down administrative rules and orders that exceed the powers granted by the Parent Act|Option D|The doctrine of ultra vires dictates that any delegated legislation exceeding the scope, purpose, or authority conferred by the Enabling Act is illegal and will be invalidated by the courts.
9.1|Which of the following functions serves as a primary legislative control over delegated legislation|Parliamentary review and scrutiny of subsidiary instruments|Direct budgetary allocation to executive regulatory departments|Appointment of junior civil servants to executive agencies|Conducting executive cabinet meetings behind closed doors|Option A|Parliament exercises oversight and control over delegated legislation by reviewing subsidiary instruments to ensure they align with legislative intent and statutory limits.
9.1|Why is official publication in a government gazette considered a crucial requirement for delegated legislation|It ensures that executive officials receive financial bonuses for rule-making|It provides formal public notification and legal notice to citizens before the rules take effect|It transfers ownership of the regulatory agency to the judicial branch|It allows the executive arm to amend the constitution without legislative consent|Option B|Publication in the official gazette gives citizens formal notice of new regulations, ensuring transparency and satisfying a fundamental requirement of legality.
9.1|Which branch of government holds the ultimate judicial authority to invalidate delegated legislation that violates the ultra vires doctrine|The Executive Cabinet|The National Assembly|The Judiciary|The Civil Service Commission|Option C|The judiciary possesses the constitutional power of judicial review, enabling courts to strike down subsidiary legislation that falls outside the limits set by the Enabling Act.
9.1|What happens when a piece of delegated legislation is successfully challenged under the doctrine of ultra vires|The Entire Parent Act is permanently repealed by the President|The offending regulation or order is declared null, void, and unenforceable|The responsible minister is automatically impeached by parliament|The judiciary rewrites the regulation to comply with current administrative policies|Option B|When a regulation is found to be ultra vires, only the unauthorized portion or rule is struck down and rendered null and void, leaving the Parent Act intact.
9.1|Which of the following best describes the main reason why modern legislatures delegate law-making powers to executive agencies|Legislators lack the technical expertise and time required to draft detailed technical regulations|To completely abolish the separation of powers between the executive and the legislature|To allow executive ministers to alter fundamental constitutional rights at will|To bypass the judiciary entirely in criminal prosecution matters|Option A|Delegation is necessary because modern governance requires specialized technical expertise and handling of complex details that the legislature lacks the time and specialized knowledge to manage directly.
9.1|Which oversight mechanism involves checking whether an administrative agency has complied with procedural requirements set out in the Parent Act|Judicial review and statutory interpretation|Executive reshuffling of ministerial portfolios|Legislative audit of party campaign financing|Popular referendums on executive policy statements|Option A|Judicial review examines whether administrative agencies followed proper statutory procedures and stayed within the jurisdictional boundaries defined by the Parent Act.
9.1|In the hierarchy of laws within the Nigerian legal framework, what is the subordinate status of delegated legislation relative to the Enabling Act|Delegated legislation overrides the Enabling Act in case of direct operational conflict|Delegated legislation enjoys equal constitutional weight with the parent statute|Delegated legislation is subordinate to and must strictly conform with the provisions of the Parent Act|Delegated legislation supersedes constitutional provisions during a state of emergency|Option C|Delegated legislation is strictly subordinate to its Parent Act and can never legally contradict or exceed the scope of the statute from which it derives its authority.
7.1|Which political philosopher is primarily credited with the formal articulation of the doctrine of separation of powers in 1748?|John Locke|Jean-Jacques Rousseau|Baron de Montesquieu|Thomas Hobbes|Option C|Baron de Montesquieu formally articulated the doctrine in 1748 emphasizing that separate bodies should exercise distinct functions to prevent tyranny.
7.1|According to Montesquieu's classical doctrine of separation of powers, how many distinct functions of government are identified?|Two|Three|Four|Five|Option B|Montesquieu identified three distinct functions of government which are legislation, execution, and adjudication.
7.1|Which of the following best describes the primary objective of implementing a separation of powers within a state?|To maximize administrative efficiency and revenue generation|To prevent the concentration of absolute power and avert tyranny|To ensure the judiciary completely dominates the legislature|To eliminate the need for any checks and balances|Option B|Separation of powers ensures that state authority is fragmented among different branches to safeguard individual liberty and prevent authoritarianism.
7.1|In the context of the separation of powers framework, which branch is primarily responsible for the adjudication of laws?|The Executive branch|The Legislature|The Judiciary|The Bureaucracy|Option C|The judiciary is the separate body tasked with adjudication, interpreting the laws, and administering justice.
7.1|Which governmental mechanism allows one branch of government to block or restrict actions taken by another branch?|Executive decree|Checks and balances|Fiscal centralization|Unitary administration|Option B|Checks and balances refer to the institutional mechanisms that allow each branch to limit the powers of the other branches.
7.1|Which of the following is a classic legislative check over the executive branch?|Judicial review|Executive veto|Impeachment and budget approval|Issuing executive orders|Option C|The legislature checks the executive through powers such as impeachment and the authorization of the national budget.
7.1|How does the judicial branch typically exercise a check on the legislative and executive branches?|Through the power of the purse|Through executive orders|Through judicial review of laws and actions|Through impeachment proceedings|Option C|Judicial review enables the judiciary to declare legislative and executive actions unconstitutional, serving as a vital check on power.
7.1|Which constitutional power empowers the executive branch to reject a bill passed by the legislature?|Veto power|Judicial review|Impeachment power|Prerogative spending|Option A|The veto is a primary executive check that allows the head of government to reject legislative bills before they become law.
7.1|Which of the following functions corresponds directly to the executive branch in Montesquieu's framework?|Lawmaking|Law execution and enforcement|Legal adjudication and constitutional interpretation|Budget drafting exclusively by unelected bureaucrats|Option B|The executive branch is responsible for enforcing and administering laws passed by the legislature.
7.1|What is the ultimate consequence if legislative, executive, and judicial powers are concentrated in the exact same body of people, according to Montesquieu?|Enhanced national unity|Absolute efficiency|The rise of tyranny and loss of political liberty|Immediate economic growth|Option C|Montesquieu argued that merging these powers inevitably leads to the total loss of liberty and the emergence of tyranny.
